payload.title: Western Pressure, Unequal Treaties, and Foreign Privilege in Qing China
payload.set_intro:
Historical source (real document)
(secondary source)
China: A Country Study (excerpt on Western trade and unequal treaties since the Opium War)
Robert L. Worden, Andrea Matles Savada and Ronald E. Dolan, eds., Federal Research Division, Library of Congress, 1988 (research completed 1987). Library of Congress, Federal Research Division (Country Studies; full text via Internet Archive OCR). Reuse: public domain (U.S. government work, 17 U.S.C. 105; the Library of Congress states all other text and graphics are in the public domain). excerpted (one contiguous passage); whitespace normalized; OCR line-break hyphenation rejoined; no wording changed.
Context: This reference book was written for the U.S. government in the 1980s.

"In the nineteenth century, European nations used military force to initiate sustained trade with China. From the time of the Opium War (1839-42) until the founding of the People's Republic in 1949, various Western countries and, starting in the 1890s, Japan compelled China to agree to a series of unequal treaties that enabled foreigners to establish essentially autonomous economic bases and operate with privileged status in China. Foreign privileges were abolished when the People's Republic came into being (see Emergence of Modern China, ch. 1)."

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Briefly describe ONE claim the authors make about how foreign powers gained trade or privileges in China.
parts.model_answer: The authors claim that European nations used military force, starting with the Opium War of 1839 to 1842, to open sustained trade with China instead of reaching it through equal negotiation.

rubric_rows.criterion: The response accurately describes one claim in the excerpt, for example that European nations used military force to begin sustained trade, that China was compelled to sign a series of unequal treaties starting with the Opium War, that these treaties let foreigners set up essentially autonomous economic bases, that foreigners operated with privileged status, that Japan joined the Western powers in imposing treaties from the 1890s, or that these privileges lasted until the People's Republic abolished them in 1949.
required_elements: The authors claim that European nations used military force, starting with the Opium War of 1839 to 1842, to open sustained trade with China instead of reaching it through equal negotiation.
The authors describe the treaties China signed as unequal because China was compelled to agree to them, and the treaties let foreigners operate with privileged status inside China.
The authors argue that the treaties allowed foreigners to set up essentially autonomous economic bases in China, which means places largely outside Chinese control.
The authors note that Japan joined the Western powers in imposing unequal treaties starting in the 1890s, and that these foreign privileges lasted until the People's Republic abolished them in 1949.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE specific treaty, war, or other development from the period 1839 to 1900 that supports the authors' claim that foreigners gained a privileged status in China. Do not use the Opium War itself as your example.
parts.model_answer: The Treaty of Nanjing (1842) forced the Qing to cede Hong Kong to Britain, open five treaty ports including Shanghai and Guangzhou, pay an indemnity, and end the Cohong monopoly. British merchants gained trading bases the Qing could not regulate on its own terms.

rubric_rows.criterion: The response explains one specific, accurate development from 1839 to 1900, other than the Opium War itself, that shows foreigners gaining privileged status, such as the Treaty of Nanjing, extraterritoriality and most-favored-nation clauses, the Second Opium War and the Treaties of Tianjin and Convention of Beijing, the Treaty of Shimonoseki, the scramble for leased territories and spheres of influence in 1897 and 1898, or the Open Door notes. The response has to connect the example to foreign privilege or autonomy.
required_elements: The Treaty of Nanjing (1842) forced the Qing to cede Hong Kong to Britain, open five treaty ports including Shanghai and Guangzhou, pay an indemnity, and end the Cohong monopoly. British merchants gained trading bases the Qing could not regulate on its own terms.

Supplementary treaties in 1843 and 1844, including the Treaty of the Bogue with Britain and the Treaty of Wangxia with the United States, gave foreigners extraterritoriality and most-favored-nation status. Foreigners accused of crimes were tried by their own consuls instead of Chinese courts, and any privilege one power gained passed to the others.

After the Second Opium War (1856 to 1860), the Treaties of Tianjin and the Convention of Beijing opened more ports, legalized the opium trade, allowed foreign diplomats to live in Beijing, and let missionaries travel and work in the interior, which widened foreign privilege well beyond the coast.

In the Treaty of Shimonoseki (1895), which ended the Sino-Japanese War, China ceded Taiwan to Japan, paid a large indemnity, and gave Japan the right to open factories in treaty ports. Afterward, in 1897 and 1898, Germany, Russia, Britain, and France took leased territories such as Jiaozhou Bay and Port Arthur and claimed spheres of influence.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE similarity OR ONE difference between China's experience of Western pressure and Japan's experience of Western pressure in the period 1850 to 1900.
parts.model_answer: Similarity: Both China and Japan were forced into unequal treaties. After Commodore Perry's arrival in 1853 and 1854, Japan signed the Treaty of Kanagawa and then the Harris Treaty of 1858, which opened treaty ports, fixed low tariffs, and gave Westerners extraterritoriality, terms much like the ones China accepted after its wars with Britain.

rubric_rows.criterion: The response explains one accurate similarity or difference between China and Japan from 1850 to 1900. Possible similarities are that both were forced into treaties granting treaty ports, low fixed tariffs, and extraterritoriality, or that both tried to adopt Western technology. Possible differences are that Meiji Japan centralized and industrialized quickly, revised its unequal treaties, and became an imperial power that defeated China in 1895, while Qing self-strengthening was limited and China lost more territory and sovereignty.
required_elements: Similarity: Both China and Japan were forced into unequal treaties. After Commodore Perry's arrival in 1853 and 1854, Japan signed the Treaty of Kanagawa and then the Harris Treaty of 1858, which opened treaty ports, fixed low tariffs, and gave Westerners extraterritoriality, terms much like the ones China accepted after its wars with Britain.

Similarity: Both states tried to adopt Western military technology to resist foreign pressure. China's Self-Strengthening Movement, led by officials such as Li Hongzhang and Zeng Guofan, built arsenals and shipyards like the Jiangnan Arsenal, while Japan's Meiji government built a modern army and navy.

Difference: Japan's Meiji Restoration of 1868 created a centralized government that carried out state-led industrialization and wide institutional reform. By 1899 Japan had ended extraterritoriality, while China's reforms were limited by a conservative court and by regional leaders, and the Hundred Days' Reform of 1898 was reversed by Empress Dowager Cixi.

Difference: By the 1890s Japan had become an imperial power itself, defeating China in 1894 and 1895 and taking Taiwan, while China kept losing territory and sovereignty to both Western powers and Japan.

Scoring guide (ALTON reference — not official AP scoring). This question is worth 3 points.
Part A (0-1): The response accurately describes one claim in the excerpt, for example that European nations used military force to begin sustained trade, that China was compelled to sign a series of unequal treaties starting with the Opium War, that these treaties let foreigners set up essentially autonomous economic bases, that foreigners operated with privileged status, that Japan joined the Western powers in imposing treaties from the 1890s, or that these privileges lasted until the People's Republic abolished them in 1949.
   - 1: The response accurately describes one claim from the excerpt about how foreign powers gained trade access or privileges in China.
   - 0: The response does not accurately describe a claim from the excerpt, misreads it, or just copies a phrase without saying what it means.
Part B (0-1): The response explains one specific, accurate development from 1839 to 1900, other than the Opium War itself, that shows foreigners gaining privileged status, such as the Treaty of Nanjing, extraterritoriality and most-favored-nation clauses, the Second Opium War and the Treaties of Tianjin and Convention of Beijing, the Treaty of Shimonoseki, the scramble for leased territories and spheres of influence in 1897 and 1898, or the Open Door notes. The response has to connect the example to foreign privilege or autonomy.
   - 1: The response explains one specific, accurate development from 1839 to 1900 and shows how it gave foreigners privileges or autonomous bases in China.
   - 0: The response gives no specific development, uses only the Opium War in general terms, is outside the stated years, is inaccurate, or does not connect the example to foreign privilege.
Part C (0-1): The response explains one accurate similarity or difference between China and Japan from 1850 to 1900. Possible similarities are that both were forced into treaties granting treaty ports, low fixed tariffs, and extraterritoriality, or that both tried to adopt Western technology. Possible differences are that Meiji Japan centralized and industrialized quickly, revised its unequal treaties, and became an imperial power that defeated China in 1895, while Qing self-strengthening was limited and China lost more territory and sovereignty.
   - 1: The response explains one accurate similarity or difference between how China and Japan experienced or responded to Western pressure from 1850 to 1900, with specific evidence for both countries.
   - 0: The response does not compare the two countries, names only one country, makes an inaccurate claim, or stays outside 1850 to 1900.
Note: Each part is scored on its own and earns 0 or 1 point. Do not penalize spelling of Chinese or Japanese names if the reference is clear.
Note: In part B, a response that only restates the Opium War or uses the excerpt's general words (unequal treaties, privileged status) with no specific example does not earn the point. The Treaty of Nanjing is acceptable because the excerpt does not name it.
Note: In part B, the Boxer Uprising of 1899 to 1900 and the foreign military intervention of 1900 are inside the stated years and may be accepted if the response ties them to foreign privilege, for example the foreign troops sent to Beijing or the claims of foreign powers in China. The Boxer Protocol (September 1901) is dated after 1900, so it is credited only as a later consequence that the response explains from the 1900 events, never as the main development.
Note: In part C, a comparison needs a real point of connection. Two unrelated facts about each country do not earn the point unless the response makes the similarity or difference explicit.
Note: Do not credit claims that China had no trade with Europeans before the 1830s. Trade went on earlier through the Canton system, so the excerpt's phrase about initiating sustained trade refers to trade on new, forced terms.

Sample response, high score (3/3; Part A 1, Part B 1, Part C 1):
(A) The authors claim that European nations used military force to open sustained trade with China on their own terms, beginning with the Opium War. After that, China was compelled to sign a series of unequal treaties that let foreigners set up essentially autonomous economic bases and operate with privileged status inside China.

(B) The Treaty of Nanjing (1842), and the supplementary treaty with Britain signed the next year, support this claim. The treaty gave Hong Kong to Britain, opened five treaty ports including Shanghai and Canton, and set low fixed tariffs that China could not change. The 1843 supplement granted extraterritoriality, so British subjects in China were tried in their own consular courts instead of Chinese courts, and a most-favored-nation clause meant any privilege later given to another power automatically went to Britain too. This created the kind of privileged, semi-autonomous foreign presence the authors describe.

(C) China and Japan were similar at first because both were forced into unequal treaties. After Commodore Perry's arrival in 1853-54, Japan signed treaties that opened ports and gave Westerners extraterritoriality and fixed tariffs, just like China. The big difference is how each country responded. After the Meiji Restoration in 1868, Japan centralized power and industrialized quickly, got rid of extraterritoriality by 1899, and defeated China in the Sino-Japanese War of 1894-95. Qing self-strengthening was limited by conservative officials and a weak central government, so China kept losing territory and sovereignty, for example by giving up Taiwan in the Treaty of Shimonoseki.
   - "European nations used military force to open sustained trade with China on their own terms" - Earns the point. It describes a claim from the excerpt accurately and in the student's own words, and "on their own terms" avoids implying there was no trade before the war.
   - "British subjects in China were tried in their own consular courts instead of Chinese courts" - Earns the point. It gives a specific, accurate development (the Treaty of Nanjing and its 1843 supplement) that is not the Opium War itself, and it explains how extraterritoriality and the most-favored-nation clause gave foreigners privileges.
   - "This created the kind of privileged, semi-autonomous foreign presence the authors describe." - This sentence ties the evidence back to the authors' claim, as the rubric requires.
   - "The big difference is how each country responded." - Earns the point. It states the difference outright and backs up both sides with evidence: Meiji industrialization, the end of extraterritoriality by 1899, and the 1894-95 war on Japan's side, and limited self-strengthening and the loss of Taiwan on China's side. All of it falls within 1850-1900.

These treaties let foreigners set up their own economic bases in China and have a privileged status there, instead of following Chinese rules the way they would have before.

(B) One development that supports this is the Treaty of Nanjing in 1842, which ended the first Opium War. Under it China had to open several treaty ports, such as Shanghai and Guangzhou, to British merchants, and it gave Britain the island of Hong Kong. whap_frq.title: Western Pressure, Unequal Treaties, and Foreign Privilege in Qing China

prompt.scenario: In the period c. 1750 to c. 1900, Western states used trade, diplomacy, and armed force to change the terms on which the Qing dynasty dealt with foreign merchants and governments. The excerpt comes from a reference study of China that a research division of the Library of Congress prepared for the United States government in the 1980s.
requirements: Each part asks for ONE answer. Answer each part in a few sentences.
Parts B and C require specific historical evidence that goes beyond what the excerpt states.
Responses to part B must come from the years 1839 to 1900, and responses to part C must come from the years 1850 to 1900.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Briefly describe ONE claim the authors make about how foreign powers gained trade or privileges in China.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE specific treaty, war, or other development from the period 1839 to 1900 that supports the authors' claim that foreigners gained a privileged status in China. Do not use the Opium War itself as your example.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE similarity OR ONE difference between China's experience of Western pressure and Japan's experience of Western pressure in the period 1850 to 1900.

sources.title: China: A Country Study (excerpt on Western trade and unequal treaties since the Opium War)

Library of Congress, Federal Research Division (Country Studies; full text via Internet Archive OCR). sources.context: This reference book was written for the U.S. government in the 1980s.
sources.body: In the nineteenth century, European nations used military force to initiate sustained trade with China. From the time of the Opium War (1839-42) until the founding of the People's Republic in 1949, various Western countries and, starting in the 1890s, Japan compelled China to agree to a series of unequal treaties that enabled foreigners to establish essentially autonomous economic bases and operate with privileged status in China. Foreign privileges were abolished when the People's Republic came into being (see Emergence of Modern China, ch. 1).

rows.name: Part A

descriptors.0: The response does not accurately describe a claim from the excerpt, misreads it, or just copies a phrase without saying what it means.
descriptors.1: The response accurately describes one claim from the excerpt about how foreign powers gained trade access or privileges in China.

rows.task_specific: The response accurately describes one claim in the excerpt, for example that European nations used military force to begin sustained trade, that China was compelled to sign a series of unequal treaties starting with the Opium War, that these treaties let foreigners set up essentially autonomous economic bases, that foreigners operated with privileged status, that Japan joined the Western powers in imposing treaties from the 1890s, or that these privileges lasted until the People's Republic abolished them in 1949.

rows.name: Part B

descriptors.0: The response gives no specific development, uses only the Opium War in general terms, is outside the stated years, is inaccurate, or does not connect the example to foreign privilege.
descriptors.1: The response explains one specific, accurate development from 1839 to 1900 and shows how it gave foreigners privileges or autonomous bases in China.

rows.task_specific: The response explains one specific, accurate development from 1839 to 1900, other than the Opium War itself, that shows foreigners gaining privileged status, such as the Treaty of Nanjing, extraterritoriality and most-favored-nation clauses, the Second Opium War and the Treaties of Tianjin and Convention of Beijing, the Treaty of Shimonoseki, the scramble for leased territories and spheres of influence in 1897 and 1898, or the Open Door notes. The response has to connect the example to foreign privilege or autonomy.

rows.name: Part C

descriptors.0: The response does not compare the two countries, names only one country, makes an inaccurate claim, or stays outside 1850 to 1900.
descriptors.1: The response explains one accurate similarity or difference between how China and Japan experienced or responded to Western pressure from 1850 to 1900, with specific evidence for both countries.

rows.task_specific: The response explains one accurate similarity or difference between China and Japan from 1850 to 1900. Possible similarities are that both were forced into treaties granting treaty ports, low fixed tariffs, and extraterritoriality, or that both tried to adopt Western technology. Possible differences are that Meiji Japan centralized and industrialized quickly, revised its unequal treaties, and became an imperial power that defeated China in 1895, while Qing self-strengthening was limited and China lost more territory and sovereignty.

scoring_notes: Each part is scored on its own and earns 0 or 1 point. Do not penalize spelling of Chinese or Japanese names if the reference is clear.

In part B, a response that only restates the Opium War or uses the excerpt's general words (unequal treaties, privileged status) with no specific example does not earn the point. The Treaty of Nanjing is acceptable because the excerpt does not name it.

In part B, the Boxer Uprising of 1899 to 1900 and the foreign military intervention of 1900 are inside the stated years and may be accepted if the response ties them to foreign privilege, for example the foreign troops sent to Beijing or the claims of foreign powers in China. The Boxer Protocol (September 1901) is dated after 1900, so it is credited only as a later consequence that the response explains from the 1900 events, never as the main development.
In part C, a comparison needs a real point of connection. Two unrelated facts about each country do not earn the point unless the response makes the similarity or difference explicit.

Do not credit claims that China had no trade with Europeans before the 1830s. Trade went on earlier through the Canton system, so the excerpt's phrase about initiating sustained trade refers to trade on new, forced terms.

doc_uses.usable_for: Identifying the claim that military force opened sustained trade and that unequal treaties gave foreigners autonomous economic bases and privileged status in China from 1839 to 1949.
doc_uses.sourcing: A secondary reference work written by area specialists for the Library of Congress Federal Research Division in the 1980s. Its overview of the treaty system dates from decades after the events, and it uses the term unequal treaties, a label that became standard in Chinese and scholarly discussion of these agreements.

evidence_map.line: Foreign privileges in China came through forced treaties
supports: Treaties of Tianjin and Convention of Beijing
complicates: Trade with Europeans already took place under the Canton system before 1839
Qing officials took part in some negotiations and later tried to reform through self-strengthening

a: The authors claim that European nations used military force, starting with the Opium War of 1839 to 1842, to open sustained trade with China instead of reaching it through equal negotiation.
The authors describe the treaties China signed as unequal because China was compelled to agree to them, and the treaties let foreigners operate with privileged status inside China.
The authors argue that the treaties allowed foreigners to set up essentially autonomous economic bases in China, which means places largely outside Chinese control.
The authors note that Japan joined the Western powers in imposing unequal treaties starting in the 1890s, and that these foreign privileges lasted until the People's Republic abolished them in 1949.
b: The Treaty of Nanjing (1842) forced the Qing to cede Hong Kong to Britain, open five treaty ports including Shanghai and Guangzhou, pay an indemnity, and end the Cohong monopoly. British merchants gained trading bases the Qing could not regulate on its own terms.

Supplementary treaties in 1843 and 1844, including the Treaty of the Bogue with Britain and the Treaty of Wangxia with the United States, gave foreigners extraterritoriality and most-favored-nation status. Foreigners accused of crimes were tried by their own consuls instead of Chinese courts, and any privilege one power gained passed to the others.

After the Second Opium War (1856 to 1860), the Treaties of Tianjin and the Convention of Beijing opened more ports, legalized the opium trade, allowed foreign diplomats to live in Beijing, and let missionaries travel and work in the interior, which widened foreign privilege well beyond the coast.

In the Treaty of Shimonoseki (1895), which ended the Sino-Japanese War, China ceded Taiwan to Japan, paid a large indemnity, and gave Japan the right to open factories in treaty ports. Afterward, in 1897 and 1898, Germany, Russia, Britain, and France took leased territories such as Jiaozhou Bay and Port Arthur and claimed spheres of influence.
c: Similarity: Both China and Japan were forced into unequal treaties. After Commodore Perry's arrival in 1853 and 1854, Japan signed the Treaty of Kanagawa and then the Harris Treaty of 1858, which opened treaty ports, fixed low tariffs, and gave Westerners extraterritoriality, terms much like the ones China accepted after its wars with Britain.

Similarity: Both states tried to adopt Western military technology to resist foreign pressure. China's Self-Strengthening Movement, led by officials such as Li Hongzhang and Zeng Guofan, built arsenals and shipyards like the Jiangnan Arsenal, while Japan's Meiji government built a modern army and navy.

Difference: Japan's Meiji Restoration of 1868 created a centralized government that carried out state-led industrialization and wide institutional reform. By 1899 Japan had ended extraterritoriality, while China's reforms were limited by a conservative court and by regional leaders, and the Hundred Days' Reform of 1898 was reversed by Empress Dowager Cixi.

Difference: By the 1890s Japan had become an imperial power itself, defeating China in 1894 and 1895 and taking Taiwan, while China kept losing territory and sovereignty to both Western powers and Japan.

common_pitfalls: Using the Opium War itself as the part B answer, even though the excerpt already names it and the prompt excludes it.
Claiming China had no trade with the West before the Opium War. Trade went on through the Canton system, and the war changed the terms of trade.
Saying the excerpt explains why the treaties were unequal in detail. It states that foreigners gained autonomous economic bases and privileged status but does not list specific treaty terms.
Answering part C about Japan alone, or saying Japan was never subject to unequal treaties.
Mixing up the Taiping Rebellion with the Boxer Uprising, or presenting the Taiping Rebellion as a treaty that gave foreigners privileges in part B.
Using events from after 1900, such as the 1911 revolution or 1949, as the main evidence for parts B or C.
Assuming the authors had a particular political purpose. The context line establishes only that the study was written for the United States government in the 1980s.
facts: The First Opium War between Britain and Qing China lasted from 1839 to 1842 and ended with the Treaty of Nanjing.
The Treaty of Nanjing ceded Hong Kong Island to Britain, opened five treaty ports (Guangzhou, Xiamen, Fuzhou, Ningbo, and Shanghai), required an indemnity, and ended the Cohong system.
Before the Opium War, European trade with China was limited to Guangzhou (Canton) under the Canton system, in place from 1757.
Extraterritoriality and most-favored-nation clauses were granted in the treaties of 1843 and 1844, including the Treaty of Wangxia with the United States.

The Second Opium War (1856 to 1860) produced the Treaties of Tianjin (1858) and the Convention of Beijing (1860), which legalized opium imports, opened more ports, and allowed foreign legations in Beijing. British and French troops burned the Summer Palace in 1860.
The Qing created the Zongli Yamen in 1861 to handle foreign affairs.
The Sino-Japanese War of 1894 to 1895 ended with the Treaty of Shimonoseki, under which China ceded Taiwan, recognized Korean independence, and paid an indemnity.
In 1897 and 1898 foreign powers took leased territories, including Germany at Jiaozhou Bay, Russia at Port Arthur, and Britain at Weihaiwei and the New Territories of Hong Kong.
The United States issued the Open Door notes in 1899 and 1900.
The Boxer Uprising (1899 to 1901) was put down by an eight-nation force and ended with the Boxer Protocol of 1901.
Japan signed the Treaty of Kanagawa in 1854 and the Harris Treaty in 1858. The Meiji Restoration took place in 1868, and Japan's extraterritoriality agreements with the Western powers ended in 1899.

samples.essay:
(A) The authors claim that European nations used military force to open sustained trade with China on their own terms, beginning with the Opium War. After that, China was compelled to sign a series of unequal treaties that let foreigners set up essentially autonomous economic bases and operate with privileged status inside China.

(B) The Treaty of Nanjing (1842), and the supplementary treaty with Britain signed the next year, support this claim. The treaty gave Hong Kong to Britain, opened five treaty ports including Shanghai and Canton, and set low fixed tariffs that China could not change. The 1843 supplement granted extraterritoriality, so British subjects in China were tried in their own consular courts instead of Chinese courts, and a most-favored-nation clause meant any privilege later given to another power automatically went to Britain too. This created the kind of privileged, semi-autonomous foreign presence the authors describe.

(C) China and Japan were similar at first because both were forced into unequal treaties. After Commodore Perry's arrival in 1853-54, Japan signed treaties that opened ports and gave Westerners extraterritoriality and fixed tariffs, just like China. The big difference is how each country responded. After the Meiji Restoration in 1868, Japan centralized power and industrialized quickly, got rid of extraterritoriality by 1899, and defeated China in the Sino-Japanese War of 1894-95. Qing self-strengthening was limited by conservative officials and a weak central government, so China kept losing territory and sovereignty, for example by giving up Taiwan in the Treaty of Shimonoseki.

fact_flags.where: Rubric Part B list of acceptable examples: 'or the Open Door notes'
fact_flags.detail: The Open Door notes (1899–1900) were U.S. diplomatic circulars to the other powers asking them to preserve equal commercial access within their spheres of influence; they were not agreements imposed on China and did not themselves grant foreigners new privileges or autonomous bases. Listing them alongside the treaties as a development that 'shows foreigners gaining privileged status' is a stretch; at most they presuppose the spheres of influence created by the 1897–98 leaseholds. Consider dropping them or requiring the response to tie them explicitly to the spheres of influence.

payload.title: Migration, Immigration, and the Remaking of American Society and Politics, 1607-1865

parts.label: A
parts.prompt:
Between the founding of Jamestown and the end of the Civil War, people kept arriving in and moving across North America. English, Scots-Irish, German, and later Irish and Chinese migrants came, voluntarily or as bound laborers. Enslaved Africans were transported by force. Settlers moved west across the Appalachians and on toward the Pacific, and Native nations were removed from their homelands. These movements changed who lived where, how people worked, and what political conflicts Americans fought over.

Evaluate the extent to which migration and immigration changed American society and politics from 1607 to 1865.

In your response you should do the following:
- Respond to the prompt with a historically defensible thesis or claim that establishes a line of reasoning.
- Describe a broader historical context relevant to the prompt.
- Support an argument in response to the prompt using at least two pieces of specific and relevant evidence.
- Use historical reasoning (causation, comparison, or continuity and change) to frame or structure an argument that addresses the prompt.
- Demonstrate a complex understanding of the historical development that is the focus of the prompt.
- You are not expected to address the entire time period. You may focus on any developments within the span from 1607 to 1865.
parts.model_answer:
From the start, the English colonies were built by people who came from somewhere else, and by people who were forced to come. Between 1607 and 1865 migration did a lot to change American society and politics. It shaped how labor was organized, it caused conflict over land with Native nations, and in the 1850s it helped break apart the party system. However, migration did not create these divisions alone. It mostly deepened conflicts that already existed over slavery and land, so its effect was large but it worked through older problems.

Migration in this period was tied to bigger changes in the Atlantic world. England followed mercantilism and wanted colonies that produced cash crops like tobacco, which needed a lot of workers. Later, in the 1800s, the market revolution brought canals, railroads and factories that needed cheap labor, while the Irish potato famine and the failed revolutions of 1848 in Europe pushed millions of people to leave. Ideas like Manifest Destiny also encouraged Americans to believe they had a right to move west.

In the colonial Chesapeake, migration changed the labor system. At first planters relied on indentured servants from England, and the headright system gave land to people who paid for a servant's passage. But when freed servants could not get good land, they became angry, and in Bacon's Rebellion in 1676 poor whites and some Black servants attacked Native Americans and burned Jamestown. After this, planters turned more to enslaved Africans brought by the Atlantic slave trade, because they seemed less of a threat. So migration first created a servant society, and then forced migration created a slave society with strict racial laws. This shows one type of migration causing a change to another type.

Westward migration also changed politics a lot. As settlers moved across the Appalachians and into the Southeast, they wanted Native land. Andrew Jackson signed the Indian Removal Act in 1830, and the Cherokee were forced out on the Trail of Tears even after the Supreme Court ruled for them in Worcester v. Georgia. For Native nations this was the biggest change of all, since they lost their homelands. For white Americans, expansion raised the question of whether new territories would be slave or free, which led to fights like the Kansas-Nebraska Act in 1854, when settlers from both sides rushed into Kansas and violence broke out.

Immigration from Europe made these political conflicts worse. Large numbers of Irish Catholics came in the 1840s and 1850s and settled in cities like Boston and New York, where they worked in factories and on docks. Many native-born Protestants feared them, and the Know-Nothing Party grew by attacking immigrants. Together with the fight over Kansas, this helped destroy the Whig Party, and many former Whigs and Know-Nothings joined the new Republican Party. Germans, many of whom settled farms in the Midwest, often opposed slavery spreading west, which also helped the Republicans.

Still, there was continuity. Even with all these new people, slavery remained the central issue, and the South stayed mostly a plantation society that few immigrants moved to. Immigrants did not start the sectional conflict; they mostly shifted which party people voted for and made the North larger and stronger, which mattered in the Civil War. Overall, migration changed American society and politics to a great extent, but mainly by speeding up and reshaping older conflicts over land and slavery instead of creating brand new ones.

rubric_rows.criterion: A defensible claim that evaluates how far migration and immigration changed American society and politics between 1607 and 1865, and that sets up a line of reasoning, for example by naming the areas of change (labor systems, sectional politics, nativism, western expansion) or by weighing change against continuity. The thesis must appear in the introduction or conclusion.

Describes broader developments that frame the argument, such as English mercantilism and the Atlantic labor market, the market revolution and the growth of industry, European famine and the revolutions of 1848, or the ideology of Manifest Destiny. The description must be more than a phrase and must connect to the prompt.

Thesis/claim (0-1): A defensible claim that evaluates how far migration and immigration changed American society and politics between 1607 and 1865, and that sets up a line of reasoning, for example by naming the areas of change (labor systems, sectional politics, nativism, western expansion) or by weighing change against continuity. The thesis must appear in the introduction or conclusion.

   - 1: Describes a broader historical context relevant to migration and immigration in this period and ties it to the argument.
   - 0: Gives no relevant context, or only a passing phrase.

Earning 2 points requires that the evidence actually support the argument.

Sample response, high score (6/6; Thesis/claim 1, Contextualization 1, Evidence 2, Analysis and reasoning 2):
From the start, the English colonies were built by people who came from somewhere else, and by people who were forced to come. Between 1607 and 1865 migration did a lot to change American society and politics. It shaped how labor was organized, it caused conflict over land with Native nations, and in the 1850s it helped break apart the party system. However, migration did not create these divisions alone. It mostly deepened conflicts that already existed over slavery and land, so its effect was large but it worked through older problems.

Migration in this period was tied to bigger changes in the Atlantic world. England followed mercantilism and wanted colonies that produced cash crops like tobacco, which needed a lot of workers. Later, in the 1800s, the market revolution brought canals, railroads and factories that needed cheap labor, while the Irish potato famine and the failed revolutions of 1848 in Europe pushed millions of people to leave. Ideas like Manifest Destiny also encouraged Americans to believe they had a right to move west.

In the colonial Chesapeake, migration changed the labor system. At first planters relied on indentured servants from England, and the headright system gave land to people who paid for a servant's passage. But when freed servants could not get good land, they became angry, and in Bacon's Rebellion in 1676 poor whites and some Black servants attacked Native Americans and burned Jamestown. After this, planters turned more to enslaved Africans brought by the Atlantic slave trade, because they seemed less of a threat. So migration first created a servant society, and then forced migration created a slave society with strict racial laws. This shows one type of migration causing a change to another type.

Westward migration also changed politics a lot. As settlers moved across the Appalachians and into the Southeast, they wanted Native land. Andrew Jackson signed the Indian Removal Act in 1830, and the Cherokee were forced out on the Trail of Tears even after the Supreme Court ruled for them in Worcester v. Georgia. For Native nations this was the biggest change of all, since they lost their homelands. For white Americans, expansion raised the question of whether new territories would be slave or free, which led to fights like the Kansas-Nebraska Act in 1854, when settlers from both sides rushed into Kansas and violence broke out.

Immigration from Europe made these political conflicts worse. Large numbers of Irish Catholics came in the 1840s and 1850s and settled in cities like Boston and New York, where they worked in factories and on docks. Many native-born Protestants feared them, and the Know-Nothing Party grew by attacking immigrants. Together with the fight over Kansas, this helped destroy the Whig Party, and many former Whigs and Know-Nothings joined the new Republican Party. Germans, many of whom settled farms in the Midwest, often opposed slavery spreading west, which also helped the Republicans.

Still, there was continuity. Even with all these new people, slavery remained the central issue, and the South stayed mostly a plantation society that few immigrants moved to. Immigrants did not start the sectional conflict; they mostly shifted which party people voted for and made the North larger and stronger, which mattered in the Civil War. Overall, migration changed American society and politics to a great extent, but mainly by speeding up and reshaping older conflicts over land and slavery instead of creating brand new ones.
   - "migration did not create these divisions alone. It mostly deepened conflicts that already existed over slavery and land" - Defensible claim about the extent of change, with a line of reasoning (labor, land, parties) and a qualification. Earns the point.
   - "England followed mercantilism and wanted colonies that produced cash crops like tobacco" - Describes mercantilism, the market revolution, the famine and 1848, and Manifest Destiny, and ties them to labor demand and migration. Earns the point.
   - "Bacon's Rebellion in 1676" - Specific, accurate evidence that supports the argument about the move from servitude to slavery.
   - "the Know-Nothing Party grew by attacking immigrants" - Ties Irish immigration to the collapse of the Whigs. With Indian removal and Kansas-Nebraska, the evidence supports the argument, so it earns 2 points. The Know-Nothing and German sections could use more detail, such as election results.
   - "one type of migration causing a change to another type" - Clear causal reasoning that links migration to changes in the labor system.
   - "Still, there was continuity." - Weighs change against continuity and compares Native and white experiences across periods. That is enough complexity for the second point, though the explanation is fairly short.

Sample response, middle score (3/6; Thesis/claim 1, Contextualization 0, Evidence 1, Analysis and reasoning 1):
Migration and immigration changed American society and politics a great deal between 1607 and 1865, especially in how people worked and in the political fights that divided the country. Migration changed labor systems, it created new groups that Americans argued about, and it pushed the nation toward sectional conflict, so the change was large.

In the early colonial period, England was building an empire and wanted colonies that could make money for the mother country. Many English people left because land was scarce and jobs were hard to find at home. This led to the Atlantic movement of people that filled the colonies with workers.

One example of how migration changed society is the Atlantic slave trade. Enslaved Africans were brought by force to the southern colonies to grow tobacco, rice, and later cotton. Before this, the Chesapeake colonies used indentured servants, who worked for a number of years in exchange for passage to America. After Bacon's Rebellion in 1676, when poor former servants rebelled against the Virginia government, planters turned more toward enslaved Africans for labor. Slavery became a main part of southern society and it stayed until the Civil War.

Another example is Irish immigration in the 1840s. Many Irish people came to the United States because of the potato famine, and most of them were Catholic. They settled in cities in the North and worked in low paying jobs. Some native-born Protestants did not like them, and this led to nativism and the Know-Nothing movement in the 1850s. The Know-Nothings wanted to limit the power of immigrants and Catholics. German immigrants also came in this period and many moved to the Midwest.

Westward movement also changed things. Settlers crossed the Appalachians and moved toward the Pacific, and Native Americans were removed from their land, such as in the Indian Removal Act of 1830 which led to the Trail of Tears. This made more room for farms and for the spread of slavery, which caused arguments in Congress about whether new states would be free or slave.

In conclusion, migration changed America in many ways. It brought slavery, it brought new immigrant groups that caused nativism, and it moved people west where the question of slavery got worse. Although some things stayed the same, such as the importance of farming, the changes from migration were mostly bigger and helped lead to the Civil War.

   - "After Bacon's Rebellion in 1676, when poor former servants rebelled against the Virginia government, planters turned more toward enslaved Africans for labor." - Accurate, specific evidence (Bacon's Rebellion, shift from indentured servitude to slavery). Described correctly, though only partly used to argue.
   - "Many Irish people came to the United States because of the potato famine, and most of them were Catholic." - Second accurate specific example (Irish famine immigration, Know-Nothings). Evidence is described but mostly stated rather than used to weigh how much change occurred, so it earns 1 of 2.
   - "Another example is Irish immigration in the 1840s." - Uses some causation (the famine leading to nativism and the Know-Nothings, Bacon's Rebellion leading to slavery) to frame the examples, which earns the first reasoning point. The examples are still taken one at a time with little comparison, so there is no complexity point.
   - "Although some things stayed the same, such as the importance of farming, the changes from migration were mostly bigger" - Gestures at continuity but does not explain or support it, so there is no complex understanding or qualification.

defensible_theses: Migration and immigration changed American society and politics a great deal between 1607 and 1865. Bound and enslaved labor migration shaped colonial economies and racial hierarchies. Westward settlement and large-scale Irish and German immigration later pushed sectional and nativist conflicts to the center of national politics.

Migration changed the makeup and geography of American society, but its political effects mostly intensified older conflicts over land, labor, and slavery rather than creating new ones. Western expansion repeatedly reopened the question of slavery's spread, from the Northwest Ordinance to the Kansas-Nebraska Act.

The political effects of migration grew sharply after 1830. Colonial migration mainly reshaped labor and frontier relations with Native peoples. Mass immigration and westward expansion in the antebellum era, by contrast, reorganized the party system, producing the Know-Nothings and the Republican Party, and helped bring on the Civil War.
contextualization_ideas: English colonization in a mercantilist Atlantic world created high demand for labor, which drew indentured servants and led to the forced transport of enslaved Africans to the Chesapeake, the Carolinas, and the Caribbean.
The market revolution, with canals, railroads, and factories, created jobs and transportation routes that pulled immigrants into Northern cities and moved settlers into the Old Northwest.

Europe's crises in the 1840s, especially the Irish potato famine and the failed revolutions of 1848 in the German states, together with Manifest Destiny and the Mexican-American War, set off large waves of movement in the 1840s and 1850s.
outside_evidence: Headright system and indentured servitude in the Chesapeake tobacco economy in the 1600s
Bacon's Rebellion (1676) and the shift from indentured servants toward enslaved African labor
The Puritan Great Migration to Massachusetts Bay in the 1630s and its tightly organized town society
Scots-Irish and German migration through Pennsylvania into the backcountry in the 1700s, which brought religious diversity and frontier tensions
Proclamation of 1763, which restricted settlement west of the Appalachians and angered colonists
Naturalization Act of 1790, limiting naturalization to free white persons, and the Alien and Sedition Acts of 1798, which raised the residency requirement for citizenship
Northwest Ordinance of 1787, which organized western settlement and banned slavery in the Northwest Territory
Missouri Compromise of 1820, a sectional crisis set off by westward expansion
Erie Canal (1825), which carried settlers and immigrant laborers westward and connected the Great Lakes to New York City
Indian Removal Act of 1830 and the Trail of Tears (1838-1839)
Irish immigration after the potato famine (1845-1852), Irish workers in Northern cities and at the Lowell mills, and Irish ties to the Democratic Party
Philadelphia nativist riots of 1844 and the rise of the Know-Nothing (American) Party in the 1850s
German immigration after the revolutions of 1848 and German settlement in the Midwest
Mormon migration to the Great Salt Lake valley in 1847
Oregon Trail migration in the 1840s
California Gold Rush (1848-1849), Chinese immigration, and California's Foreign Miners' Tax of 1850
Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854) and Bleeding Kansas, where settlers on both sides of the slavery question tried to control the territory
Homestead Act of 1862, which encouraged western settlement under the Republican free-soil program
reasoning_types: Causation: how migration led to labor systems, nativism, sectional conflict, and new parties
Continuity and change: comparing colonial migration patterns with antebellum mass immigration and westward expansion
Comparison: contrasting voluntary and forced migration, or the reception of Irish and German immigrants
common_pitfalls: Writing only about immigration after 1880, such as Ellis Island or the Chinese Exclusion Act, which falls outside the span
Listing waves of migration without evaluating the extent of change in society and politics
Leaving out forced migration of enslaved Africans and removed Native peoples, or not connecting it to the prompt
Treating westward expansion only as a story of geography without linking it to the debate over slavery's expansion
Giving context that is just a sentence about 'America was growing' with no specific development
Confusing the Know-Nothings of the 1850s with later nativist groups, or mixing up the dates of the Irish famine
facts: Jamestown was founded in 1607.
Bacon's Rebellion occurred in Virginia in 1676.
The Proclamation of 1763 barred colonial settlement west of the Appalachian Mountains.
The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 prohibited slavery in the Northwest Territory.
The Naturalization Act of 1790 limited naturalization to free white persons.
The Missouri Compromise was passed in 1820.
The Erie Canal opened in 1825.
The Indian Removal Act was signed in 1830.
The Irish potato famine lasted from about 1845 to 1852 and caused large-scale emigration to the United States.
Revolutions broke out across the German states in 1848 and failed, and many Germans emigrated afterward.
Gold was discovered in California in 1848, and the Gold Rush peaked in 1849.
The Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 allowed popular sovereignty in those territories.
The Know-Nothing (American) Party was an anti-immigrant, anti-Catholic party that reached its peak in the mid-1850s.
The Homestead Act was passed in 1862.

payload.title: Federal Power Versus State Power and the Shaping of the Nation, 1787-1877

parts.label: A
parts.prompt:
From the drafting of the Constitution to the end of Reconstruction, Americans argued again and again about how power should be divided between the national government and the states. These arguments came up over taxation, banking, tariffs, westward expansion, slavery, and the rights of citizens.

Evaluate the extent to which debates over the power of the federal government relative to the states changed the United States from 1787 to 1877. You are not expected to address the entire time period.

In your response you should do the following:
- Respond to the prompt with a historically defensible thesis or claim that establishes a line of reasoning.
- Describe a broader historical context relevant to the prompt.
- Support an argument in response to the prompt using at least two pieces of specific and relevant evidence.
- Use historical reasoning (for example, causation, comparison, or continuity and change) to frame or structure an argument that addresses the prompt.
- Use evidence to corroborate, qualify, or modify an argument that addresses the prompt, showing a complex understanding.
parts.model_answer:
After the Revolution, Americans were suspicious of any strong central government because they had just fought a war against a king and Parliament who taxed them without consent. Because of this, the Articles of Confederation gave almost all power to the states. Congress could not tax, could not regulate trade between states, and could not raise an army without the states agreeing. When farmers in Massachusetts rose up in Shays' Rebellion in 1786 over debts and taxes, the national government could do almost nothing, and many leaders decided a stronger government was needed. This tension between fear of tyranny and the need for a working national government shaped arguments for the next ninety years.

From 1787 to 1877, debates over federal versus state power changed the United States a great deal by creating a much stronger national government, especially after the Civil War, but the change was not complete because states kept control over many rights, and after 1877 the South was able to use states' rights again to limit Black citizens.

The first big debate was over the Constitution itself. Federalists like Hamilton and Madison argued in the Federalist Papers that a stronger government would protect liberty better, while Anti-Federalists worried it would crush the states. The compromise was the Bill of Rights, and the Tenth Amendment said powers not given to the federal government belonged to the states. This shows the nation changed by having a real national government, but the states' role was still protected. Soon after, Hamilton's national bank caused another fight. Jefferson said the Constitution did not allow a bank, but Hamilton used the elastic clause. In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), John Marshall's Supreme Court ruled that the bank was constitutional and that Maryland could not tax it, which made federal law supreme over the states.

States' rights arguments did not go away, though. In the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions of 1798, Jefferson and Madison argued states could judge the Alien and Sedition Acts unconstitutional. John C. Calhoun built on this idea in the Nullification Crisis of 1832, when South Carolina declared the tariff void. Jackson threatened to use force with the Force Bill, and a compromise tariff ended the crisis. Interestingly, the side that wanted states' rights changed depending on the issue. New England Federalists at the Hartford Convention complained about federal power during the War of 1812, and Southerners who talked about states' rights supported the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, which made Northern states help return escaped slaves. This shows the debate was often really about slavery and economic interests more than a principle.

These arguments eventually led to secession. After Lincoln was elected in 1860, South Carolina and other Southern states claimed they had the right to leave the Union. The Union victory in the Civil War settled that states could not secede, which was the biggest change in the whole period. Then the Reconstruction Amendments greatly expanded federal power. The Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery, and the Fourteenth Amendment made everyone born in the U.S. a citizen and said no state could deny equal protection of the laws. For the first time, the federal government was protecting individual rights against the states.

However, this change was limited. After the Compromise of 1877, federal troops left the South, and Southern states passed laws that took away Black voting rights and set up segregation. So even though the Constitution had changed, states still had a lot of power in practice. Overall, debates over federal and state power transformed the nation by making the Union permanent and creating national citizenship, but the continuing power of the states meant the promise of Reconstruction was not fulfilled until much later, during the civil rights movement.

rubric_rows.criterion: A historically defensible claim that judges how far debates over federal versus state power changed the nation between 1787 and 1877, and that sets up a line of reasoning, for example by naming the ways it changed (a stronger national government, sectional crisis and war, new definitions of citizenship) and what stayed the same.

Describes a broader context relevant to the prompt, such as the weaknesses of the Articles of Confederation and Shays' Rebellion, Revolutionary-era fears of centralized power drawn from the conflict with Britain, or the market revolution and westward expansion that raised new questions about federal authority.

Specific examples such as the ratification debate, the Bill of Rights, Hamilton's bank, the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions, McCulloch v. Maryland, the Nullification Crisis, the Bank War, the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, Dred Scott, secession, the Reconstruction Amendments, and the Compromise of 1877.

Uses causation, comparison, or continuity and change to structure the essay, for example tracing how arguments for states' rights moved from the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions to nullification to secession, and how the Civil War and Reconstruction Amendments strengthened federal power. Complexity might mean explaining both change and continuity (for example, federal power over civil rights grew but then weakened after 1877), noting that sides switched positions depending on the issue (New England Federalists at the Hartford Convention, Southern support for the federal Fugitive Slave Act), or tying the topic to a later period.

Sample response, middle score (5/6; Thesis/claim 1, Contextualization 1, Evidence 2, Analysis and reasoning 1):
Debates over federal power versus state power changed the United States a great deal between 1787 and 1877, because they moved the country from a loose union of states toward a stronger national government, but some of the change was limited since states kept a lot of power and the federal government pulled back from Reconstruction at the end.

Before 1787 the United States was run under the Articles of Confederation. Americans had just fought Britain because they feared a distant central government that taxed them, so the Articles gave Congress very little power. Congress could not tax and could not force states to follow its decisions. Problems like Shays' Rebellion in Massachusetts in 1786 and 1787, where farmers in debt shut down courts, made many leaders think the national government was too weak. This led to the Constitutional Convention, which created a stronger federal government but still left many powers to the states.

One example of the debate was the fight over Hamilton's national bank in the 1790s. Hamilton wanted a Bank of the United States to help the economy and handle the national debt. Jefferson and Madison said the Constitution did not say Congress could create a bank, so it was unconstitutional, and they wanted a strict reading of the Constitution. Washington sided with Hamilton, and the bank was created using the idea of implied powers from the necessary and proper clause. Later, in McCulloch v. Maryland in 1819, the Supreme Court under John Marshall said Maryland could not tax the national bank and that the federal government had implied powers. This shows the national government getting stronger over time.

Another example is the Nullification Crisis. In 1832 South Carolina said it could nullify the federal tariff because it hurt Southern farmers. John C. Calhoun argued that states could cancel federal laws they thought were unconstitutional. President Jackson, even though he liked limiting government in other ways, said the Union could not be broken and threatened to use force. A compromise tariff was passed in 1833 and South Carolina backed down. This showed that states' rights arguments were strong in the South, and the same kind of argument came back later with secession in 1860 and 1861.

The biggest change came with the Civil War and Reconstruction. After the North won, the Thirteenth, Fourteenth, and Fifteenth Amendments were added, which ended slavery, made African Americans citizens, and protected their right to vote. These gave the federal government power to enforce rights against the states, which was a big change from 1787. However, there was also continuity, because by the Compromise of 1877 federal troops left the South and Southern states went back to controlling their own affairs, so African Americans lost many protections.

In conclusion, the debates changed the country by making the federal government much stronger, especially after the Civil War, but the struggle between the two levels never fully ended.
   - "changed the United States a great deal between 1787 and 1877, because they moved the country from a loose union of states toward a stronger national government, but some of the change was limited since states kept a lot of power" - Defensible thesis that judges the extent of change and previews a line of reasoning (stronger national government, but limited by state power and the end of Reconstruction). Earns the thesis point, though the categories of change are not very specific.
   - "Problems like Shays' Rebellion in Massachusetts in 1786 and 1787, where farmers in debt shut down courts, made many leaders think the national government was too weak." - Describes relevant context (Articles of Confederation weakness, fear of central power from Britain, Shays' Rebellion) and links it to the Constitutional Convention. Brief but connected to the argument, so it earns the context point.
   - "Washington sided with Hamilton, and the bank was created using the idea of implied powers from the necessary and proper clause." - Accurate, specific evidence about the bank debate and McCulloch v. Maryland. It is mostly described rather than analyzed, with little explanation of how the debate changed the balance of power.
   - "A compromise tariff was passed in 1833 and South Carolina backed down." - Second specific example (Nullification Crisis) that is accurate and relevant. It is linked to later secession, but the causal link is stated rather than explained, so evidence support is only partly developed.
   - "This shows the national government getting stronger over time." - Reasoning is present (continuity and change) but thin: it asserts a conclusion without explaining how the ruling actually shifted power from states to the federal government.
   - "However, there was also continuity, because by the Compromise of 1877 federal troops left the South and Southern states went back to controlling their own affairs" - Qualifies the argument by weighing change against continuity, which moves toward complexity. It is brief and not developed with multiple causes or perspectives, so it does not fully earn the second analysis point.

defensible_theses: Debates over federal versus state power changed the nation a great deal: arguments that started with the ratification debate and the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions grew into nullification and secession, and the Union victory together with the Reconstruction Amendments made national authority supreme over the states.

Debates over federal power changed the nation only partly: the Civil War ended secession and slavery, but after Reconstruction ended in 1877 states kept broad control over voting, policing, and civil rights, so in practice much of the older balance continued.

Federal-state debates mattered mostly as a tool in fights over slavery and economic interest, which explains why groups switched sides; the debates changed the nation by turning sectional conflict into constitutional crisis, which ended in war and a more centralized Union.
contextualization_ideas: Under the Articles of Confederation (ratified 1781) Congress could not tax or regulate commerce, and Shays' Rebellion (1786-1787) convinced many leaders that a stronger central government was needed.
Revolutionary-era distrust of distant, centralized authority, shaped by the conflict with Parliament over taxation, made many Americans wary of national power.
The market revolution, westward expansion, and the growth of cotton slavery raised new questions about tariffs, internal improvements, banking, and whether slavery could spread into the territories.
outside_evidence: The ratification debate of 1787-1788 between Federalists and Anti-Federalists, which led to the Bill of Rights (1791), including the Tenth Amendment reserving powers to the states.
Alexander Hamilton's financial plan and the First Bank of the United States (1791), defended through a loose reading of the necessary and proper clause.
Washington's use of federal militia to put down the Whiskey Rebellion (1794).
The Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions (1798), written by Madison and Jefferson against the Alien and Sedition Acts.
The Hartford Convention (1814-1815), where New England Federalists opposed to the War of 1812 proposed constitutional amendments.
McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) and Gibbons v. Ogden (1824) under Chief Justice John Marshall, which affirmed federal supremacy and broad federal power over interstate commerce.
The Nullification Crisis (1832-1833): South Carolina tried to nullify the tariffs of 1828 and 1832, Congress passed the Force Bill, and the Compromise Tariff of 1833 ended the crisis.
Andrew Jackson's 1832 veto of the recharter of the Second Bank of the United States.
Worcester v. Georgia (1832) and Georgia's refusal to comply, followed by Cherokee removal.
The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 and Northern personal liberty laws that resisted it.
The Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854) and popular sovereignty; Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857).
The secession of Southern states in 1860-1861 after Lincoln's election, and the Civil War.
Wartime expansion of federal power: the Homestead Act and Pacific Railway Act (1862), the National Banking Acts, and the federal draft.
The Thirteenth (1865), Fourteenth (1868), and Fifteenth (1870) Amendments; the Reconstruction Acts of 1867; the Freedmen's Bureau; the Enforcement Acts of 1870-1871.
The Slaughterhouse Cases (1873), which read the Fourteenth Amendment narrowly, and the Compromise of 1877, which ended federal military support for Reconstruction governments.
reasoning_types: Continuity and change over time (from the Tenth Amendment and compact theory to the supremacy of the Union after the Civil War)
Causation (how federal-state disputes contributed to secession and war)
Comparison (Federalist versus Anti-Federalist views; Jeffersonian versus Hamiltonian readings of the Constitution)
common_pitfalls: Describing events without judging the extent of change the prompt asks about.
Treating states' rights as a fixed regional position and ignoring cases where sides switched (Hartford Convention; Southern support for a strong federal Fugitive Slave Act).
Writing a general essay about slavery without linking it to the federal-state balance of power.
Using evidence from after 1877 (such as Plessy v. Ferguson) as main support, rather than as a link to a later period.
Mixing up court cases, for example claiming that McCulloch v. Maryland was about commerce.
Getting dates wrong or confusing the First and Second Banks of the United States.
facts: The Constitution was drafted in 1787 and ratified in 1788; the Bill of Rights was ratified in 1791.
The Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions were adopted in 1798.
McCulloch v. Maryland was decided in 1819.
South Carolina's Ordinance of Nullification was issued in 1832; the Force Bill and the Compromise Tariff passed in 1833.
Jackson vetoed the recharter of the Second Bank in 1832.
Dred Scott v. Sandford was decided in 1857.
South Carolina seceded in December 1860.
The Thirteenth Amendment was ratified in 1865, the Fourteenth in 1868, and the Fifteenth in 1870.
The Compromise of 1877 settled the disputed 1876 election and ended Reconstruction.
