Maryland (1819), John Marshall's Supreme Court ruled that the bank was constitutional and that Maryland could not tax it, which made federal law supreme over the states.

States' rights arguments did not go away, though. In the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions of 1798, Jefferson and Madison argued states could judge the Alien and Sedition Acts unconstitutional. John C. Calhoun built on this idea in the Nullification Crisis of 1832, when South Carolina declared the tariff void. Jackson threatened to use force with the Force Bill, and a compromise tariff ended the crisis. Interestingly, the side that wanted states' rights changed depending on the issue. New England Federalists at the Hartford Convention complained about federal power during the War of 1812, and Southerners who talked about states' rights supported the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, which made Northern states help return escaped slaves. This shows the debate was often really about slavery and economic interests more than a principle.

These arguments eventually led to secession. After Lincoln was elected in 1860, South Carolina and other Southern states claimed they had the right to leave the Union. The Union victory in the Civil War settled that states could not secede, which was the biggest change in the whole period. Then the Reconstruction Amendments greatly expanded federal power. The Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery, and the Fourteenth Amendment made everyone born in the U.S. a citizen and said no state could deny equal protection of the laws. For the first time, the federal government was protecting individual rights against the states.

However, this change was limited. After the Compromise of 1877, federal troops left the South, and Southern states passed laws that took away Black voting rights and set up segregation. So even though the Constitution had changed, states still had a lot of power in practice. Overall, debates over federal and state power transformed the nation by making the Union permanent and creating national citizenship, but the continuing power of the states meant the promise of Reconstruction was not fulfilled until much later, during the civil rights movement.

annotations.quote: debates over federal versus state power changed the United States a great deal by creating a much stronger national government
annotations.comment: Defensible thesis that judges extent (great deal but not complete) and sets a line of reasoning: stronger government, war, limits after 1877.

annotations.quote: When farmers in Massachusetts rose up in Shays' Rebellion in 1786
annotations.comment: Context of Articles weakness and Revolutionary fear of central power, tied to the ongoing tension the essay traces.

annotations.quote: In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), John Marshall's Supreme Court ruled that the bank was constitutional and that Maryland could not tax it
annotations.comment: Specific evidence used to support the claim that federal supremacy grew.

annotations.quote: The Fourteenth Amendment made everyone born in the U.S. a citizen
annotations.comment: Specific evidence connected to the argument about federal protection of rights against states; with nullification and secession earns 2.

annotations.quote: Calhoun built on this idea in the Nullification Crisis of 1832
annotations.comment: Traces continuity of states' rights arguments from 1798 to nullification to secession, a causal line of reasoning.

annotations.quote: the side that wanted states' rights changed depending on the issue
annotations.comment: Complexity: Hartford Convention and the Fugitive Slave Act show positions switched, which qualifies the argument.

annotations.quote: However, this change was limited. After the Compromise of 1877
annotations.comment: Weighs change against continuity; the explanation of later Jim Crow laws is brief, which keeps this short of a top-level essay.

samples.essay:
Debates over federal power versus state power changed the United States a great deal between 1787 and 1877, because they moved the country from a loose union of states toward a stronger national government, but some of the change was limited since states kept a lot of power and the federal government pulled back from Reconstruction at the end.

Before 1787 the United States was run under the Articles of Confederation. Americans had just fought Britain because they feared a distant central government that taxed them, so the Articles gave Congress very little power. Congress could not tax and could not force states to follow its decisions. Problems like Shays' Rebellion in Massachusetts in 1786 and 1787, where farmers in debt shut down courts, made many leaders think the national government was too weak. This led to the Constitutional Convention, which created a stronger federal government but still left many powers to the states.

One example of the debate was the fight over Hamilton's national bank in the 1790s. Hamilton wanted a Bank of the United States to help the economy and handle the national debt. Jefferson and Madison said the Constitution did not say Congress could create a bank, so it was unconstitutional, and they wanted a strict reading of the Constitution. Washington sided with Hamilton, and the bank was created using the idea of implied powers from the necessary and proper clause. Later, in McCulloch v. Maryland in 1819, the Supreme Court under John Marshall said Maryland could not tax the national bank and that the federal government had implied powers. This shows the national government getting stronger over time.

Another example is the Nullification Crisis. In 1832 South Carolina said it could nullify the federal tariff because it hurt Southern farmers. John C. Calhoun argued that states could cancel federal laws they thought were unconstitutional. President Jackson, even though he liked limiting government in other ways, said the Union could not be broken and threatened to use force. A compromise tariff was passed in 1833 and South Carolina backed down. This showed that states' rights arguments were strong in the South, and the same kind of argument came back later with secession in 1860 and 1861.

The biggest change came with the Civil War and Reconstruction. After the North won, the Thirteenth, Fourteenth, and Fifteenth Amendments were added, which ended slavery, made African Americans citizens, and protected their right to vote. These gave the federal government power to enforce rights against the states, which was a big change from 1787. However, there was also continuity, because by the Compromise of 1877 federal troops left the South and Southern states went back to controlling their own affairs, so African Americans lost many protections.

In conclusion, the debates changed the country by making the federal government much stronger, especially after the Civil War, but the struggle between the two levels never fully ended.

annotations.quote: changed the United States a great deal between 1787 and 1877, because they moved the country from a loose union of states toward a stronger national government, but some of the change was limited since states kept a lot of power
annotations.comment: Defensible thesis that judges the extent of change and previews a line of reasoning (stronger national government, but limited by state power and the end of Reconstruction). Earns the thesis point, though the categories of change are not very specific.

annotations.quote: Problems like Shays' Rebellion in Massachusetts in 1786 and 1787, where farmers in debt shut down courts, made many leaders think the national government was too weak.
annotations.comment: Describes relevant context (Articles of Confederation weakness, fear of central power from Britain, Shays' Rebellion) and links it to the Constitutional Convention. Brief but connected to the argument, so it earns the context point.

annotations.quote: Washington sided with Hamilton, and the bank was created using the idea of implied powers from the necessary and proper clause.
annotations.comment: Accurate, specific evidence about the bank debate and McCulloch v. Maryland. It is mostly described rather than analyzed, with little explanation of how the debate changed the balance of power.

annotations.quote: A compromise tariff was passed in 1833 and South Carolina backed down.
annotations.comment: Second specific example (Nullification Crisis) that is accurate and relevant. It is linked to later secession, but the causal link is stated rather than explained, so evidence support is only partly developed.

annotations.quote: This shows the national government getting stronger over time.
annotations.comment: Reasoning is present (continuity and change) but thin: it asserts a conclusion without explaining how the ruling actually shifted power from states to the federal government.

annotations.quote: However, there was also continuity, because by the Compromise of 1877 federal troops left the South and Southern states went back to controlling their own affairs
annotations.comment: Qualifies the argument by weighing change against continuity, which moves toward complexity. It is brief and not developed with multiple causes or perspectives, so it does not fully earn the second analysis point.

samples.essay:
Debates over federal and state power were very important in United States history from 1787 to 1877. The country argued about this issue many times and it changed in some ways, but the debates also stayed important throughout the period. This essay will show that the debates changed the United States a lot.

The debates were a big part of American history because Americans did not agree on how much power the government should have. Some people wanted a strong national government and other people wanted the states to have more say. This made many problems for the country and led to a lot of conflict over time.

One example is the Civil War. The Southern states left the Union because they believed the states had the right to decide about slavery. The North fought to keep the country together. After the war the federal government became stronger than it was before. This shows that the debate changed the country.

Another example is the Reconstruction period. The government passed new amendments after the war, including the Thirteenth Amendment, which ended slavery. This changed the country because the federal government took on more power over what states could do.

In conclusion, the debates over federal power changed the United States in many ways between 1787 and 1877. They caused a war and led to a stronger national government, even though people still argued about it afterward.

annotations.quote: This essay will show that the debates changed the United States a lot.
annotations.comment: Thesis only restates the prompt with a vague 'a lot'. It names no specific ways the nation changed and sets up no line of reasoning, so it earns no thesis point.

annotations.quote: Some people wanted a strong national government and other people wanted the states to have more say.
annotations.comment: General background with no specific events, such as the Articles of Confederation or Revolutionary-era fears of central power, and it is not tied to the argument. No contextualization credit.

annotations.quote: The Southern states left the Union because they believed the states had the right to decide about slavery.
annotations.comment: Secession is a relevant example but is described only generally, with no dates, specific events or details. It is the main example and is not developed.

annotations.quote: The government passed new amendments after the war, including the Thirteenth Amendment, which ended slavery.
annotations.comment: A second relevant example (the Thirteenth Amendment) is identified, and the next sentence does say the federal government took on more power over the states. Together the two examples earn the first evidence point, but both are thin and neither is developed into an argument about federal and state power, so the second evidence point is not earned.

annotations.quote: After the war the federal government became stronger than it was before.
annotations.comment: States a change in one sentence and gives no causal explanation of how the debates produced it. It also ignores continuity, such as the weakening of federal power by 1877. The essay mostly lists and asserts, so there is no reasoning credit.

payload.title: The Market Revolution and American Lives, 1815-1860
payload.set_intro:
Historical source (real document)
These documents are real historical sources (excerpts are cut verbatim from the repository text; [...] marks an omission). Documents 4 and 7 are images shown below the documents.

Document 1 (primary source)
Andrew Jackson, Veto Message Regarding the Bank of the United States (excerpt)
Andrew Jackson, President of the United States, 1832 (July 10). Avalon Project, Yale Law School (transcription). Reuse: public domain (U.S. government work; published before 1929). excerpted (one contiguous passage); whitespace normalized; no wording changed.
Context: A message to the Senate explaining why the President refused to sign a bill renewing the charter of the Second Bank of the United States, an issue in the 1832 election.

"It is to be regretted that the rich and powerful too often bend the acts of government to their selfish purposes. Distinctions in society will always exist under every just government. Equality of talents, of education, or of wealth can not be produced by human institutions. In the full enjoyment of the gifts of Heaven and the fruits of superior industry, economy, and virtue, every man is equally entitled to protection by law; but when the laws undertake to add to these natural and just advantages artificial distinctions, to grant titles, gratuities, and exclusive privileges, to make the rich richer and the potent more powerful, the humble members of society-the farmers, mechanics, and laborers-who have neither the time nor the means of securing like favors to themselves, have a right to complain of the injustice of their Government. There are no necessary evils in government. Its evils exist only in its abuses. If it would confine itself to equal protection, and, as Heaven does its rains, shower its favors alike on the high and the low, the rich and the poor, it would be an unqualified blessing."

———

Document 2 (primary source)
Loom and Spindle, or Life among the Early Mill Girls (excerpt on Lowell)
Harriet Hanson Robinson (recalling Lowell mill life of the 1830s and 1840s), 1898. Project Gutenberg eBook #72757. Reuse: public domain in the United States (published before 1929). excerpted (two segments joined by [...]); whitespace normalized; no wording changed.
Context: Written in 1898 by a woman who began work in a Lowell, Massachusetts, cotton mill as a child in the 1830s; the passages describe Lowell in 1848 and a workers' "turn out" (strike) there in October 1836.

"In 1848 over one-half of the depositors in the Lowell Institution for Savings were mill-girls, and over one-third of the whole sum deposited belonged to them [...] Cutting down the wages was not their only grievance, nor the only cause of this strike. Hitherto the corporations had paid twenty-five cents a week towards the board of each operative, and now it was their purpose to have the girls pay the sum; and this, in addition to the cut in the wages, would make a difference of at least one dollar a week. It was estimated that as many as twelve or fifteen hundred girls turned out, and walked in procession through the streets."

———

Document 3 (primary source)
Democracy in America, vol. 2: Causes of the Restless Spirit of Americans in the Midst of Their Prosperity (excerpt)
Alexis de Tocqueville (French observer; translated by Henry Reeve), 1840 (vol. 2; English translation). Project Gutenberg eBook #816. Reuse: public domain in the United States (published before 1929). excerpted (one contiguous passage); whitespace normalized; no wording changed.
Context: Written by a French visitor who toured the United States in 1831-32 and published this volume in France in 1840; the English translation is by Henry Reeve.

"It is strange to see with what feverish ardor the Americans pursue their own welfare; and to watch the vague dread that constantly torments them lest they should not have chosen the shortest path which may lead to it. A native of the United States clings to this world's goods as if he were certain never to die; and he is so hasty in grasping at all within his reach, that one would suppose he was constantly afraid of not living long enough to enjoy them. He clutches everything, he holds nothing fast, but soon loosens his grasp to pursue fresh gratifications. In the United States a man builds a house to spend his latter years in it, and he sells it before the roof is on: he plants a garden, and lets it just as the trees are coming into bearing: he brings a field into tillage, and leaves other men to gather the crops: he embraces a profession, and gives it up: he settles in a place, which he soon afterwards leaves, to carry his changeable longings elsewhere."

———

Document 4 (print)
[View of Lowell, Massachusetts at the confluence of the Merrimack and Concord rivers, with a row of textile mills or factories mainly along the Merrimack River]
Unattributed (title devised by Library of Congress staff), c. 1840 (LoC date 1840). Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division (Popular Graphic Arts). Reuse: public domain (unattributed print c. 1840; LoC reports no known restrictions). unmodified except LoC's 1024px reference JPEG (hand-colored print on its mount).
Context: A print of unknown authorship, dated c. 1840 by the Library of Congress, showing the textile mills of Lowell, Massachusetts, seen across a river and meadow.

The image for this document is shown below the documents, labeled Document 4. Select the image to open it full size.

———

Document 5 (primary source)
Walden, 'Economy' (excerpt on the railroad)
Henry David Thoreau, 1854. Project Gutenberg eBook #205. Reuse: public domain in the United States (published before 1929; author died 1862). excerpted (one contiguous passage); whitespace normalized; no wording changed.
Context: Thoreau lived beside Walden Pond near Concord, Massachusetts, in 1845-47 and published his account of that life, which criticizes the pace of commercial life, in 1854.

"But if we stay at home and mind our business, who will want railroads? We do not ride on the railroad; it rides upon us. Did you ever think what those sleepers are that underlie the railroad? Each one is a man, an Irish-man, or a Yankee man. The rails are laid on them, and they are covered with sand, and the cars run smoothly over them."

———

Document 6 (table)
Resident population of the United States by region, 1800-1860 (selected census years)
U.S. Census Bureau (Campbell Gibson and Kay Jung, compilers of Working Paper 56), 2002 compilation of decennial census counts for 1800-1860. U.S. Census Bureau. Reuse: public domain (U.S. government work). four decennial years chosen from the compiled tables; the Northeast, Midwest (North Central), South and West totals and the U.S. total copied by code; sums of regions checked to equal the U.S. total in every year; the West Region has no entry before 1850 and is shown as a dash.
Context: Census counts for 1800-1860 compiled and published by the Census Bureau in 2002. Modern census regions are applied to every year, the West has no entry before 1850, and the South's total includes enslaved people.

| Year | Northeast | Midwest | South | West | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1800 | 2,635,576 | 51,006 | 2,621,901 | – | 5,308,483 |
| 1820 | 4,359,916 | 859,305 | 4,419,232 | – | 9,638,453 |
| 1840 | 6,761,082 | 3,351,542 | 6,950,729 | – | 17,063,353 |
| 1860 | 10,594,268 | 9,096,716 | 11,133,361 | 618,976 | 31,443,321 |

———

Document 7 (map)
Map showing the distribution of the slave population of the southern states of the United States. Compiled from the census of 1860
E. Hergesheimer (drawn); Henry S. Graham (publisher, Washington); certified by Census Office, Dept. of the Interior, 1861 (Washington, September 1861). Library of Congress, Geography and Map Division. Reuse: public domain (published 1861, before 1929; LoC GMD free to use and reuse). unmodified except LoC's IIIF 12.5% rendering (1313x1048 px).
Context: Drawn from 1860 census data (certified by the Census Office) and published in Washington in September 1861, during the Civil War; darker shading marks counties where a larger share of the population was enslaved.

The image for this document is shown below the documents, labeled Document 7. Select the image to open it full size.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt:
Between 1815 and 1860, canals, steamboats and railroads, new factories and a growing cotton trade drew more Americans into buying and selling in distant markets. Historians often call these developments the market revolution.

Evaluate the extent to which the market revolution changed the lives of Americans between 1815 and 1860.

In your response you should do the following:
- Respond to the prompt with a historically defensible thesis or claim that establishes a line of reasoning.
- Describe a broader historical context relevant to the prompt.
- Support an argument in response to the prompt using at least four documents.
- Use at least one additional piece of specific historical evidence (beyond that found in the documents) relevant to an argument about the prompt.
- For at least two documents, explain how or why the document's point of view, purpose, historical situation, and/or audience is relevant to an argument.
- Demonstrate a complex understanding of the historical development that is the focus of the prompt, using evidence to corroborate, qualify, or modify an argument that addresses the question.
parts.model_answer:
After the War of 1812, a wave of nationalism led leaders such as Henry Clay to promote the American System of internal improvements, a protective tariff and a national bank. The Erie Canal, opened in 1825, cut the cost of shipping between the Great Lakes and New York City, and steamboats and early railroads did the same elsewhere. At the same moment, Eli Whitney's cotton gin made short-staple cotton enormously profitable and pushed planters and enslaved people into the Southwest. Between 1815 and 1860 the market revolution changed the lives of Americans to a large extent, but unevenly: it transformed the work, movement and expectations of many Northern and Western families, it deepened slavery in the South, and almost everywhere it created insecurities that critics noticed.

The documents show how deeply the market reshaped free Americans' work and movement. In Document 2, Harriet Robinson reports that mill girls made up more than half of the depositors at Lowell's savings institution in 1848 and owned over a third of the money deposited, which suggests that wages gave young women money and a measure of independence that farm daughters had rarely had. Document 6 shows a larger shift: the Midwest grew from about 51,000 people in 1800 to more than 9 million in 1860, a population that settled where canals and railroads could carry crops to Eastern and foreign buyers. Document 3 points to a change in habits of mind. Tocqueville describes Americans who sell a house before the roof is finished, give up one profession for another and move on to new places, a restless pursuit of gain that suits an economy built on buying, selling and moving.

The same documents show that change came with conflict and limits. Robinson also describes the 1836 turn out, when workers protested a wage cut and new charges for board, so the factory system did not simply deliver prosperity. She wrote in 1898, six decades later, as a former mill girl proud of her fellow operatives, so her picture of independence may be warmer than the experience of every worker, yet her description of the strike shows that workers understood the corporations' power. Document 4, an unsigned print of the Lowell mills, shows tidy brick buildings beside open meadow with no workers or crowding. Because its maker and purpose are unknown, it is best read as a picture of how the new industrial town could be presented to reassure viewers, not as evidence about conditions inside. In Document 1, Andrew Jackson's veto message, written during an election campaign and aimed at farmers and laborers, attacks the Bank for favoring "the rich and powerful," which shows that many Americans feared that new financial institutions served a few. The Panic of 1837, which brought a severe depression, showed how exposed ordinary families had become to distant financial shocks.

The market revolution did not transform life for everyone. Document 7, a map made from the 1860 census, shows the heaviest concentrations of enslaved people in counties along the lower Mississippi River and on the South Carolina coast. This is the other side of the story told by Documents 2 and 4: New England's mills depended on cotton grown by enslaved labor, and the demand for cotton fed the domestic slave trade that sold people from the Upper South to the Deep South. For roughly four million enslaved Americans in 1860, the market meant sale and forced movement rather than opportunity. The map was drawn from federal census data and published in 1861, during the Civil War, a reminder that economic integration also sharpened the conflict between slave and free regions. Document 5 adds a further qualification. Thoreau argues that people do not ride the railroad but are ridden upon by it, and he points to the Irish and Yankee laborers who laid its track. He was a writer who chose to live simply at Walden Pond and was not a typical worker, but his criticism shows that material progress did not satisfy everyone.

In sum, the market revolution profoundly changed life in the North and West by creating wage labor, commercial farming and mobility, but it also hardened slavery in the South and left many people anxious about debt, wages and power. The extent of change depended on region, race, gender and class, which is why Jackson, Thoreau and the striking Lowell workers could all find reasons to protest.

rubric_rows.criterion: A defensible claim that evaluates the extent to which the market revolution changed Americans' lives, 1815-1860, and sets up a line of reasoning, for example large change for many Northern and Western families with deepening slavery and new insecurity, or limited and uneven change that depended on region, race and class.

Describes broader context such as post-War of 1812 nationalism and the American System, the transportation revolution (National Road, steamboats, Erie Canal), early industrialization, or cotton and the spread of slavery, and ties it to the prompt.

Uses document content to support claims about change and its limits, for example wages and savings (Doc 2), settlement of the Midwest (Doc 6), restlessness and mobility (Doc 3), the factory town image (Doc 4), distrust of privilege (Doc 1), criticism of commercial growth (Doc 5), and the distribution of slavery (Doc 7).

Uses at least one specific piece of evidence not in the documents, such as the Erie Canal, the Panic of 1837, the cotton gin and the domestic slave trade, Commonwealth v. Hunt (1842), Irish immigration, or the cult of domesticity.

Explains how point of view, purpose, historical situation or audience matters for at least two documents, for example Robinson's 1898 memory as a former mill girl (Doc 2), Jackson's election-year audience (Doc 1), the unknown maker of the print (Doc 4), Thoreau's chosen simple life (Doc 5), or the French visitor's generalizations (Doc 3).

Shows complex understanding, for example by weighing opportunity against dependence and conflict, by qualifying 'change' with region, race, gender and class differences, by linking the cotton market and slavery to the textile mills, or by using documents that disagree to modify the claim.

payload.reference_text:
Scoring guide (ALTON reference — not official AP scoring). This question is worth 7 points.
Thesis/claim (0-1): A defensible claim that evaluates the extent to which the market revolution changed Americans' lives, 1815-1860, and sets up a line of reasoning, for example large change for many Northern and Western families with deepening slavery and new insecurity, or limited and uneven change that depended on region, race and class.
   - 1: Gives a historically defensible thesis that evaluates the extent of change in Americans' lives and sets up a line of reasoning, in the introduction or conclusion.
   - 0: Gives no defensible thesis, only restates the prompt, or does not evaluate the extent of change in Americans' lives.
Contextualization (0-1): Describes broader context such as post-War of 1812 nationalism and the American System, the transportation revolution (National Road, steamboats, Erie Canal), early industrialization, or cotton and the spread of slavery, and ties it to the prompt.
   - 1: Describes a broader historical context before, during or continuing through 1815 to 1860 and connects it to the prompt.
   - 0: Gives no relevant context, or only a passing reference.
Evidence from the documents (0-2): Uses document content to support claims about change and its limits, for example wages and savings (Doc 2), settlement of the Midwest (Doc 6), restlessness and mobility (Doc 3), the factory town image (Doc 4), distrust of privilege (Doc 1), criticism of commercial growth (Doc 5), and the distribution of slavery (Doc 7).
   - 2: Uses the content of at least four documents to support an argument in response to the prompt.
   - 1: Accurately describes the content of at least three documents in a way that addresses the topic.
   - 0: Uses fewer than three documents or only quotes or summarizes without connecting them to the topic.
Evidence beyond the documents (0-1): Uses at least one specific piece of evidence not in the documents, such as the Erie Canal, the Panic of 1837, the cotton gin and the domestic slave trade, Commonwealth v. Hunt (1842), Irish immigration, or the cult of domesticity.
   - 1: Uses at least one specific, accurate piece of outside evidence relevant to an argument about the prompt.
   - 0: Gives no specific outside evidence, or the evidence is irrelevant or inaccurate.
Sourcing (point of view, purpose, situation, audience) (0-1): Explains how point of view, purpose, historical situation or audience matters for at least two documents, for example Robinson's 1898 memory as a former mill girl (Doc 2), Jackson's election-year audience (Doc 1), the unknown maker of the print (Doc 4), Thoreau's chosen simple life (Doc 5), or the French visitor's generalizations (Doc 3).
   - 1: Explains how or why the point of view, purpose, historical situation or audience of at least two documents matters to an argument.
   - 0: Gives no sourcing analysis, or sourcing for only one document.
Complex understanding (0-1): Shows complex understanding, for example by weighing opportunity against dependence and conflict, by qualifying 'change' with region, race, gender and class differences, by linking the cotton market and slavery to the textile mills, or by using documents that disagree to modify the claim.
   - 1: Shows a complex understanding through sophisticated argumentation or effective use of evidence that corroborates, qualifies or modifies the argument.
   - 0: Does not show a complex understanding, or makes only a brief phrase or reference.
Note: The thesis may argue for great, moderate or limited change as long as it is defensible and evaluates extent.
Note: Document 6's South total includes enslaved people; Document 7 shows where enslaved people lived but does not itself state any link to the market, so that link must come from outside knowledge.
Note: Outside evidence must differ from evidence used for contextualization to earn both points.
Note: Simply naming an author or date does not count as sourcing; the student must explain why the source's perspective or situation matters.
Note: ALTON reference — not official AP scoring: model scores are an ALTON estimate and no AP score is implied.

Evidence map (which documents support or complicate each line of reasoning):
- Large change in Northern and Western working life: wages, mills, migration and new habits of mind. Supports: Document 2, 3, 4, 6. Complicates: Document 5.
- Change was uneven: the market's growth also deepened slavery and left many lives untouched. Supports: Document 7, 6. Complicates: Document 4, 2.
- Change brought new insecurity, conflict and criticism, so gains were mixed. Supports: Document 1, 5, 2, 3. Complicates: Document 4.
- The market's institutions became a political fight over who benefited. Supports: Document 1. Complicates: Document 5.

Using the documents (use and sourcing):
- Document 1: Shows that banking and credit, the machinery of the new market economy, were contested: Jackson says government should give 'equal protection' and attacks privileges that make 'the rich richer'. Supports claims about new economic inequality and political conflict; corroborates Thoreau's distrust of commercial growth. Sourcing: A veto message addressed to the Senate during the 1832 campaign. Jackson, a slaveholding planter who needed the votes of farmers and laborers, framed the veto as a defense of ordinary people; supporters of the Bank argued that it steadied credit and currency, so the purpose is political as well as constitutional.
- Document 2: Shows opportunity and some independence for young women (mill girls were more than half of the depositors at Lowell's savings institution in 1848) and also tension (the 1836 turn out over a wage cut and new board charges). Supports both 'large change' and 'change with conflict'. Sourcing: A memoir written in 1898, some sixty years after the events, by a former mill girl who later became a suffrage activist. She was a child in 1836, and hindsight and pride in the operatives shape the account; the audience is readers of a book about the early mill girls.
- Document 3: Describes a restless, mobile, gain-seeking people who change homes and occupations quickly and feel uneasy even in prosperity; supports a change in habits and attitudes, and the insecurity that came with commercial life. Sourcing: A French aristocrat generalizing for readers in France after a trip of about nine months in 1831-32; sweeping claims about 'Americans' that overlook enslaved people and the experience of women, and a comparison with European society shapes his view.
- Document 4: A visual of the new factory town: a row of mills set in open country. Supports the claim that industry became part of the landscape and was presented as orderly; can also be used to ask what the picture leaves out (workers, enslaved cotton growers). Sourcing: An unattributed print whose maker and purpose are unknown. It shows no workers, crowding or noise, so a student can ask whether it was made to reassure viewers; it cannot be used as evidence of working conditions.
- Document 5: Argues that railroads and commerce had not improved ordinary lives ('it rides upon us') and notes that laborers, Irish and Yankee, built the track. Supports uneven gains and criticism of the new economy. Sourcing: A Massachusetts writer who chose a simple life at Walden Pond and wrote provocatively for educated Boston readers in 1854; he is not a typical worker, and he describes the track builders from the outside.
- Document 6: Quantifies the shift of population: the Midwest grew from 51,006 (1800) to 9,096,716 (1860) while the South grew from about 2.6 to 11.1 million. Supports claims about westward movement into regions linked to markets; shows nothing about causes or quality of life. Sourcing: Official counts compiled long after the events (2002) for a reference publication; there is no argument or persuasion in the table, but it measures numbers of people, not lives, and the South's total includes enslaved people, so its growth is not a measure of free people's market opportunity.
- Document 7: Shows the 1860 concentration of enslaved people along the lower Mississippi River and on the South Carolina coast. Supports the claim that for millions the market revolution meant expanded bondage, not new opportunity. Sourcing: A map drawn from federal census data and published in Washington during the Civil War; it shows where enslaved people lived in 1860 but says nothing about the cotton trade directly, so students must connect it to cotton and the market with outside knowledge.

Sample response, high score (7/7; Thesis/claim 1, Contextualization 1, Evidence from the documents 2, Evidence beyond the documents 1, Sourcing (point of view, purpose, situation, audience) 1, Complex understanding 1):
After the War of 1812, a wave of nationalism led leaders such as Henry Clay to promote the American System of internal improvements, a protective tariff and a national bank. The Erie Canal, opened in 1825, cut the cost of shipping between the Great Lakes and New York City, and steamboats and early railroads did the same elsewhere. At the same moment, Eli Whitney's cotton gin made short-staple cotton enormously profitable and pushed planters and enslaved people into the Southwest. Between 1815 and 1860 the market revolution changed the lives of Americans to a large extent, but unevenly: it transformed the work, movement and expectations of many Northern and Western families, it deepened slavery in the South, and almost everywhere it created insecurities that critics noticed.

The documents show how deeply the market reshaped free Americans' work and movement. In Document 2, Harriet Robinson reports that mill girls made up more than half of the depositors at Lowell's savings institution in 1848 and owned over a third of the money deposited, which suggests that wages gave young women money and a measure of independence that farm daughters had rarely had. Document 6 shows a larger shift: the Midwest grew from about 51,000 people in 1800 to more than 9 million in 1860, a population that settled where canals and railroads could carry crops to Eastern and foreign buyers. Document 3 points to a change in habits of mind. Tocqueville describes Americans who sell a house before the roof is finished, give up one profession for another and move on to new places, a restless pursuit of gain that suits an economy built on buying, selling and moving.

The same documents show that change came with conflict and limits. Robinson also describes the 1836 turn out, when workers protested a wage cut and new charges for board, so the factory system did not simply deliver prosperity. She wrote in 1898, six decades later, as a former mill girl proud of her fellow operatives, so her picture of independence may be warmer than the experience of every worker, yet her description of the strike shows that workers understood the corporations' power. Document 4, an unsigned print of the Lowell mills, shows tidy brick buildings beside open meadow with no workers or crowding. Because its maker and purpose are unknown, it is best read as a picture of how the new industrial town could be presented to reassure viewers, not as evidence about conditions inside. In Document 1, Andrew Jackson's veto message, written during an election campaign and aimed at farmers and laborers, attacks the Bank for favoring "the rich and powerful," which shows that many Americans feared that new financial institutions served a few. The Panic of 1837, which brought a severe depression, showed how exposed ordinary families had become to distant financial shocks.

The market revolution did not transform life for everyone. Document 7, a map made from the 1860 census, shows the heaviest concentrations of enslaved people in counties along the lower Mississippi River and on the South Carolina coast. This is the other side of the story told by Documents 2 and 4: New England's mills depended on cotton grown by enslaved labor, and the demand for cotton fed the domestic slave trade that sold people from the Upper South to the Deep South. For roughly four million enslaved Americans in 1860, the market meant sale and forced movement rather than opportunity. The map was drawn from federal census data and published in 1861, during the Civil War, a reminder that economic integration also sharpened the conflict between slave and free regions. Document 5 adds a further qualification. Thoreau argues that people do not ride the railroad but are ridden upon by it, and he points to the Irish and Yankee laborers who laid its track. He was a writer who chose to live simply at Walden Pond and was not a typical worker, but his criticism shows that material progress did not satisfy everyone.

In sum, the market revolution profoundly changed life in the North and West by creating wage labor, commercial farming and mobility, but it also hardened slavery in the South and left many people anxious about debt, wages and power. The extent of change depended on region, race, gender and class, which is why Jackson, Thoreau and the striking Lowell workers could all find reasons to protest.
   - "it transformed the work, movement and expectations of many Northern and Western families, it deepened slavery in the South" - Defensible thesis that evaluates the extent of change and sets up a line of reasoning (large change in the North and West, deepened slavery, insecurity).
   - "The Erie Canal, opened in 1825, cut the cost of shipping between the Great Lakes and New York City" - Context paragraph (post-1812 nationalism, American System, transportation revolution, cotton gin) tied to the prompt.
   - "mill girls made up more than half of the depositors at Lowell's savings institution in 1848" - Accurate use of Document 2 to support a claim; with Documents 6, 3, 4, 1 and 7 this reaches the two-point documents row.
   - "The Panic of 1837, which brought a severe depression" - Specific outside evidence not found in the documents.
   - "Because its maker and purpose are unknown, it is best read as a picture of how the new industrial town could be presented" - Sourcing: explains how purpose and unknown authorship limit Document 4 (and, elsewhere, Robinson's 1898 hindsight and Jackson's election-year audience).
   - "the demand for cotton fed the domestic slave trade" - Complexity: links Northern mills, cotton and slavery, and qualifies 'change' with region, race and class.

Sample response, middle score (5/7; Thesis/claim 1, Contextualization 1, Evidence from the documents 2, Evidence beyond the documents 1, Sourcing (point of view, purpose, situation, audience) 0, Complex understanding 0):
After the War of 1812, Americans embraced a national economy, building roads and banks and putting up a protective tariff to tie the states together. The market revolution changed American lives a lot between 1815 and 1860 because it connected people to markets and gave them new kinds of work. For example, the Erie Canal, finished in 1825, made it cheaper to ship crops, so farmers in the West could sell to people in far away cities. Many people also moved west to find land and new opportunities.

Several documents show these changes. Document 2 says that in 1848 over half of the people with savings in a Lowell bank were mill girls. This shows that women had new jobs and earned wages, which gave them more independence. Document 6 is a table of population by region. The Midwest grew from 51,006 people in 1800 to 9,096,716 in 1860, which shows that a huge number of people moved west. Document 4 is a picture of the Lowell mills that looks clean and peaceful, so the new factories seemed like a good thing for the towns where they were built.

Not everyone liked the changes, though. In Document 1, Andrew Jackson says that the Bank helps the rich and powerful and that farmers, mechanics, and laborers have a right to complain. This shows people worried that the new economy was unfair. Document 5, by Thoreau, says the railroad rides on people, and that men who build the track are like sleepers. This shows that some people thought workers were being used by the new economy.

Also, the market revolution did not help everyone in the same way. Document 7 is a map that shows that in the South there were many enslaved people, especially near the Mississippi River. These people did not get opportunities from the market and were treated as property. So the changes were not the same for every group.

In conclusion, the market revolution changed lives a great deal for many Americans because of new jobs and new transportation, but it was not the same for everyone, since enslaved people and workers faced problems.
   - "After the War of 1812, Americans embraced a national economy, building roads and banks and putting up a protective tariff to tie the states together." - Describes a broader development after the War of 1812 (a national economy, roads, banks and the tariff) and ties it to the market revolution, so it earns the context point. The Erie Canal is not used here; it is kept as the separate outside example below.
   - "The market revolution changed American lives a lot between 1815 and 1860 because it connected people to markets and gave them new kinds of work." - A claim that answers the prompt; the line of reasoning is thin until the last paragraph, where it adds unevenness.
   - "Document 6 is a table of population by region." - Accurate description and use of documents (2, 6, 4, 1, 5, 7) addresses the topic, but explanations stay at the level of summary.
   - "the Erie Canal, finished in 1825, made it cheaper to ship crops" - A specific outside fact that is different from the context sentence above, so it earns the outside-evidence point. It is used as an example rather than as a developed context paragraph.
   - "This shows that women had new jobs and earned wages" - Interprets the document but never asks who wrote it or why, so there is no sourcing credit.

Sample response, low score (1/7; Thesis/claim 0, Contextualization 0, Evidence from the documents 1, Evidence beyond the documents 0, Sourcing (point of view, purpose, situation, audience) 0, Complex understanding 0):
The market revolution changed things a lot in America. There were new inventions and new ways to travel so people could buy and sell more things. It changed the lives of many people in the North and also the South.

Document 2 says that girls in Lowell had savings in the bank, so they were earning money. Document 6 is a table about how many people lived in different parts of the country, and the Midwest got much bigger, so people were moving west. Document 1 is about the Bank and Andrew Jackson did not like it because it helped rich people. Document 7 is a map of slaves in the South, so a lot of people there did not get the same chances.

The market revolution was a good thing because it made life better for many people, but some people had problems like the slaves in the South. In conclusion, the market revolution changed a lot of lives between 1815 and 1860.
   - "The market revolution changed things a lot in America." - Restates the prompt with no line of reasoning, so the thesis row is not earned.
   - "Document 2 says that girls in Lowell had savings in the bank." - Names what documents say without explaining how they answer the question; this earns at most one point for describing document content.
   - "Document 7 is a map of slaves in the South." - Mentions the map but does not use it to support an argument.
   - "In conclusion, the market revolution changed a lot of lives between 1815 and 1860." - No context, no outside evidence, no sourcing and no complexity.

ush_frq.title: The Market Revolution and American Lives, 1815-1860

prompt.scenario: Between 1815 and 1860, canals, steamboats and railroads, new factories and a growing cotton trade drew more Americans into buying and selling in distant markets. Historians often call these developments the market revolution.
prompt.task: Evaluate the extent to which the market revolution changed the lives of Americans between 1815 and 1860.
requirements: Respond to the prompt with a historically defensible thesis or claim that establishes a line of reasoning.
Describe a broader historical context relevant to the prompt.
Support an argument in response to the prompt using at least four documents.
Use at least one additional piece of specific historical evidence (beyond that found in the documents) relevant to an argument about the prompt.
For at least two documents, explain how or why the document's point of view, purpose, historical situation, and/or audience is relevant to an argument.

sources.title: Andrew Jackson, Veto Message Regarding the Bank of the United States (excerpt)
sources.attribution: Andrew Jackson, President of the United States, 1832 (July 10). Avalon Project, Yale Law School (transcription). Reuse: public domain (U.S. government work; published before 1929). excerpted (one contiguous passage); whitespace normalized; no wording changed.
sources.body: It is to be regretted that the rich and powerful too often bend the acts of government to their selfish purposes. Distinctions in society will always exist under every just government. Equality of talents, of education, or of wealth can not be produced by human institutions. In the full enjoyment of the gifts of Heaven and the fruits of superior industry, economy, and virtue, every man is equally entitled to protection by law; but when the laws undertake to add to these natural and just advantages artificial distinctions, to grant titles, gratuities, and exclusive privileges, to make the rich richer and the potent more powerful, the humble members of society-the farmers, mechanics, and laborers-who have neither the time nor the means of securing like favors to themselves, have a right to complain of the injustice of their Government. There are no necessary evils in government. Its evils exist only in its abuses. If it would confine itself to equal protection, and, as Heaven does its rains, shower its favors alike on the high and the low, the rich and the poor, it would be an unqualified blessing.

sources.title: Loom and Spindle, or Life among the Early Mill Girls (excerpt on Lowell)
sources.attribution: Harriet Hanson Robinson (recalling Lowell mill life of the 1830s and 1840s), 1898. Project Gutenberg eBook #72757. Reuse: public domain in the United States (published before 1929). excerpted (two segments joined by [...]); whitespace normalized; no wording changed.
sources.body: In 1848 over one-half of the depositors in the Lowell Institution for Savings were mill-girls, and over one-third of the whole sum deposited belonged to them [...] Cutting down the wages was not their only grievance, nor the only cause of this strike. Hitherto the corporations had paid twenty-five cents a week towards the board of each operative, and now it was their purpose to have the girls pay the sum; and this, in addition to the cut in the wages, would make a difference of at least one dollar a week. It was estimated that as many as twelve or fifteen hundred girls turned out, and walked in procession through the streets.

sources.title: Democracy in America, vol. 2: Causes of the Restless Spirit of Americans in the Midst of Their Prosperity (excerpt)
sources.attribution: Alexis de Tocqueville (French observer; translated by Henry Reeve), 1840 (vol. 2; English translation). Project Gutenberg eBook #816. Reuse: public domain in the United States (published before 1929). excerpted (one contiguous passage); whitespace normalized; no wording changed.
sources.body: It is strange to see with what feverish ardor the Americans pursue their own welfare; and to watch the vague dread that constantly torments them lest they should not have chosen the shortest path which may lead to it. A native of the United States clings to this world's goods as if he were certain never to die; and he is so hasty in grasping at all within his reach, that one would suppose he was constantly afraid of not living long enough to enjoy them. He clutches everything, he holds nothing fast, but soon loosens his grasp to pursue fresh gratifications. In the United States a man builds a house to spend his latter years in it, and he sells it before the roof is on: he plants a garden, and lets it just as the trees are coming into bearing: he brings a field into tillage, and leaves other men to gather the crops: he embraces a profession, and gives it up: he settles in a place, which he soon afterwards leaves, to carry his changeable longings elsewhere.

rows.name: Thesis/claim

descriptors.0: Gives no defensible thesis, only restates the prompt, or does not evaluate the extent of change in Americans' lives.
descriptors.1: Gives a historically defensible thesis that evaluates the extent of change in Americans' lives and sets up a line of reasoning, in the introduction or conclusion.

rows.task_specific: A defensible claim that evaluates the extent to which the market revolution changed Americans' lives, 1815-1860, and sets up a line of reasoning, for example large change for many Northern and Western families with deepening slavery and new insecurity, or limited and uneven change that depended on region, race and class.

rows.name: Contextualization

descriptors.0: Gives no relevant context, or only a passing reference.
descriptors.1: Describes a broader historical context before, during or continuing through 1815 to 1860 and connects it to the prompt.

rows.task_specific: Describes broader context such as post-War of 1812 nationalism and the American System, the transportation revolution (National Road, steamboats, Erie Canal), early industrialization, or cotton and the spread of slavery, and ties it to the prompt.

rows.name: Evidence from the documents

descriptors.0: Uses fewer than three documents or only quotes or summarizes without connecting them to the topic.
descriptors.1: Accurately describes the content of at least three documents in a way that addresses the topic.
descriptors.2: Uses the content of at least four documents to support an argument in response to the prompt.

rows.task_specific: Uses document content to support claims about change and its limits, for example wages and savings (Doc 2), settlement of the Midwest (Doc 6), restlessness and mobility (Doc 3), the factory town image (Doc 4), distrust of privilege (Doc 1), criticism of commercial growth (Doc 5), and the distribution of slavery (Doc 7).

rows.name: Evidence beyond the documents

descriptors.0: Gives no specific outside evidence, or the evidence is irrelevant or inaccurate.
descriptors.1: Uses at least one specific, accurate piece of outside evidence relevant to an argument about the prompt.

rows.task_specific: Uses at least one specific piece of evidence not in the documents, such as the Erie Canal, the Panic of 1837, the cotton gin and the domestic slave trade, Commonwealth v. Hunt (1842), Irish immigration, or the cult of domesticity.

rows.name: Sourcing (point of view, purpose, situation, audience)

descriptors.0: Gives no sourcing analysis, or sourcing for only one document.
descriptors.1: Explains how or why the point of view, purpose, historical situation or audience of at least two documents matters to an argument.

rows.task_specific: Explains how point of view, purpose, historical situation or audience matters for at least two documents, for example Robinson's 1898 memory as a former mill girl (Doc 2), Jackson's election-year audience (Doc 1), the unknown maker of the print (Doc 4), Thoreau's chosen simple life (Doc 5), or the French visitor's generalizations (Doc 3).

rows.name: Complex understanding

descriptors.0: Does not show a complex understanding, or makes only a brief phrase or reference.
descriptors.1: Shows a complex understanding through sophisticated argumentation or effective use of evidence that corroborates, qualifies or modifies the argument.

rows.task_specific: Shows complex understanding, for example by weighing opportunity against dependence and conflict, by qualifying 'change' with region, race, gender and class differences, by linking the cotton market and slavery to the textile mills, or by using documents that disagree to modify the claim.

scoring_notes: The thesis may argue for great, moderate or limited change as long as it is defensible and evaluates extent.
Document 6's South total includes enslaved people; Document 7 shows where enslaved people lived but does not itself state any link to the market, so that link must come from outside knowledge.
Outside evidence must differ from evidence used for contextualization to earn both points.
Simply naming an author or date does not count as sourcing; the student must explain why the source's perspective or situation matters.
ALTON reference — not official AP scoring: model scores are an ALTON estimate and no AP score is implied.

defensible_theses: The market revolution changed American lives to a great extent in the North and West by creating wage labor, commercial farming and mobility, but the change was uneven: it deepened slavery in the South, and it brought insecurity and conflict even where it brought opportunity.

The market revolution transformed how many free Americans worked and thought, yet its benefits were unequal and contested, so its overall effect on lives was significant but mixed rather than uniformly progressive.

Although canals, mills and migration reshaped parts of the country, the market revolution changed the lives of enslaved people and of many rural or poor Americans very little or for the worse, so the extent of change was limited and depended on region, race and class.

Cotton gin and the spread of cotton and slavery into the Southwest

Comparison (region, race, gender and class)

evidence_map.line: Large change in Northern and Western working life: wages, mills, migration and new habits of mind
Change was uneven: the market's growth also deepened slavery and left many lives untouched
Change brought new insecurity, conflict and criticism, so gains were mixed
The market's institutions became a political fight over who benefited

common_pitfalls: Describing canals and factories without explaining how daily lives changed.
Treating the market revolution as uniform and ignoring slavery and regional differences.
Summarizing documents one at a time instead of grouping them to support claims.
Reading Document 4 (a print of unknown purpose) as proof of good working conditions.
Treating the South's population growth in Document 6 as growth in free people's opportunity: the total includes enslaved people.
Naming a document's author or date without explaining why the perspective matters (no sourcing credit).
Using events after 1860 as the main evidence.
facts: The Erie Canal opened in 1825 and linked the Hudson River with Lake Erie.
Andrew Jackson vetoed the bill to recharter the Second Bank of the United States on July 10, 1832.
The Lowell, Massachusetts, cotton mills began operating in the 1820s and employed many young New England women.
Lowell mill workers 'turned out' (struck) in 1834 and again in October 1836.
The 1860 census counted about 3.95 million enslaved people.
The Panic of 1837 began a depression that lasted into the 1840s.
Tocqueville toured the United States in 1831-32; the second volume of Democracy in America appeared in 1840.
Walden was published in 1854.
Eli Whitney patented the cotton gin in 1794.

Tocqueville describes Americans who sell a house before the roof is finished, give up one profession for another and move on to new places, a restless pursuit of gain that suits an economy built on buying, selling and moving.

The same documents show that change came with conflict and limits. Robinson also describes the 1836 turn out, when workers protested a wage cut and new charges for board, so the factory system did not simply deliver prosperity. She wrote in 1898, six decades later, as a former mill girl proud of her fellow operatives, so her picture of independence may be warmer than the experience of every worker, yet her description of the strike shows that workers understood the corporations' power. Document 4, an unsigned print of the Lowell mills, shows tidy brick buildings beside open meadow with no workers or crowding. Because its maker and purpose are unknown, it is best read as a picture of how the new industrial town could be presented to reassure viewers, not as evidence about conditions inside. In Document 1, Andrew Jackson's veto message, written during an election campaign and aimed at farmers and laborers, attacks the Bank for favoring "the rich and powerful," which shows that many Americans feared that new financial institutions served a few. The Panic of 1837, which brought a severe depression, showed how exposed ordinary families had become to distant financial shocks.

The market revolution did not transform life for everyone. Document 7, a map made from the 1860 census, shows the heaviest concentrations of enslaved people in counties along the lower Mississippi River and on the South Carolina coast. This is the other side of the story told by Documents 2 and 4: New England's mills depended on cotton grown by enslaved labor, and the demand for cotton fed the domestic slave trade that sold people from the Upper South to the Deep South. For roughly four million enslaved Americans in 1860, the market meant sale and forced movement rather than opportunity. The map was drawn from federal census data and published in 1861, during the Civil War, a reminder that economic integration also sharpened the conflict between slave and free regions. Document 5 adds a further qualification. Thoreau argues that people do not ride the railroad but are ridden upon by it, and he points to the Irish and Yankee laborers who laid its track. He was a writer who chose to live simply at Walden Pond and was not a typical worker, but his criticism shows that material progress did not satisfy everyone.

In sum, the market revolution profoundly changed life in the North and West by creating wage labor, commercial farming and mobility, but it also hardened slavery in the South and left many people anxious about debt, wages and power. The extent of change depended on region, race, gender and class, which is why Jackson, Thoreau and the striking Lowell workers could all find reasons to protest.

annotations.quote: it transformed the work, movement and expectations of many Northern and Western families, it deepened slavery in the South
annotations.comment: Defensible thesis that evaluates the extent of change and sets up a line of reasoning (large change in the North and West, deepened slavery, insecurity).

annotations.quote: The Erie Canal, opened in 1825, cut the cost of shipping between the Great Lakes and New York City
annotations.comment: Context paragraph (post-1812 nationalism, American System, transportation revolution, cotton gin) tied to the prompt.

annotations.quote: mill girls made up more than half of the depositors at Lowell's savings institution in 1848
annotations.comment: Accurate use of Document 2 to support a claim; with Documents 6, 3, 4, 1 and 7 this reaches the two-point documents row.

annotations.quote: The Panic of 1837, which brought a severe depression
annotations.comment: Specific outside evidence not found in the documents.

annotations.quote: Because its maker and purpose are unknown, it is best read as a picture of how the new industrial town could be presented
annotations.comment: Sourcing: explains how purpose and unknown authorship limit Document 4 (and, elsewhere, Robinson's 1898 hindsight and Jackson's election-year audience).

annotations.quote: the demand for cotton fed the domestic slave trade
annotations.comment: Complexity: links Northern mills, cotton and slavery, and qualifies 'change' with region, race and class.

samples.essay:
After the War of 1812, Americans embraced a national economy, building roads and banks and putting up a protective tariff to tie the states together. The market revolution changed American lives a lot between 1815 and 1860 because it connected people to markets and gave them new kinds of work. For example, the Erie Canal, finished in 1825, made it cheaper to ship crops, so farmers in the West could sell to people in far away cities. Many people also moved west to find land and new opportunities.

Several documents show these changes. Document 2 says that in 1848 over half of the people with savings in a Lowell bank were mill girls. This shows that women had new jobs and earned wages, which gave them more independence. Document 6 is a table of population by region. The Midwest grew from 51,006 people in 1800 to 9,096,716 in 1860, which shows that a huge number of people moved west. Document 4 is a picture of the Lowell mills that looks clean and peaceful, so the new factories seemed like a good thing for the towns where they were built.

Not everyone liked the changes, though. In Document 1, Andrew Jackson says that the Bank helps the rich and powerful and that farmers, mechanics, and laborers have a right to complain. This shows people worried that the new economy was unfair. Document 5, by Thoreau, says the railroad rides on people, and that men who build the track are like sleepers. This shows that some people thought workers were being used by the new economy.

Also, the market revolution did not help everyone in the same way. Document 7 is a map that shows that in the South there were many enslaved people, especially near the Mississippi River. These people did not get opportunities from the market and were treated as property. So the changes were not the same for every group.

In conclusion, the market revolution changed lives a great deal for many Americans because of new jobs and new transportation, but it was not the same for everyone, since enslaved people and workers faced problems.

annotations.quote: After the War of 1812, Americans embraced a national economy, building roads and banks and putting up a protective tariff to tie the states together.
annotations.comment: Describes a broader development after the War of 1812 (a national economy, roads, banks and the tariff) and ties it to the market revolution, so it earns the context point. The Erie Canal is not used here; it is kept as the separate outside example below.

annotations.quote: The market revolution changed American lives a lot between 1815 and 1860 because it connected people to markets and gave them new kinds of work.
annotations.comment: A claim that answers the prompt; the line of reasoning is thin until the last paragraph, where it adds unevenness.

annotations.quote: Document 6 is a table of population by region.
annotations.comment: Accurate description and use of documents (2, 6, 4, 1, 5, 7) addresses the topic, but explanations stay at the level of summary.

annotations.quote: the Erie Canal, finished in 1825, made it cheaper to ship crops
annotations.comment: A specific outside fact that is different from the context sentence above, so it earns the outside-evidence point. It is used as an example rather than as a developed context paragraph.

annotations.quote: This shows that women had new jobs and earned wages
annotations.comment: Interprets the document but never asks who wrote it or why, so there is no sourcing credit.

samples.essay:
The market revolution changed things a lot in America. There were new inventions and new ways to travel so people could buy and sell more things. It changed the lives of many people in the North and also the South.

Document 2 says that girls in Lowell had savings in the bank, so they were earning money. Document 6 is a table about how many people lived in different parts of the country, and the Midwest got much bigger, so people were moving west. Document 1 is about the Bank and Andrew Jackson did not like it because it helped rich people. Document 7 is a map of slaves in the South, so a lot of people there did not get the same chances.

The market revolution was a good thing because it made life better for many people, but some people had problems like the slaves in the South. In conclusion, the market revolution changed a lot of lives between 1815 and 1860.

annotations.comment: Restates the prompt with no line of reasoning, so the thesis row is not earned.

provenance.note: The prompt, rubric, evidence map and sample essays are ALTON-authored practice material; all seven documents are real historical sources (see sources[].source_registry_id).

thesis_space: The market revolution changed American lives to a great extent in the North and West by creating wage labor, commercial farming and mobility, but the change was uneven: it deepened slavery in the South, and it brought insecurity and conflict even where it brought opportunity.

The market revolution transformed how many free Americans worked and thought, yet its benefits were unequal and contested, so its overall effect on lives was significant but mixed rather than uniformly progressive.

Although canals, mills and migration reshaped parts of the country, the market revolution changed the lives of enslaved people and of many rural or poor Americans very little or for the worse, so the extent of change was limited and depended on region, race and class.

evidence_map.line: Large change in Northern and Western working life: wages, mills, migration and new habits of mind
Change was uneven: the market's growth also deepened slavery and left many lives untouched
Change brought new insecurity, conflict and criticism, so gains were mixed
The market's institutions became a political fight over who benefited

fact_verdicts.note: Quotation matches the July 10, 1832 veto message; context and sourcing (Senate address, election year, Jackson a slaveholding planter, Bank supporters' credit argument) are accurate.

Excerpts match Loom and Spindle (1898); Robinson began as a doffer in 1835 at age ten, was a child during the October 1836 turn-out, and later was a suffrage activist. Figures (25 cents board, one dollar a week, 1,200-1,500 strikers, 1848 savings depositors) are as in the book.
Reeve translation passage is accurate; tour of roughly nine months in 1831-32 and 1840 publication of vol. 2 are correct.

Alt text and notes match the attached image: hand-colored print, mills and spires along the far bank, river and meadow, foreground tree at right, no visible crowding or labor. Provenance and c. 1840 date consistent with LoC record.
Walden passage accurate; Walden residence 1845-47 and 1854 publication correct. Reading of 'sleepers' as laborers (Irish and Yankee) is a defensible gloss of Thoreau's metaphor.
Regional totals match Gibson & Jung Working Paper 56 and sum to the U.S. total in every year; the note's figures (51,006 to 9,096,716; South ~2.6 to 11.1 million) are correctly read.
Alt text matches the Hergesheimer map (county shading, darkest along the lower Mississippi and the South Carolina coast, shade legend, 1860 census table); provenance and September 1861 date correct.
Standard, answerable 'evaluate the extent' prompt; the seven documents allow great, mixed, or limited-change theses.
Assignments are defensible; Doc 1's link to the market revolution (bank/credit as market institution) is somewhat indirect but conventional in APUSH framing.
Task-specific language, notes on Doc 6/Doc 7, and the context-vs-outside-evidence rule are consistent with AP scoring practice.
All dates correct (Erie Canal 1825, Panic of 1837, cotton gin 1794, Commonwealth v. Hunt 1842, telegraph 1844, Gibbons v. Ogden 1824).
All facts verified, including 1834 and October 1836 Lowell turn-outs and ~3.95 million enslaved in 1860.

Document readings and outside evidence (American System, Erie Canal, cotton gin, Panic of 1837, domestic slave trade, ~4 million enslaved in 1860) are accurate; sourcing and complexity claims stay within what the documents show. Score of 6 is a reasonable estimate (arguably 7).

Document claims accurate; the inference that the clean-looking print means factories 'seemed like a good thing' is a mild overreach typical of a mid-level essay and consistent with the intended score of 4 (no sourcing, no separate outside evidence).
Document summaries are accurate if thin; thesis plus minimal document use fits an intended score of 2.
