payload.title: Population of Kansas, Nebraska, and the Dakotas, 1870-1900
payload.set_intro:
Historical source (real document)
(table)
Total population of Kansas, Nebraska, North Dakota and South Dakota, census counts 1870-1900
Campbell Gibson and Kay Jung, U.S. Census Bureau, Population Division, 2002 (Working Paper No. 56, Sept. 2002; figures from decennial censuses). U.S. Census Bureau. Reuse: public domain (U.S. government work). excerpted (selected rows/columns; values unchanged). Census Bureau, Working Paper No. 56. Each figure is the total population at the census year shown. For North and South Dakota, the 1870 and 1880 figures are for the area of the present state, and the source notes that the division of Dakota Territory's population between the two is partly estimated.

The table for this source appears below.

stimulus.description: The total population of Kansas, Nebraska, North Dakota, and South Dakota in each census year from 1870 to 1900.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Briefly identify ONE trend or pattern shown in the table between 1870 and 1900.
parts.model_answer: Population grew rapidly in all four areas between 1870 and 1890; Kansas rose from 364,399 to 1,427,096 and Nebraska from 122,993 to 1,058,910.

rubric_rows.criterion: Students identify one accurate trend or pattern from the table. Acceptable answers include: rapid population growth in all four areas from 1870 to 1890; Kansas and Nebraska growing very little between 1890 and 1900 while North and South Dakota kept growing; or the Dakotas growing from very small populations in 1870 to more than 300,000 by 1900.
required_elements: Population grew rapidly in all four areas between 1870 and 1890; Kansas rose from 364,399 to 1,427,096 and Nebraska from 122,993 to 1,058,910.
Kansas and Nebraska grew very little in the 1890s (1,427,096 to 1,470,495 and 1,058,910 to 1,066,300), while North and South Dakota kept growing.
North and South Dakota grew from very small populations in 1870 (2,405 and 11,776) to more than 300,000 each by 1900.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE specific historical cause of the trend or pattern you identified in part A.
parts.model_answer: The Homestead Act of 1862 offered 160 acres of public land to settlers who lived on and improved it for five years, which drew farm families to the Plains and raised the population.

rubric_rows.criterion: Students explain one specific historical cause that fits the trend they named in part A. Examples: the Homestead Act's 160-acre claims; federal land grants to railroads under the Pacific Railway Acts, along with railroad promotion of settlement; immigrant recruitment in Europe; or drought, falling crop prices and the Panic of 1893 for the slowdown in the 1890s.
required_elements: The Homestead Act of 1862 offered 160 acres of public land to settlers who lived on and improved it for five years, which drew farm families to the Plains and raised the population.
Federal land grants under the Pacific Railway Acts led railroads to build lines across the Plains and to sell land and advertise for settlers, so population grew quickly once track reached an area.
Railroads and state immigration boards recruited settlers in Europe, including Germans and Scandinavians, which brought many new residents to the Plains states.
Drought, falling crop prices, and the Panic of 1893 ruined many Plains farmers in the early 1890s, which explains why growth in Kansas and Nebraska nearly stopped.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE specific effect of, or development related to, the settlement of the Great Plains in the period 1865 to 1898.
parts.model_answer: Settlement and railroad building helped destroy the bison herds and pushed Plains nations onto reservations, and the Dawes Act of 1887 later divided reservation land into individual allotments.

rubric_rows.criterion: Students explain one specific effect of, or development connected to, Plains settlement from 1865 to 1898. Examples: Native nations displaced, the bison destroyed, and the Dawes Act passed; farmer protest through the Grange, the Farmers' Alliances, and the Populist Party; regulation of railroad rates through Granger laws and the Interstate Commerce Act, and of grain-warehouse charges in Munn v. Illinois; the 1890 census report that a frontier line no longer existed; or greater commercial farming for national and world markets.
required_elements: Settlement and railroad building helped destroy the bison herds and pushed Plains nations onto reservations, and the Dawes Act of 1887 later divided reservation land into individual allotments.

Farmers who resented railroad rates, debt, and low prices organized the Grange and the Farmers' Alliances and later formed the Populist Party, whose 1892 Omaha Platform called for government ownership of railroads and free coinage of silver.

Farmer pressure led to state Granger laws regulating railroad rates and grain-elevator charges. In Munn v. Illinois (1877), a case about grain-warehouse charges rather than railroads, the Supreme Court upheld state power to regulate businesses that affect the public interest, and Congress later passed the Interstate Commerce Act of 1887.
The Superintendent of the Census reported in 1890 that a frontier line no longer existed, and Frederick Jackson Turner made that report the starting point of his 1893 frontier thesis.

payload.reference_text:
Scoring guide (ALTON practice rubric, not official College Board scoring). This question is worth 3 points.
Part A (0-1): Students identify one accurate trend or pattern from the table. Acceptable answers include: rapid population growth in all four areas from 1870 to 1890; Kansas and Nebraska growing very little between 1890 and 1900 while North and South Dakota kept growing; or the Dakotas growing from very small populations in 1870 to more than 300,000 by 1900.
   - 1: The response accurately identifies one trend or pattern shown in the table, such as Kansas rising from about 364,000 in 1870 to about 1,427,000 in 1890.
   - 0: The response misreads the table, gives a vague statement, or names no trend that the data support.
Part B (0-1): Students explain one specific historical cause that fits the trend they named in part A. Examples: the Homestead Act's 160-acre claims; federal land grants to railroads under the Pacific Railway Acts, along with railroad promotion of settlement; immigrant recruitment in Europe; or drought, falling crop prices and the Panic of 1893 for the slowdown in the 1890s.
   - 1: The response explains how one specific, accurate development from the period caused or contributed to the trend identified in part A.
   - 0: The response gives no cause, gives a cause from the wrong period, or does not explain how the cause connects to the trend.
Part C (0-1): Students explain one specific effect of, or development connected to, Plains settlement from 1865 to 1898. Examples: Native nations displaced, the bison destroyed, and the Dawes Act passed; farmer protest through the Grange, the Farmers' Alliances, and the Populist Party; regulation of railroad rates through Granger laws and the Interstate Commerce Act, and of grain-warehouse charges in Munn v. Illinois; the 1890 census report that a frontier line no longer existed; or greater commercial farming for national and world markets.
   - 1: The response explains one specific, accurate effect of or development related to Great Plains settlement between 1865 and 1898.
   - 0: The response gives no effect, an inaccurate one, or one outside the period or not connected to Plains settlement.
Note: Each part is worth one point. Parts are scored separately, but part B must explain a cause of a trend that the data actually show.
Note: In part A, accept an accurate reading of any column. Students do not need to quote exact numbers.
Note: In part B, a bare name such as 'the Homestead Act' with no explanation does not earn the point. The response must show how the development produced the trend.
Note: In part C, accept effects on Native peoples, farmers, railroads, politics, or the national economy if they are tied to western settlement in the period.
Acceptable answers for A: Population grew rapidly in all four areas between 1870 and 1890; Kansas rose from 364,399 to 1,427,096 and Nebraska from 122,993 to 1,058,910. / Kansas and Nebraska grew very little in the 1890s (1,427,096 to 1,470,495 and 1,058,910 to 1,066,300), while North and South Dakota kept growing. / North and South Dakota grew from very small populations in 1870 (2,405 and 11,776) to more than 300,000 each by 1900.
Acceptable answers for B: The Homestead Act of 1862 offered 160 acres of public land to settlers who lived on and improved it for five years, which drew farm families to the Plains and raised the population. / Federal land grants under the Pacific Railway Acts led railroads to build lines across the Plains and to sell land and advertise for settlers, so population grew quickly once track reached an area. / Railroads and state immigration boards recruited settlers in Europe, including Germans and Scandinavians, which brought many new residents to the Plains states. / Drought, falling crop prices, and the Panic of 1893 ruined many Plains farmers in the early 1890s, which explains why growth in Kansas and Nebraska nearly stopped.
Acceptable answers for C: Settlement and railroad building helped destroy the bison herds and pushed Plains nations onto reservations, and the Dawes Act of 1887 later divided reservation land into individual allotments. / Farmers who resented railroad rates, debt, and low prices organized the Grange and the Farmers' Alliances and later formed the Populist Party, whose 1892 Omaha Platform called for government ownership of railroads and free coinage of silver. / Farmer pressure led to state Granger laws regulating railroad rates and grain-elevator charges. In Munn v. Illinois (1877), a case about grain-warehouse charges rather than railroads, the Supreme Court upheld state power to regulate businesses that affect the public interest, and Congress later passed the Interstate Commerce Act of 1887. / The Superintendent of the Census reported in 1890 that a frontier line no longer existed, and Frederick Jackson Turner made that report the starting point of his 1893 frontier thesis.

Sample response, high score (3/3; Part A 1, Part B 1, Part C 1):
(A) One trend in the table is that Kansas and Nebraska grew very fast between 1870 and 1890. Kansas went from 364,399 people in 1870 to 1,427,096 in 1890, and Nebraska went from 122,993 to 1,058,910.

(B) One cause of this growth was the Homestead Act of 1862, which gave settlers 160 acres of public land if they lived on it and farmed it for five years. Land that cost almost nothing drew families from the East and from Europe to places like Kansas and Nebraska, so the population multiplied.

(C) One effect of Plains settlement was that farmers organized politically. Plains farmers depended on railroads to ship their wheat and corn and resented high rates, debt, and falling crop prices, so they joined the Grange and the Farmers' Alliances and later formed the Populist Party, whose 1892 Omaha Platform called for government ownership of the railroads and free coinage of silver.
   - "Kansas went from 364,399 people in 1870 to 1,427,096 in 1890" - Reads the table correctly and gives exact figures to show the growth trend from 1870 to 1890. Earns the Part A point.
   - "gave settlers 160 acres of public land if they lived on it and farmed it for five years" - Names an accurate, specific cause with correct details from the right period. It goes beyond a bare name of the act.
   - "so the population multiplied" - Connects the cause to the trend from part A, which the rubric requires. Earns the Part B point.
   - "formed the Populist Party" - Gives an accurate development tied to Plains settlement between 1865 and 1898.
   - "whose 1892 Omaha Platform called for government ownership of the railroads" - Backs the effect with specific, accurate evidence tied to farmers' complaints about railroads. Earns the Part C point.

Sample response, middle score (2/3; Part A 1, Part B 0, Part C 1):
(A) The population in all four places grew a lot between 1870 and 1890. For example, South Dakota went from 11,776 people in 1870 to 328,808 in 1890.

(B) A cause of this was the Homestead Act. It was passed in 1862 and many people moved to the Plains because of it.

(C) One effect of the settlement of the Great Plains was that Native Americans were pushed off their land. As settlers and railroads spread across the Plains, the buffalo herds were destroyed and Plains nations were forced onto reservations. Later the Dawes Act of 1887 broke up reservation land into individual allotments.
   - "South Dakota went from 11,776 people in 1870 to 328,808 in 1890" - Accurate figures from the table support a clear trend. This earns the Part A point.
   - "many people moved to the Plains because of it" - Names a valid cause but never says what the Homestead Act offered or how it drew settlers, so it only restates the trend. No credit for Part B.
   - "the buffalo herds were destroyed and Plains nations were forced onto reservations" - Accurate and specific development tied to settlement and railroad building.
   - "the Dawes Act of 1887 broke up reservation land into individual allotments" - Correct evidence from the period. This earns the Part C point.

Sample response, low score (1/3; Part A 1, Part B 0, Part C 0):
(A) One trend is that the population of these places went up between 1870 and 1900. For Kansas it went from 364,399 to 1,470,495.

(B) The population went up because people wanted to move to the Plains and there was a lot of land there.

(C) Settlement of the Great Plains was important in American history. People moved west and built farms and towns, and the country grew.
   - "For Kansas it went from 364,399 to 1,470,495." - Accurate reading of the table, so this earns the Part A point.
   - "people wanted to move to the Plains and there was a lot of land there" - Restates the trend and names no specific development such as the Homestead Act or railroad land grants. No credit for Part B.
   - "Settlement of the Great Plains was important in American history" - A vague claim of importance. Part C needs one specific, accurate effect such as farmer protest or Native displacement.

payload.title: Prose Fiction Analysis: The Open Boat
payload.set_intro:
Public-domain source text — Stephen Crane, The Open Boat (Section I, excerpt), The Open Boat and Other Stories (London: Heinemann, 1898 print)
The Open Boat
by Stephen Crane
The following passage from a short story is by Stephen Crane (1897). This is an excerpt.

```passage
    None of them knew the colour of the sky. Their eyes
glanced level, and were fastened upon the waves that
swept toward them. These waves were of the hue of slate,
save for the tops, which were of foaming white, and all
of the men knew the colours of the sea. The horizon
narrowed and widened, and dipped and rose, and at all
times its edge was jagged with waves that seemed thrust
up in points like rocks.

    Many a man ought to have a bath-tub larger than the
boat which here rode upon the sea. These waves were most
wrongfully and barbarously abrupt and tall, and each
froth-top was a problem in small boat navigation.

    The cook squatted in the bottom and looked with both
eyes at the six inches of gunwale which separated him
from the ocean. His sleeves were rolled over his fat
forearms, and the two flaps of his unbuttoned vest
dangled as he bent to bail out the boat. Often he said:
"Gawd! That was a narrow clip." As he remarked it he
invariably gazed eastward over the broken sea.

    The oiler, steering with one of the two oars in the
boat, sometimes raised himself suddenly to keep clear of
water that swirled in over the stern. It was a thin
little oar and it seemed often ready to snap.

    The correspondent, pulling at the other oar, watched
the waves and wondered why he was there.

    The injured captain, lying in the bow, was at this
time buried in that profound dejection and indifference
which comes, temporarily at least, to even the bravest
and most enduring when, willy nilly, the firm fails, the
army loses, the ship goes down. The mind of the master
of a vessel is rooted deep in the timbers of her, though
he commanded for a day or a decade, and this captain had
on him the stern impression of a scene in the greys of
dawn of seven turned faces, and later a stump of a
top-mast with a white ball on it that slashed to and fro
at the waves, went low and lower, and down. Thereafter
there was something strange in his voice. Although
steady, it was deep with mourning, and of a quality
beyond oration or tears.

    "Keep 'er a little more south, Billie," said he.

    "'A little more south,' sir," said the oiler in the
stern.

    A seat in this boat was not unlike a seat upon a
bucking broncho, and, by the same token, a broncho is
not much smaller. The craft pranced and reared, and
plunged like an animal. As each wave came, and she rose
for it, she seemed like a horse making at a fence
outrageously high. The manner of her scramble over these
walls of water is a mystic thing, and, moreover, at the
top of them were ordinarily these problems in white
water, the foam racing down from the summit of each
wave, requiring a new leap, and a leap from the air.
Then, after scornfully bumping a crest, she would slide,
and race, and splash down a long incline, and arrive
bobbing and nodding in front of the next menace.

    A singular disadvantage of the sea lies in the fact
that after successfully surmounting one wave you
discover that there is another behind it just as
important and just as nervously anxious to do something
effective in the way of swamping boats. In a ten-foot
dingey one can get an idea of the resources of the sea
in the line of waves that is not probable to the average
experience which is never at sea in a dingey. As each
slaty wall of water approached, it shut all else from
the view of the men in the boat, and it was not
difficult to imagine that this particular wave was the
final outburst of the ocean, the last effort of the grim
water. There was a terrible grace in the move of the
waves, and they came in silence, save for the snarling
of the crests.
```

parts.prompt:
The following passage is from "The Open Boat," a short story by Stephen Crane (1897 in the original). In this passage, a narrator describes four shipwrecked men (a cook, an oiler, a correspondent, and their injured captain) as they work to keep a small dinghy afloat on a rough, dangerous sea.

Read the passage closely. Then write an essay in which you analyze how Stephen Crane uses literary elements and techniques to convey the men's mortal danger through a narrative stance that moves between wry, almost comic detachment and close, sober attention to their fear, exhaustion, and grief.

Your essay should:
- Respond to the prompt with a thesis that offers a defensible interpretation of the passage.
- Use specific evidence from the passage, and explain how that evidence supports your line of reasoning.
- Explain how multiple literary elements and techniques contribute to the meaning you describe.
- Write clearly, with appropriate grammar and punctuation.
parts.model_answer:
In this passage from "The Open Boat," Stephen Crane's narrator can't seem to decide whether the shipwreck is a joke or a funeral. He compares the dinghy to a bath-tub and a bronco, then turns without warning to a captain mourning his drowned crew. This shifting stance doesn't soften the danger. It measures it. The wry detachment shows how absurdly small the men are against the sea, and the close attention to each man shows what that smallness costs. Together they suggest that the sea's apparent hostility is something the men project onto an ocean that does not care about them at all.

The passage opens close and sober. "None of them knew the colour of the sky" is a flat, plain sentence, but it tells us the men cannot afford to look up even once. Their world has shrunk to waves of "the hue of slate," and the horizon that "narrowed and widened" seems almost to breathe. Then the narrator abruptly pulls back: "Many a man ought to have a bath-tub larger than the boat." The hyperbole is funny because it drops a safe, domestic image into an ocean where it doesn't belong. A bathtub is the most harmless water there is, and the joke makes us feel how ridiculous it is to cross a sea in something smaller. In the same way, calling each wave "a problem in small boat navigation" borrows the dry language of a textbook. The understatement is comic, yet the word "each" quietly reminds us that the problems never stop.

In the middle section the narrator moves in on the men one at a time, and the sentences become short and separate, as if each man is alone in his own fear. The cook stares at the "six inches of gunwale" between him and drowning, a measurement so exact it mirrors his tunnel vision. The oiler's oar is "thin little" and "seemed often ready to snap," and those small words make their only way of steering seem pitiful. The correspondent gets a single sentence: he "watched the waves and wondered why he was there." After the jokes its plainness stands out, because no irony protects him here. The captain's paragraph is the gravest. The list "the firm fails, the army loses, the ship goes down" widens his loss into every human failure, and the image of "seven turned faces" and the mast going "low and lower, and down" slows the rhythm until the last "down" lands like the sinking itself. His voice is "beyond oration or tears," a grief language can't hold, which may be exactly why the narrator needs humor everywhere else.

When the narrator goes back to comedy, it has gotten darker. The boat is "a bucking broncho" and "a horse making at a fence outrageously high," images that turn survival into a rodeo stunt. The waves are "nervously anxious to do something effective in the way of swamping boats," bureaucratic diction that makes the sea sound like an eager employee. It's funny, but it is also relentless, since there is always "another behind it just as important." The sea is personified in "wrongfully and barbarously" and "the snarling of the crests," which shows the men experiencing it as an enemy, and even the boat is given a living attitude when she goes "scornfully bumping a crest." But the last lines complicate this. The waves have "a terrible grace" and "came in silence," which suggests something beautiful and indifferent, not angry. The snarling exists only at the crests, almost as if the anger is what the men hear rather than what the sea intends.

So the humor in this passage is not an escape from danger. It lets the narrator stand far enough back to see how tiny the boat is, while the sober moments show from the inside what being that tiny feels like. Crane needs both, because the joke and the grief are telling the same truth.

rubric_rows.criterion: A defensible thesis must make a claim about how the passage presents the men's danger through the narrator's shifting or divided stance. For example, it might argue that ironic understatement and comic comparisons sharpen the sense of peril instead of softening it, or that the narrator's distance and the men's narrowed, intimate view together show human smallness before a sea that seems hostile but is really indifferent. A thesis that only restates the situation ('the men are in danger on the sea') or only lists devices ('Crane uses similes and personification') without saying what they do for this idea does not earn the point. A thesis that names only one attitude can earn the point if it makes a defensible interpretive claim about how the danger is presented, but stronger responses recognize the tension between humor and gravity.

Strong responses pick specific evidence from both sides of the tension and explain how each works. On the detached or comic side: the bath-tub hyperbole, the 'problem in small boat navigation' understatement, the bucking broncho and horse-at-a-fence comparisons, and the mock-formal claim that waves are 'nervously anxious to do something effective in the way of swamping boats.' On the intimate or grave side: the opening narrowed vision ('None of them knew the colour of the sky'), the 'six inches of gunwale,' the oar 'ready to snap,' the correspondent wondering 'why he was there,' and the captain's memory of 'seven turned faces' and the mast going 'low and lower, and down.' Commentary at the 4 level explains how particular word choices create the effect. For example, the formal, bureaucratic diction applied to waves makes the threat seem absurd and also relentless, and the short, flat sentences about each man show how small and isolated each one is. Commentary also links these choices back to the thesis throughout. A 3 has relevant evidence and some explanation but is uneven or mostly about one side. A 2 mostly summarizes or names devices with thin explanation. A 1 gives little relevant evidence.

Sophistication might mean explaining how the humor itself carries the dread, so that the irony is a way of coping with the danger or of measuring it, not an escape from it. It might mean showing that personification of the sea ('wrongfully,' 'snarling') records how the men perceive the sea while hinting that the sea has no intent at all ('a terrible grace,' 'they came in silence'). It might also mean tracing how the structure moves: from narrowed sight, to a portrait of each man, to the captain's grief, to the larger, generalized reflection on endless waves, and explaining what that movement shows about the limits of human perspective. The point needs sustained complexity throughout the essay, not a single passing remark or vague praise of Crane's 'realism.'

Sample essay (mid; scored 4/6: thesis 1, evidence 3, sophistication 0)
In this passage from "The Open Boat," Stephen Crane shows the danger the four men are in by switching between a joking, distant narrator and a serious one who pays close attention to what the men feel. The humor makes the sea seem almost silly at first, but it ends up making the danger feel more real, because the men are so small next to it.

The passage begins with the serious side. "None of them knew the colour of the sky" tells the reader that the men can only look at the waves in front of them, so their view is very narrow. The waves are described as "slate" with "foaming white" tops, and the horizon is "jagged" like rocks. This imagery makes the sea seem hard and sharp instead of soft, so the reader feels how threatening it is even before any man is described.

Then the narrator changes tone and becomes funny. He says "Many a man ought to have a bath-tub larger than the boat." This is hyperbole, and it makes the boat seem tiny and silly. The narrator also calls each wave "a problem in small boat navigation," which is an understatement because the problem could actually kill them. The humor makes the narrator seem calm and far away, but the reader still understands the boat could be swamped. Later the boat is compared to a "bucking broncho" and a horse "making at a fence." These comparisons are playful, but they also show the boat is being thrown around and has to keep jumping the next wave. Crane also says the waves are "nervously anxious to do something effective in the way of swamping boats." Using business-like words for the waves is funny, but it also shows the waves never stop trying.

The narrator gets serious again when he describes the men one at a time. The cook looks at "six inches of gunwale" which separates him from the ocean, and this exact detail shows how close death is. The oar is "thin" and "ready to snap," which makes their only tool seem weak. The correspondent "wondered why he was there," which is a short simple sentence that shows he feels lost and alone. The most serious part is the captain, who remembers "seven turned faces" and the mast that went "low and lower, and down." The repetition in that phrase makes the sinking feel slow, and the captain's voice is "deep with mourning." Here there is no joking at all.

In conclusion, Crane uses humor and seriousness together. The comic comparisons show the narrator standing back from the scene, and the details about the men show the fear and grief up close. Together they show that the men are very small and the danger is very real.
- Row A: "The humor makes the sea seem almost silly at first, but it ends up making the danger feel more real, because the men are so small next to it." - Defensible thesis that addresses the humor/gravity tension and says what the humor does for the danger. It is somewhat general, but it answers the prompt and earns the point.
- Row B: ""None of them knew the colour of the sky" tells the reader that the men can only look at the waves in front of them" - Specific quotation with a reasonable explanation of the narrowed view. The commentary stays fairly simple and does not tie the point back strongly to the narrator's stance.
- Row B: "This is hyperbole, and it makes the boat seem tiny and silly." - Names a technique and gives a brief effect, but the commentary is thin and repetitive. It does not explain how the exaggeration carries the danger.
- Row B: "Using business-like words for the waves is funny, but it also shows the waves never stop trying." - Good attempt to explain how diction works on both the comic and threatening sides. It is brief and not developed.
- Row B: "The repetition in that phrase makes the sinking feel slow, and the captain's voice is "deep with mourning."" - Uses specific evidence from the grave side and explains one technique, repetition. The analysis is short and the passage's structure is not examined further.
- Row C: "The humor makes the narrator seem calm and far away, but the reader still understands the boat could be swamped." - Touches on the tension between detachment and peril, but only in passing. The essay does not sustain this idea, so sophistication is not earned.

Sample essay (low; scored 2/6: thesis 0, evidence 2, sophistication 0)
In the passage from The Open Boat, Stephen Crane shows four men in a small boat on a rough sea. The narrator sometimes sounds funny and sometimes serious, and Crane uses imagery and comparisons to show the men are in danger.

At the start the men only look at the waves. "None of them knew the colour of the sky" shows that they are focused on the sea and cannot look at anything else. The waves are described as slate colored with white tops, and the horizon is jagged like rocks. This shows the sea is dangerous.

Then the narrator gets kind of funny. He says "Many a man ought to have a bath-tub larger than the boat." This is a joke because the boat is so small. He also compares the boat to a bucking broncho and a horse jumping a fence. These comparisons make the boat seem alive and they show how hard it is to stay afloat. The narrator also says the waves are "nervously anxious" to swamp boats, which is another funny line, but it still shows the waves are a threat.

The narrator also describes each man. The cook bails the boat and says "Gawd! That was a narrow clip." The oiler steers with a thin oar that seems ready to snap. The correspondent wonders why he is there. The captain is hurt and sad because his ship went down. His voice is "deep with mourning." These details show the men are scared and tired and sad.

In conclusion, Crane uses humor and serious description to show the men are in mortal danger. The comparisons and the details about each man make the reader feel how scary the sea is, and the ending says the waves are grim and silent.

- Row B: "This shows the sea is dangerous." - Commentary is a general restatement of the prompt's premise. It does not explain how the color imagery or the jagged horizon creates the sense of danger.
- Row B: "This is a joke because the boat is so small." - Identifies the bath-tub hyperbole but explains only that it is funny, not how the comic exaggeration conveys or heightens the peril.
- Row C: "which is another funny line, but it still shows the waves are a threat." - Gestures at the humor and threat together but does not analyze the mock-formal diction or why the joke makes the threat feel relentless. This is a missed opportunity for sophistication.
- Row B: "These details show the men are scared and tired and sad." - Relevant details (oar ready to snap, captain's mourning) are quoted or paraphrased, but the commentary is a general summary with no explanation of technique, so evidence stays at a low level.

prompt.lead: The following passage is from "The Open Boat," a short story by Stephen Crane (1897 in the original). In this passage, a narrator describes four shipwrecked men (a cook, an oiler, a correspondent, and their injured captain) as they work to keep a small dinghy afloat on a rough, dangerous sea.
prompt.task: Read the passage closely. Then write an essay in which you analyze how Stephen Crane uses literary elements and techniques to convey the men's mortal danger through a narrative stance that moves between wry, almost comic detachment and close, sober attention to their fear, exhaustion, and grief.
requirements: Respond to the prompt with a thesis that offers a defensible interpretation of the passage.
Use specific evidence from the passage, and explain how that evidence supports your line of reasoning.
Explain how multiple literary elements and techniques contribute to the meaning you describe.
Write clearly, with appropriate grammar and punctuation.

passage.title: The Open Boat
passage.headnote: The following passage from a short story is by Stephen Crane (1897). This is an excerpt.
stanzas: None of them knew the colour of the sky. Their eyes
glanced level, and were fastened upon the waves that
swept toward them. These waves were of the hue of slate,
save for the tops, which were of foaming white, and all
of the men knew the colours of the sea. The horizon
narrowed and widened, and dipped and rose, and at all
times its edge was jagged with waves that seemed thrust
up in points like rocks.
Many a man ought to have a bath-tub larger than the
boat which here rode upon the sea. These waves were most
wrongfully and barbarously abrupt and tall, and each
froth-top was a problem in small boat navigation.
The cook squatted in the bottom and looked with both
eyes at the six inches of gunwale which separated him
from the ocean. His sleeves were rolled over his fat
forearms, and the two flaps of his unbuttoned vest
dangled as he bent to bail out the boat. Often he said:
"Gawd! That was a narrow clip." As he remarked it he
invariably gazed eastward over the broken sea.
The oiler, steering with one of the two oars in the
boat, sometimes raised himself suddenly to keep clear of
water that swirled in over the stern. It was a thin
little oar and it seemed often ready to snap.
The correspondent, pulling at the other oar, watched
the waves and wondered why he was there.
The injured captain, lying in the bow, was at this
time buried in that profound dejection and indifference
which comes, temporarily at least, to even the bravest
and most enduring when, willy nilly, the firm fails, the
army loses, the ship goes down. The mind of the master
of a vessel is rooted deep in the timbers of her, though
he commanded for a day or a decade, and this captain had
on him the stern impression of a scene in the greys of
dawn of seven turned faces, and later a stump of a
top-mast with a white ball on it that slashed to and fro
at the waves, went low and lower, and down. Thereafter
there was something strange in his voice. Although
steady, it was deep with mourning, and of a quality
beyond oration or tears.
"Keep 'er a little more south, Billie," said he.
"'A little more south,' sir," said the oiler in the
stern.
A seat in this boat was not unlike a seat upon a
bucking broncho, and, by the same token, a broncho is
not much smaller. The craft pranced and reared, and
plunged like an animal. As each wave came, and she rose
for it, she seemed like a horse making at a fence
outrageously high. The manner of her scramble over these
walls of water is a mystic thing, and, moreover, at the
top of them were ordinarily these problems in white
water, the foam racing down from the summit of each
wave, requiring a new leap, and a leap from the air.
Then, after scornfully bumping a crest, she would slide,
and race, and splash down a long incline, and arrive
bobbing and nodding in front of the next menace.
A singular disadvantage of the sea lies in the fact
that after successfully surmounting one wave you
discover that there is another behind it just as
important and just as nervously anxious to do something
effective in the way of swamping boats. In a ten-foot
dingey one can get an idea of the resources of the sea
in the line of waves that is not probable to the average
experience which is never at sea in a dingey. As each
slaty wall of water approached, it shut all else from
the view of the men in the boat, and it was not
difficult to imagine that this particular wave was the
final outburst of the ocean, the last effort of the grim
water. There was a terrible grace in the move of the
waves, and they came in silence, save for the snarling
of the crests.

rows.name: Thesis

descriptors.0: No defensible thesis: the response only restates the prompt, summarizes or describes the text, makes a comment that does not answer the prompt, or never states an interpretation that needs to be defended.
descriptors.1: The response states a defensible interpretation that answers the prompt (it may take more than one sentence and may appear anywhere in the essay).

rows.task_specific: A defensible thesis must make a claim about how the passage presents the men's danger through the narrator's shifting or divided stance. For example, it might argue that ironic understatement and comic comparisons sharpen the sense of peril instead of softening it, or that the narrator's distance and the men's narrowed, intimate view together show human smallness before a sea that seems hostile but is really indifferent. A thesis that only restates the situation ('the men are in danger on the sea') or only lists devices ('Crane uses similes and personification') without saying what they do for this idea does not earn the point. A thesis that names only one attitude can earn the point if it makes a defensible interpretive claim about how the danger is presented, but stronger responses recognize the tension between humor and gravity.

rows.name: Evidence and commentary

descriptors.0: Restates the thesis or the prompt, repeats given information, or offers irrelevant material; no usable evidence or commentary.
descriptors.1: Evidence is mostly general; the response summarizes or paraphrases and does not explain how the evidence supports an argument.
descriptors.2: Some specific, relevant evidence, mixed with generalities. Explains how some evidence relates to the argument, but no line of reasoning is established or it is faulty.
descriptors.3: Specific evidence for the claims in a line of reasoning, and explains how some of that evidence supports the line of reasoning, including how at least one literary element or technique contributes to meaning.
descriptors.4: Specific evidence supports every claim in a line of reasoning, the commentary consistently explains how the evidence supports it, and it explains how multiple literary elements or techniques contribute to meaning. Errors that interfere with communication prevent this level.

rows.task_specific: Strong responses pick specific evidence from both sides of the tension and explain how each works. On the detached or comic side: the bath-tub hyperbole, the 'problem in small boat navigation' understatement, the bucking broncho and horse-at-a-fence comparisons, and the mock-formal claim that waves are 'nervously anxious to do something effective in the way of swamping boats.' On the intimate or grave side: the opening narrowed vision ('None of them knew the colour of the sky'), the 'six inches of gunwale,' the oar 'ready to snap,' the correspondent wondering 'why he was there,' and the captain's memory of 'seven turned faces' and the mast going 'low and lower, and down.' Commentary at the 4 level explains how particular word choices create the effect. For example, the formal, bureaucratic diction applied to waves makes the threat seem absurd and also relentless, and the short, flat sentences about each man show how small and isolated each one is. Commentary also links these choices back to the thesis throughout. A 3 has relevant evidence and some explanation but is uneven or mostly about one side. A 2 mostly summarizes or names devices with thin explanation. A 1 gives little relevant evidence.

rows.name: Sophistication

descriptors.0: Does not meet the criteria for the point: contextualizing is limited to sweeping generalities, other readings are only hinted at, complexity is oversimplified, or elaborate language does not advance the argument.
descriptors.1: Shows sophistication of thought or develops a complex literary argument, sustained through the essay (not a phrase): explores tensions or complexities in the text, situates the interpretation in a broader context, accounts for alternative interpretations, or uses a consistently vivid and persuasive style.

rows.task_specific: Sophistication might mean explaining how the humor itself carries the dread, so that the irony is a way of coping with the danger or of measuring it, not an escape from it. It might mean showing that personification of the sea ('wrongfully,' 'snarling') records how the men perceive the sea while hinting that the sea has no intent at all ('a terrible grace,' 'they came in silence'). It might also mean tracing how the structure moves: from narrowed sight, to a portrait of each man, to the captain's grief, to the larger, generalized reflection on endless waves, and explaining what that movement shows about the limits of human perspective. The point needs sustained complexity throughout the essay, not a single passing remark or vague praise of Crane's 'realism.'

scoring_notes: Do not reward plot summary of the men's roles in the boat unless it is tied to how the narrator presents them.
Device identification alone earns little. A response that never names a technique but explains closely how diction and comparisons create the divided stance can still earn high Row B scores.

Do not require readers to call the sea 'indifferent.' Readings that treat it as hostile are defensible if they are supported, although noticing the gap between seeming hostility and actual indifference can support Row C.
Do not reward claims about Crane's biography or about events beyond this excerpt, since the passage and headnote do not support them.
Responses may treat the humor as consolation, as irony, or as a sign of exhaustion. Any of these can be defensible if grounded in the text.

defensible_positions: The narrator's ironic understatement and comic comparisons do not lessen the danger. They make it sharper by setting the deadly situation against a calm, almost amused voice.
The passage moves between a detached, generalizing narrator and the men's narrowed, close-up perception, and this contrast stresses how small and isolated the men are before the sea.

Personifying the sea as spiteful, scornful, and snarling captures the men's fearful sense of being targeted, while 'terrible grace' and 'silence' suggest that the sea is actually impersonal and indifferent.

The brief, separate portraits of the cook, oiler, correspondent, and captain show each man shut inside his own task or thought, and the captain's quiet grief gives the passage a gravity that the humor never fully displaces.
The comparison of the boat to a bucking horse shows both how hard and how absurd the men's struggle is, presenting survival as a series of improbable leaps that never ends.

devices.quote: None of them knew the colour of the sky.
devices.effect: The story opens on narrowed sight. The men cannot look up, so their whole world shrinks to the waves, which sets up their fear and confinement.

devices.quote: Many a man ought to have a bath-tub larger than the boat which here rode upon the sea.
devices.effect: The domestic, comic comparison shows how tiny the boat is and brings in the narrator's wry detachment from the peril.

devices.quote: each froth-top was a problem in small boat navigation
devices.effect: Technical, mild wording for a possible death sentence creates irony that makes the danger feel constant and calmly measured.

devices.quote: the six inches of gunwale which separated him from the ocean
devices.effect: The exact, small measurement shows how thin the barrier between life and death is, seen through the cook's fixed stare.

devices.quote: It was a thin little oar and it seemed often ready to snap.
devices.effect: The words 'thin little' make the men's main tool feel fragile and childlike, which raises the tension.

devices.quote: watched the waves and wondered why he was there
devices.effect: The repeated w sounds and the bare sentence suggest the correspondent's dazed, existential confusion, which is a moment of inner exposure.

devices.quote: the firm fails, the army loses, the ship goes down
devices.effect: The series of parallel clauses widens the captain's dejection into a universal pattern of failure and gives his grief dignity.

devices.quote: went low and lower, and down
devices.effect: The sinking rhythm of the phrase acts out the ship's slow disappearance in the captain's memory and holds back emotion in a sober way.

devices.quote: "Keep 'er a little more south, Billie," said he.
devices.effect: The captain's brief, steady order after the account of his mourning shows duty going on under grief, which is restraint and not drama.

devices.quote: she seemed like a horse making at a fence outrageously high
devices.effect: The comparison makes the boat's struggle lively and a little comic while stressing how hard each wave is to clear.

devices.quote: just as nervously anxious to do something effective in the way of swamping boats
devices.effect: Mock-official wording gives the waves petty intent, which makes the threat funny and endless at the same time.

devices.quote: There was a terrible grace in the move of the waves
devices.effect: Joining beauty and dread shows the narrator's divided response and hints that the sea is impersonal, not malicious.

devices.quote: the snarling of the crests
devices.effect: The animal-like menace in the last image leaves the men's fearful perception of the sea as the passage's closing note.

common_pitfalls: Summarizing the jobs of the four men without analyzing how the narrator presents them.
Treating the passage as purely comic or purely tragic and missing the tension between detachment and gravity.
Listing devices such as simile and personification without explaining their effect on the idea of danger.
Claiming the sea is literally evil or intentionally cruel without considering the gap between how it seems and what it is.
Bringing in biographical claims about Crane or events from later in the story that the excerpt does not support.
Misreading the captain's indifference as cowardice instead of the grief and dejection the narrator describes.

samples.essay:
In this passage from "The Open Boat," Stephen Crane's narrator can't seem to decide whether the shipwreck is a joke or a funeral. He compares the dinghy to a bath-tub and a bronco, then turns without warning to a captain mourning his drowned crew. This shifting stance doesn't soften the danger. It measures it. The wry detachment shows how absurdly small the men are against the sea, and the close attention to each man shows what that smallness costs. Together they suggest that the sea's apparent hostility is something the men project onto an ocean that does not care about them at all.

The passage opens close and sober. "None of them knew the colour of the sky" is a flat, plain sentence, but it tells us the men cannot afford to look up even once. Their world has shrunk to waves of "the hue of slate," and the horizon that "narrowed and widened" seems almost to breathe. Then the narrator abruptly pulls back: "Many a man ought to have a bath-tub larger than the boat." The hyperbole is funny because it drops a safe, domestic image into an ocean where it doesn't belong. A bathtub is the most harmless water there is, and the joke makes us feel how ridiculous it is to cross a sea in something smaller. In the same way, calling each wave "a problem in small boat navigation" borrows the dry language of a textbook. The understatement is comic, yet the word "each" quietly reminds us that the problems never stop.

In the middle section the narrator moves in on the men one at a time, and the sentences become short and separate, as if each man is alone in his own fear. The cook stares at the "six inches of gunwale" between him and drowning, a measurement so exact it mirrors his tunnel vision. The oiler's oar is "thin little" and "seemed often ready to snap," and those small words make their only way of steering seem pitiful. The correspondent gets a single sentence: he "watched the waves and wondered why he was there." After the jokes its plainness stands out, because no irony protects him here. The captain's paragraph is the gravest. The list "the firm fails, the army loses, the ship goes down" widens his loss into every human failure, and the image of "seven turned faces" and the mast going "low and lower, and down" slows the rhythm until the last "down" lands like the sinking itself. His voice is "beyond oration or tears," a grief language can't hold, which may be exactly why the narrator needs humor everywhere else.

When the narrator goes back to comedy, it has gotten darker. The boat is "a bucking broncho" and "a horse making at a fence outrageously high," images that turn survival into a rodeo stunt. The waves are "nervously anxious to do something effective in the way of swamping boats," bureaucratic diction that makes the sea sound like an eager employee. It's funny, but it is also relentless, since there is always "another behind it just as important." The sea is personified in "wrongfully and barbarously" and "the snarling of the crests," which shows the men experiencing it as an enemy, and even the boat is given a living attitude when she goes "scornfully bumping a crest." But the last lines complicate this. The waves have "a terrible grace" and "came in silence," which suggests something beautiful and indifferent, not angry. The snarling exists only at the crests, almost as if the anger is what the men hear rather than what the sea intends.

So the humor in this passage is not an escape from danger. It lets the narrator stand far enough back to see how tiny the boat is, while the sober moments show from the inside what being that tiny feels like. Crane needs both, because the joke and the grief are telling the same truth.

annotations.quote: This shifting stance doesn't soften the danger. It measures it.
annotations.comment: Defensible, specific thesis that answers the prompt directly. It claims the two attitudes work together to convey peril instead of just restating the situation or listing devices.

annotations.quote: something the men project onto an ocean that does not care about them at all
annotations.comment: Extends the thesis into a line of reasoning (smallness, then cost, then indifference) that the body paragraphs follow.

annotations.quote: A bathtub is the most harmless water there is
annotations.comment: Commentary explains how the hyperbole works (a domestic image out of place at sea) and connects the comic side back to the danger.

annotations.quote: the word "each" quietly reminds us that the problems never stop
annotations.comment: Close attention to a single word shows how the understatement carries a sense of relentless threat. This is 4-level analysis of diction.

annotations.quote: the sentences become short and separate, as if each man is alone in his own fear
annotations.comment: Explains how sentence structure contributes to meaning, which adds a technique beyond imagery and diction.

annotations.quote: slows the rhythm until the last "down" lands like the sinking itself
annotations.comment: Specific evidence from the grave side, with commentary on sound and rhythm. The essay covers both sides of the tension with explained evidence.

annotations.quote: bureaucratic diction that makes the sea sound like an eager employee
annotations.comment: Explains how mock-formal word choice makes the threat seem absurd and relentless at once, as the task-specific rubric asks.

annotations.quote: which may be exactly why the narrator needs humor everywhere else
annotations.comment: Argues that humor is a response to grief beyond words, not an escape from it. The essay comes back to this idea instead of making it once in passing.

annotations.quote: almost as if the anger is what the men hear rather than what the sea intends
annotations.comment: Separates perceived hostility from real indifference using 'terrible grace' and 'silence.' This complexity was set up in the thesis and is followed through here.

annotations.quote: Crane needs both, because the joke and the grief are telling the same truth.
annotations.comment: The conclusion ties the tension together. Sophistication runs through the whole essay instead of sitting in one line, which earns the point.

samples.essay:
In this passage from "The Open Boat," Stephen Crane shows the danger the four men are in by switching between a joking, distant narrator and a serious one who pays close attention to what the men feel. The humor makes the sea seem almost silly at first, but it ends up making the danger feel more real, because the men are so small next to it.

The passage begins with the serious side. "None of them knew the colour of the sky" tells the reader that the men can only look at the waves in front of them, so their view is very narrow. The waves are described as "slate" with "foaming white" tops, and the horizon is "jagged" like rocks. This imagery makes the sea seem hard and sharp instead of soft, so the reader feels how threatening it is even before any man is described.

Then the narrator changes tone and becomes funny. He says "Many a man ought to have a bath-tub larger than the boat." This is hyperbole, and it makes the boat seem tiny and silly. The narrator also calls each wave "a problem in small boat navigation," which is an understatement because the problem could actually kill them. The humor makes the narrator seem calm and far away, but the reader still understands the boat could be swamped. Later the boat is compared to a "bucking broncho" and a horse "making at a fence." These comparisons are playful, but they also show the boat is being thrown around and has to keep jumping the next wave. Crane also says the waves are "nervously anxious to do something effective in the way of swamping boats." Using business-like words for the waves is funny, but it also shows the waves never stop trying.

The narrator gets serious again when he describes the men one at a time. The cook looks at "six inches of gunwale" which separates him from the ocean, and this exact detail shows how close death is. The oar is "thin" and "ready to snap," which makes their only tool seem weak. The correspondent "wondered why he was there," which is a short simple sentence that shows he feels lost and alone. The most serious part is the captain, who remembers "seven turned faces" and the mast that went "low and lower, and down." The repetition in that phrase makes the sinking feel slow, and the captain's voice is "deep with mourning." Here there is no joking at all.

In conclusion, Crane uses humor and seriousness together. The comic comparisons show the narrator standing back from the scene, and the details about the men show the fear and grief up close. Together they show that the men are very small and the danger is very real.

annotations.quote: The humor makes the sea seem almost silly at first, but it ends up making the danger feel more real, because the men are so small next to it.
annotations.comment: Defensible thesis that addresses the humor/gravity tension and says what the humor does for the danger. It is somewhat general, but it answers the prompt and earns the point.

annotations.quote: "None of them knew the colour of the sky" tells the reader that the men can only look at the waves in front of them
annotations.comment: Specific quotation with a reasonable explanation of the narrowed view. The commentary stays fairly simple and does not tie the point back strongly to the narrator's stance.

annotations.quote: This is hyperbole, and it makes the boat seem tiny and silly.
annotations.comment: Names a technique and gives a brief effect, but the commentary is thin and repetitive. It does not explain how the exaggeration carries the danger.

annotations.quote: Using business-like words for the waves is funny, but it also shows the waves never stop trying.
annotations.comment: Good attempt to explain how diction works on both the comic and threatening sides. It is brief and not developed.

annotations.quote: The repetition in that phrase makes the sinking feel slow, and the captain's voice is "deep with mourning."
annotations.comment: Uses specific evidence from the grave side and explains one technique, repetition. The analysis is short and the passage's structure is not examined further.

annotations.quote: The humor makes the narrator seem calm and far away, but the reader still understands the boat could be swamped.
annotations.comment: Touches on the tension between detachment and peril, but only in passing. The essay does not sustain this idea, so sophistication is not earned.

samples.essay:
In the passage from The Open Boat, Stephen Crane shows four men in a small boat on a rough sea. The narrator sometimes sounds funny and sometimes serious, and Crane uses imagery and comparisons to show the men are in danger.

At the start the men only look at the waves. "None of them knew the colour of the sky" shows that they are focused on the sea and cannot look at anything else. The waves are described as slate colored with white tops, and the horizon is jagged like rocks. This shows the sea is dangerous.

Then the narrator gets kind of funny. He says "Many a man ought to have a bath-tub larger than the boat." This is a joke because the boat is so small. He also compares the boat to a bucking broncho and a horse jumping a fence. These comparisons make the boat seem alive and they show how hard it is to stay afloat. The narrator also says the waves are "nervously anxious" to swamp boats, which is another funny line, but it still shows the waves are a threat.

The narrator also describes each man. The cook bails the boat and says "Gawd! That was a narrow clip." The oiler steers with a thin oar that seems ready to snap. The correspondent wonders why he is there. The captain is hurt and sad because his ship went down. His voice is "deep with mourning." These details show the men are scared and tired and sad.

In conclusion, Crane uses humor and serious description to show the men are in mortal danger. The comparisons and the details about each man make the reader feel how scary the sea is, and the ending says the waves are grim and silent.

annotations.quote: Crane uses imagery and comparisons to show the men are in danger.
annotations.comment: Thesis only says the men are in danger and lists devices. It does not make a claim about how the shifting humorous and serious stance shapes the danger, so it earns no thesis credit.

annotations.quote: This shows the sea is dangerous.
annotations.comment: Commentary is a general restatement of the prompt's premise. It does not explain how the color imagery or the jagged horizon creates the sense of danger.

annotations.quote: This is a joke because the boat is so small.
annotations.comment: Identifies the bath-tub hyperbole but explains only that it is funny, not how the comic exaggeration conveys or heightens the peril.

annotations.quote: which is another funny line, but it still shows the waves are a threat.
annotations.comment: Gestures at the humor and threat together but does not analyze the mock-formal diction or why the joke makes the threat feel relentless. This is a missed opportunity for sophistication.

annotations.quote: These details show the men are scared and tired and sad.
annotations.comment: Relevant details (oar ready to snap, captain's mourning) are quoted or paraphrased, but the commentary is a general summary with no explanation of technique, so evidence stays at a low level.

blueprint.central_idea: Four men in a tiny dinghy face waves that never stop coming. A narrator who moves between wry, ironic detachment and sober closeness to the men's perception shows how small and fragile they are, and the captain's grief and the oxymoron 'terrible grace' hint at a sea that seems hostile but is really indifferent.
blueprint.complexity: The tension in the passage comes from tone. Comic hyperbole, understatement, and mock-official diction exist alongside close-up images of fragility and a dignified portrait of mourning. Students have to explain how the humor makes the danger stronger, and they can go further by examining the gap between the men's sense of a malicious sea and the narrator's hints that it does not care about them at all.

payload.title: Poetry Analysis: Spin Cycle, Ellery Street
payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage
Spin Cycle, Ellery Street
by Marisol Teague

```passage
Eleven-forty. The change machine
eats my second five and gives back nothing,
and I let it, the way she let the landlord
keep the deposit every March.

Number nine is the only dryer that gets hot.
I learned that at seven, holding her coat
while she fed it quarters from a film can,
counting under her breath in two languages.

Her hands: chapped at the knuckle, a burn
shaped like a comma on the left thumb
from the press at Dunmore Cleaners,
a ring she turned inward so it wouldn't snag.

She folded a fitted sheet in the air
like a magician closing a box with a dove in it.
Nothing was ever lost. Nothing
was ever let go of, either.

Tomorrow the bus leaves at six.
I have packed the shirts she ironed
flat as envelopes, sealed, addressed
to a city she has never seen.

The drum turns. My clothes rise
and fall and rise, a slow tantrum
behind the round glass,
going nowhere at great speed.

I want to tell her: your hands
built me a door. I want to tell her:
I am walking out of it. Both are thank you.
Only one of them sounds like it.

The buzzer. Everything warm.
I fold the way she taught me, corners to corners,
and leave one sock in the lint trap,
so something of mine stays here, turning.
```

parts.label: A
parts.prompt:
In the poem "Spin Cycle, Ellery Street" (an original poem by Marisol Teague), the speaker waits out a wash cycle the night before leaving home and recalls the mother's hands at work.

Read the poem closely. Then write an essay in which you analyze how Marisol Teague uses poetic elements and techniques to convey the speaker's complex attitude toward leaving, in which gratitude for the mother's labor is inseparable from a wish to escape the life that labor kept going.

Your essay should:
- Respond to the prompt with a thesis that offers a defensible interpretation of the poem.
- Use specific evidence from the poem, and explain how that evidence supports your line of reasoning.
- Explain how multiple poetic elements and techniques contribute to the meaning you describe.
- Write clearly, with appropriate grammar and punctuation.
parts.model_answer:
The night before she leaves home, the speaker of Marisol Teague's "Spin Cycle, Ellery Street" sits in a laundromat doing exactly what her mother did for years, and the poem never gets past that irony. Teague uses the laundromat's circular imagery, the scarred details of the mother's hands, and line breaks that hold on and then let go to show that the speaker can only thank her mother by leaving her. Even the leaving is made out of the mother's habits. So gratitude and escape are not two separate feelings in this poem. They are one act seen from two sides.

The first stanza sets up this inheritance before the speaker admits it. When the change machine "eats my second five," she lets it, "the way she let the landlord / keep the deposit every March." The simile connects her to her mother's patience, but it is patience as giving up, and "every March" turns the loss into a yearly ritual. The memory of quarters fed from a film can, "counting under her breath in two languages," works the same way. The counting is careful and loving, the kind of labor that kept the family going, but it also shows how small and measured that life was, with every quarter tracked.

The third stanza is full of injury. The burn "shaped like a comma on the left thumb" stands out, because a comma is a pause and not a period. The mother's working life is a sentence that never gets to end. The ring "she turned inward so it wouldn't snag" suggests that even her one piece of jewelry, maybe her marriage, was turned to suit the job instead of her. Then the speaker admires her folding a sheet "like a magician closing a box with a dove in it." The image is full of wonder, but the dove is trapped. The line break that follows makes this tension happen on the page: "Nothing was ever lost. Nothing" ends the line, and the reader hangs on that second "Nothing" before the turn to "was ever let go of, either." What started as praise turns into complaint halfway through a sentence. Holding everything together and never letting anything go are the same act, and the enjambment forces us to feel both.

The shirts she ironed "flat as envelopes, sealed, addressed / to a city she has never seen" push this further. The mother's labor literally packages the speaker for departure, sending her child somewhere she herself could not go. The metaphor carries gratitude and guilt together. The dryer, meanwhile, is a "slow tantrum" with clothes "going nowhere at great speed." Calling it a tantrum gives the machine a child's frustration, which sounds like the speaker's own restlessness. The phrase also describes the mother's life, constant motion that stays in place. The repetition "rise / and fall and rise" copies the cycle the speaker is afraid of repeating.

The door metaphor is where the speaker comes closest to stating her attitude. Her repeated "I want to tell her" shows that she doesn't actually say it. Her mother's hands "built me a door," and "I am walking out of it." A reader could argue the mother is mainly confining, since she never let anything go, and the poem partly allows that reading. Sample essay (high; scored 6/6: thesis 1, evidence 4, sophistication 1)
The night before she leaves home, the speaker of Marisol Teague's "Spin Cycle, Ellery Street" sits in a laundromat doing exactly what her mother did for years, and the poem never gets past that irony. Teague uses the laundromat's circular imagery, the scarred details of the mother's hands, and line breaks that hold on and then let go to show that the speaker can only thank her mother by leaving her. Even the leaving is made out of the mother's habits. So gratitude and escape are not two separate feelings in this poem. They are one act seen from two sides.

The first stanza sets up this inheritance before the speaker admits it. When the change machine "eats my second five," she lets it, "the way she let the landlord / keep the deposit every March." The simile connects her to her mother's patience, but it is patience as giving up, and "every March" turns the loss into a yearly ritual. The memory of quarters fed from a film can, "counting under her breath in two languages," works the same way. The counting is careful and loving, the kind of labor that kept the family going, but it also shows how small and measured that life was, with every quarter tracked.

The third stanza is full of injury. The burn "shaped like a comma on the left thumb" stands out, because a comma is a pause and not a period. The mother's working life is a sentence that never gets to end. The ring "she turned inward so it wouldn't snag" suggests that even her one piece of jewelry, maybe her marriage, was turned to suit the job instead of her. Then the speaker admires her folding a sheet "like a magician closing a box with a dove in it." The image is full of wonder, but the dove is trapped. The line break that follows makes this tension happen on the page: "Nothing was ever lost. Nothing" ends the line, and the reader hangs on that second "Nothing" before the turn to "was ever let go of, either." What started as praise turns into complaint halfway through a sentence. Holding everything together and never letting anything go are the same act, and the enjambment forces us to feel both.

The shirts she ironed "flat as envelopes, sealed, addressed / to a city she has never seen" push this further. The mother's labor literally packages the speaker for departure, sending her child somewhere she herself could not go. The metaphor carries gratitude and guilt together. The dryer, meanwhile, is a "slow tantrum" with clothes "going nowhere at great speed." Calling it a tantrum gives the machine a child's frustration, which sounds like the speaker's own restlessness. The phrase also describes the mother's life, constant motion that stays in place. The repetition "rise / and fall and rise" copies the cycle the speaker is afraid of repeating.

The door metaphor is where the speaker comes closest to stating her attitude. Her repeated "I want to tell her" shows that she doesn't actually say it. Her mother's hands "built me a door," and "I am walking out of it." A reader could argue the mother is mainly confining, since she never let anything go, and the poem partly allows that reading. Leaving is the truer thanks, but it is the one her mother might not hear as thanks.

The ending refuses to settle this. The speaker folds "corners to corners," the way she was taught, so the mother's gestures go with her. Then she leaves a sock in the lint trap "so something of mine stays here, turning." This reverses "Nothing was ever lost": she deliberately lets something go, which her mother never did, but she does it so that part of her can stay. The last word, "turning," leaves her both gone and still in the cycle, which is where the poem has kept her all along.

Sample essay (mid; scored 4/6: thesis 1, evidence 3, sophistication 0)
In "Spin Cycle, Ellery Street," Marisol Teague shows a speaker who is leaving home and cannot separate being thankful to her mother from wanting to get away from the life her mother's work held up. The poem suggests that the same hard work that gave the speaker a future is also what she has to leave behind, so every thank you is also a goodbye.

The speaker's gratitude shows up first in the details about the mother's hands. They are "chapped at the knuckle" and have a burn "shaped like a comma" on the thumb. The comma is a nice image because a comma is a pause, not a stop, which could mean that the mother's work never really ends. These details make the mother's labor seem physical and real, and the speaker clearly respects it. The mother also "counting under her breath in two languages" shows how much effort she put into getting by. At the same time, the speaker remembers the landlord keeping the deposit "every March," which shows that the family was stuck in a cycle of being cheated and having little. The poem is about a laundromat, and the laundry is a good symbol of work that repeats.

The fourth stanza is where the mixed attitude is clearest. The speaker says the mother folded a sheet "like a magician closing a box with a dove in it." This is a loving comparison. Then the poem says "Nothing was ever lost. Nothing / was ever let go of, either." The line break after the second "Nothing" makes the reader stop, and the word "either" turns the praise into a complaint. Holding on to everything is a kind of care, but it is also a kind of trap, and the speaker wants to be let go. The shirts "ironed flat as envelopes" are similar. They are a gift from the mother, but they are packed and "addressed to a city she has never seen," so the mother's work is literally being sent away from her.

The dryer image of the clothes as "a slow tantrum" that is "going nowhere at great speed" shows the speaker's frustration. The tone here is more bitter and a little funny, and it seems to describe the speaker's feelings about staying in the same place as well as the laundry. Then the metaphor "your hands / built me a door" is the main idea of the poem. The door was built by the mother, but the speaker is "walking out of it." The speaker says "Both are thank you. / Only one of them sounds like it," which admits that leaving might not look like gratitude even if it is.

The ending keeps both feelings. The speaker folds "the way she taught me" and leaves one sock in the lint trap "so something of mine stays here, turning." The folding shows the mother's influence continues, and the sock turning matches the drum, so the speaker is leaving but is not fully free of the cycle. lit_frq.title: Poetry Analysis: Spin Cycle, Ellery Street

prompt.lead: In the poem "Spin Cycle, Ellery Street" (an original poem by Marisol Teague), the speaker waits out a wash cycle the night before leaving home and recalls the mother's hands at work.
prompt.task: Read the poem closely. Then write an essay in which you analyze how Marisol Teague uses poetic elements and techniques to convey the speaker's complex attitude toward leaving, in which gratitude for the mother's labor is inseparable from a wish to escape the life that labor kept going.
requirements: Respond to the prompt with a thesis that offers a defensible interpretation of the poem.
Use specific evidence from the poem, and explain how that evidence supports your line of reasoning.
Explain how multiple poetic elements and techniques contribute to the meaning you describe.
Write clearly, with appropriate grammar and punctuation.

passage.title: Spin Cycle, Ellery Street
stanzas: Eleven-forty. The change machine
eats my second five and gives back nothing,
and I let it, the way she let the landlord
keep the deposit every March.
Number nine is the only dryer that gets hot.
I learned that at seven, holding her coat
while she fed it quarters from a film can,
counting under her breath in two languages.
Her hands: chapped at the knuckle, a burn
shaped like a comma on the left thumb
from the press at Dunmore Cleaners,
a ring she turned inward so it wouldn't snag.
She folded a fitted sheet in the air
like a magician closing a box with a dove in it.
Nothing was ever lost. Nothing
was ever let go of, either.
Tomorrow the bus leaves at six.
I have packed the shirts she ironed
flat as envelopes, sealed, addressed
to a city she has never seen.
The drum turns. My clothes rise
and fall and rise, a slow tantrum
behind the round glass,
going nowhere at great speed.
I want to tell her: your hands
built me a door. I want to tell her:
I am walking out of it. Both are thank you.
Only one of them sounds like it.
The buzzer. Everything warm.
I fold the way she taught me, corners to corners,
and leave one sock in the lint trap,
so something of mine stays here, turning.

descriptors.0: No defensible thesis: the response only restates the prompt, summarizes or describes the text, makes a comment that does not answer the prompt, or never states an interpretation that needs to be defended.
descriptors.1: The response states a defensible interpretation that answers the prompt (it may take more than one sentence and may appear anywhere in the essay).

rows.name: Evidence and commentary

descriptors.0: Restates the thesis or the prompt, repeats given information, or offers irrelevant material; no usable evidence or commentary.
descriptors.1: Evidence is mostly general; the response summarizes or paraphrases and does not explain how the evidence supports an argument.
descriptors.2: Some specific, relevant evidence, mixed with generalities. Explains how some evidence relates to the argument, but no line of reasoning is established or it is faulty.
descriptors.3: Specific evidence for the claims in a line of reasoning, and explains how some of that evidence supports the line of reasoning, including how at least one literary element or technique contributes to meaning.
descriptors.4: Specific evidence supports every claim in a line of reasoning, the commentary consistently explains how the evidence supports it, and it explains how multiple literary elements or techniques contribute to meaning. Errors that interfere with communication prevent this level.

rows.task_specific: Strong responses use specific quotations such as the 'Nothing / was ever let go of' break, the 'door' metaphor, the 'slow tantrum' dryer, the envelope shirts, and the sock in the lint trap. The commentary must explain how each choice shows care that is also confinement, or departure that is also tribute. A score of 4 needs consistent links between evidence and the complex attitude across the poem. A score of 2 means the essay mostly summarizes or names devices with thin explanation.

rows.name: Sophistication

descriptors.0: Does not meet the criteria for the point: contextualizing is limited to sweeping generalities, other readings are only hinted at, complexity is oversimplified, or elaborate language does not advance the argument.
descriptors.1: Shows sophistication of thought or develops a complex literary argument, sustained through the essay (not a phrase): explores tensions or complexities in the text, situates the interpretation in a broader context, accounts for alternative interpretations, or uses a consistently vivid and persuasive style.

rows.task_specific: Sophistication may show in tracing the speaker's inheritance of the mother's gestures (counting, folding) as a kind of continuity that complicates leaving. It may also show in reading the closing image as an unresolved ending, or in analyzing how line breaks enact holding on and letting go. Calling the poem 'complex' or using elevated vocabulary does not earn the point.

scoring_notes: Award the evidence points based on how well the commentary explains the evidence, not on how many devices the essay names.
Readings that see the mother as more critical or more confining are acceptable if the text supports them.

defensible_positions: The speaker sees leaving as the fulfillment of the mother's labor, yet fears it erases her, so the poem holds thanks and guilt together.
The poem shows the mother's care as both protective and confining, and the speaker's departure as inheriting her gestures while rejecting her circumstances.
Through laundromat imagery of repetitive motion, the speaker dreads a stalled life and still cannot leave cleanly, as the final sock shows.
The speaker's restraint and small rituals reveal that love is expressed in labor rather than words, which makes saying goodbye nearly impossible.

common_pitfalls: Reading the poem as simple nostalgia or pure gratitude and ignoring the wish to escape
Listing devices without explaining how they show the divided attitude

Summarizing the stanzas in order with no argument
lines_of_reasoning: Move from the mother's work in the past to the speaker's own folding in the present
Follow motion imagery: spinning, turning, the bus, the door
Read stanza seven as the volta where the two impulses are named
