Then the metaphor "your hands / built me a door" is the main idea of the poem. The door was built by the mother, but the speaker is "walking out of it." The speaker says "Both are thank you. / Only one of them sounds like it," which admits that leaving might not look like gratitude even if it is.

The ending keeps both feelings. The speaker folds "the way she taught me" and leaves one sock in the lint trap "so something of mine stays here, turning." The folding shows the mother's influence continues, and the sock turning matches the drum, so the speaker is leaving but is not fully free of the cycle. The poem does not choose between the two feelings, which is why it feels honest.

samples.essay:
In the poem "Spin Cycle, Ellery Street" by Marisol Teague, the speaker is in a laundromat the night before leaving home. The poem talks about the mother's hands and the speaker's memories of doing laundry with her. The poet uses imagery, metaphor, and line breaks to show how the speaker feels about leaving.

In the first stanzas the speaker describes the laundromat. The change machine "eats my second five and gives back nothing" and this shows that the family did not have much money. The speaker also remembers holding her mother's coat at seven while she counted quarters. This is a memory of the mother working hard and the speaker watching her. The poet uses detail here to show the mother's life.

The third stanza is about the mother's hands. They are "chapped at the knuckle" and there is a burn from the cleaners. This imagery shows that the mother worked a lot and her hands were hurt by it. The speaker seems to respect her for this.

Later the speaker says she packed shirts that the mother ironed. They are "flat as envelopes" which is a simile. The speaker is going to a city her mother has never seen. Then the dryer is called a "slow tantrum" which shows the speaker is frustrated, like she is going nowhere.

At the end the speaker says "your hands built me a door" and that she is walking out of it. She leaves one sock in the lint trap. This shows she wants to leave but still wants something to stay. In conclusion the poet uses many techniques to show the speaker feels both thankful and wants to leave, which makes the poem about a complicated feeling.

payload.set_intro:
Public-domain source text — Anton Chekhov, The Lady with the Dog (Section I, opening), The Lady with the Dog and Other Stories, trans. Constance Garnett (1917)
The Lady with the Dog
by Anton Chekhov, translated by Constance Garnett
The following passage from a short story is by Anton Chekhov, translated by Constance Garnett (1917). This is an excerpt.

```passage
    IT was said that a new person had appeared on the
sea-front: a lady with a little dog. Dmitri Dmitritch
Gurov, who had by then been a fortnight at Yalta, and so
was fairly at home there, had begun to take an interest
in new arrivals. Sitting in Verney's pavilion, he saw,
walking on the sea-front, a fair-haired young lady of
medium height, wearing a béret; a white Pomeranian dog
was running behind her.

    And afterwards he met her in the public gardens and
in the square several times a day. She was walking
alone, always wearing the same béret, and always with
the same white dog; no one knew who she was, and every
one called her simply "the lady with the dog."

    "If she is here alone without a husband or friends,
it wouldn't be amiss to make her acquaintance," Gurov
reflected.

    He was under forty, but he had a daughter already
twelve years old, and two sons at school. He had been
married young, when he was a student in his second year,
and by now his wife seemed half as old again as he. She
was a tall, erect woman with dark eyebrows, staid and
dignified, and, as she said of herself, intellectual.
She read a great deal, used phonetic spelling, called
her husband, not Dmitri, but Dimitri, and he secretly
considered her unintelligent, narrow, inelegant, was
afraid of her, and did not like to be at home. He had
begun being unfaithful to her long ago--had been
unfaithful to her often, and, probably on that account,
almost always spoke ill of women, and when they were
talked about in his presence, used to call them "the
lower race."

    It seemed to him that he had been so schooled by
bitter experience that he might call them what he liked,
and yet he could not get on for two days together
without "the lower race." In the society of men he was
bored and not himself, with them he was cold and
uncommunicative; but when he was in the company of women
he felt free, and knew what to say to them and how to
behave; and he was at ease with them even when he was
silent. In his appearance, in his character, in his
whole nature, there was something attractive and elusive
which allured women and disposed them in his favour; he
knew that, and some force seemed to draw him, too, to
them.

    Experience often repeated, truly bitter experience,
had taught him long ago that with decent people,
especially Moscow people--always slow to move and
irresolute--every intimacy, which at first so agreeably
diversifies life and appears a light and charming
adventure, inevitably grows into a regular problem of
extreme intricacy, and in the long run the situation
becomes unbearable. But at every fresh meeting with an
interesting woman this experience seemed to slip out of
his memory, and he was eager for life, and everything
seemed simple and amusing.

    One evening he was dining in the gardens, and the
lady in the béret came up slowly to take the next table.
Her expression, her gait, her dress, and the way she did
her hair told him that she was a lady, that she was
married, that she was in Yalta for the first time and
alone, and that she was dull there.... The stories told
of the immorality in such places as Yalta are to a great
extent untrue; he despised them, and knew that such
stories were for the most part made up by persons who
would themselves have been glad to sin if they had been
able; but when the lady sat down at the next table three
paces from him, he remembered these tales of easy
conquests, of trips to the mountains, and the tempting
thought of a swift, fleeting love affair, a romance with
an unknown woman, whose name he did not know, suddenly
took possession of him.

    He beckoned coaxingly to the Pomeranian, and when
the dog came up to him he shook his finger at it. The
Pomeranian growled: Gurov shook his finger at it again.
```

parts.label: A
parts.prompt:
The following passage is from "The Lady with the Dog," a short story by Anton Chekhov (1899 in the original; English translation by Constance Garnett, 1917). In this passage, the narrator introduces Dmitri Dmitritch Gurov, a married man on holiday at Yalta, as he notices a young woman walking alone with a small white dog and begins to imagine an affair with her.

Read the passage closely. Then write an essay in which you analyze how Anton Chekhov uses literary elements and techniques to portray Gurov as a man whose claimed worldly experience and scorn for women are undercut by his dependence on them and his readiness to forget what experience has taught him.

Your essay should:
- Respond to the prompt with a thesis that offers a defensible interpretation of the passage.
- Use specific evidence from the passage, and explain how that evidence supports your line of reasoning.
- Explain how multiple literary elements and techniques contribute to the meaning you describe.
- Write clearly, with appropriate grammar and punctuation.
parts.model_answer:
Gurov thinks of himself as a man who has seen through women, but Chekhov's narrator stays just close enough to his thoughts to show that the contempt is a cover. Using a close, half-ironic narrative voice, sentences that turn on "and yet" and "but," and a final comic moment with a dog, Chekhov presents Gurov's "bitter experience" as a lesson he keeps repeating and keeps forgetting. Still, the narrator never simply sneers at him. By paying attention to his loveless marriage and his loneliness among men, Chekhov makes Gurov ridiculous and believable at once.

The irony starts with how Gurov's opinions are framed. The narrator tells us he called women "the lower race," but the explanation comes from the narrator: he was unfaithful often, and "probably on that account" spoke ill of women. That small phrase flips the cause and effect Gurov would claim. He doesn't scorn women because experience taught him to. He scorns them because he has wronged them and needs a reason. The next paragraph opens with "It seemed to him," which marks his sense of being "schooled" as his own belief, not a fact the narrator confirms. Then the sentence pivots: he could call them what he liked, "and yet he could not get on for two days together" without them. The grammar acts out the contradiction, with the boast in the first half and the dependence in the second.

Chekhov does not let the irony go cold, though. The description of Gurov's wife cuts both ways. She is "intellectual" only "as she said of herself," which mocks her pretensions, and Gurov privately judges her "unintelligent, narrow, inelegant." But the list ends with "was afraid of her, and did not like to be at home." The last item gives him away, because a man who fears his wife is not the master of women he imagines. The same goes for the line that among men he is "bored and not himself," while with women "he felt free." These details make his chasing less like conquest and more like a hunt for the only place he can be himself, so the reader pities him even while seeing through him.

The paragraph about experience repeats its lesson in the way it is built. "Experience often repeated, truly bitter experience" is insistent, almost exhausted, as if Gurov is trying to drill the lesson into himself. The long sentence that follows moves from "a light and charming adventure" to "a regular problem of extreme intricacy," and its piled-up clauses feel as tangled as the affairs it describes. Then one short "But" wipes the lesson away: the experience "seemed to slip out of his memory." Here the experience is the grammatical subject and Gurov only undergoes the forgetting: he does not choose to forget, it just happens to him, the same way "some force seemed to draw him" and the thought of an affair "suddenly took possession of him." Chekhov lets Gurov feel like the victim of his own desire, but the repeated "seemed" keeps that excuse at a distance. The Yalta gossip works the same way. Gurov despises the storytellers as people "who would themselves have been glad to sin," which describes him exactly, and a sentence later "he remembered these tales." His scorn and his temptation sit inside one sentence.

The ending shrinks this whole pattern down to a gesture. The woman has no name. She is "the lady with the dog," and Gurov reads her gait and dress as signs that she is married, alone and "dull," confident in his worldly expertise. What attracts him is a woman "whose name he did not know," in other words someone he can't really know. Then he beckons "coaxingly" to the Pomeranian, shakes his finger at it, and when "The Pomeranian growled," he does it again. Coaxing, scolding and trying again regardless is exactly how he treats women, and the growl is a warning he ignores just as he ignores his experience. It is funny, but it also suggests that Gurov, for all his claims, has learned nothing at all.

rubric_rows.criterion: A defensible thesis must make an interpretive claim about how the passage presents Gurov, and it must deal with the tension between what he says or believes (his contempt for women, his bitter experience, his scorn of Yalta gossip) and what he feels or does (needing women, forgetting his lessons, being carried away by the thought of an affair). Acceptable theses might say the narrator ironically exposes Gurov's contempt as a defense that hides his dependence, or that the passage shows a man trapped in a repeating cycle of disillusionment and renewed appetite, or that Chekhov's mix of detachment and sympathy makes Gurov both ridiculous and human. A thesis that only restates the prompt, only lists devices, only summarizes (for example, 'Gurov sees a lady and wants to meet her'), or only judges Gurov morally ('Gurov is a bad husband') without a claim about how he is portrayed does not earn the point.

Strong responses build a line of reasoning from specific textual details. Key evidence includes the reversal in 'he might call them what he liked, and yet he could not get on for two days together without "the lower race"'; the repeated 'Experience often repeated, truly bitter experience' set against 'this experience seemed to slip out of his memory'; the movement from 'a light and charming adventure' to 'a regular problem of extreme intricacy'; the ironic 'as she said of herself, intellectual' and the list of 'unintelligent, narrow, inelegant, was afraid of her'; his scorn for gossips 'who would themselves have been glad to sin' just before the same tales tempt him; the involuntary phrasing 'some force seemed to draw him' and 'suddenly took possession of him'; and the closing moment with the growling Pomeranian. Commentary has to explain how these choices show the gap between Gurov's self-image and his behavior, for example how the narrator's close, half-ironic voice ('It seemed to him') lets readers see past his own rationalizations. A score of 4 needs consistent, specific commentary that ties evidence to the thesis across the passage. A score of 3 explains several pieces of evidence well but unevenly. A score of 2 relies on summary, or names devices with little explanation. A score of 1 or 0 is mostly paraphrase or uses evidence that has nothing to do with the claim.

Sophistication can be earned by tracing the complexity in how the narrator treats Gurov, who is mocked and also understood: the irony exposes his hypocrisy while the attention to his boredom with men and his marriage makes his longing believable. It can also be earned by showing how the passage's own structure acts out the cycle it describes, with a lesson stated and then immediately forgotten. Other routes are reading the final gesture with the dog as a small comic model of his whole approach to women (coaxing, then scolding, then repeating), or noting how the lady is reduced to a label and a set of readable signs ('the lady with the dog', 'whose name he did not know') in a way that shows how Gurov sees women. The point goes to responses that develop one of these readings throughout the essay. Passing mentions or sweeping claims about Chekhov or human nature do not earn it.

In this passage from "The Lady with the Dog," Chekhov shows Gurov as a man who believes he is experienced and above women, but whose behavior proves the opposite. Through irony and a narrator who stays close to Gurov's thoughts while still pointing out his contradictions, Chekhov makes Gurov both a little ridiculous and believable, a man who says one thing and does another.

The clearest contradiction is in how Gurov talks about women. The narrator says he "almost always spoke ill of women" and called them "the lower race." This sounds like contempt, but the next paragraph undercuts it. It says "It seemed to him that he had been so schooled by bitter experience that he might call them what he liked." The phrase "It seemed to him" shows that this is only Gurov's opinion of himself, and the narrator does not agree with it. Then comes the reversal, "yet he could not get on for two days together" without them. The word "yet" turns the sentence around, so the reader sees that the name-calling is not real superiority. He actually needs women, since with men he is "bored and not himself" but with women he feels "free." So his scorn seems more like a cover for dependence.

Chekhov also uses repetition to show how Gurov forgets what he has learned. The narrator writes "Experience often repeated, truly bitter experience," which makes the lesson sound heavy and serious. The lesson is that affairs start as "a light and charming adventure" and end as "a regular problem of extreme intricacy." The contrast between "light and charming" and "extreme intricacy" shows how much trouble he knows is coming. But then "this experience seemed to slip out of his memory," and "everything seemed simple and amusing." The structure of the passage acts this out, because the lesson is stated and then forgotten right away, just as Gurov forgets it with every new woman.

The description of his wife adds to this. She is described as "as she said of herself, intellectual," which is ironic because it is her own claim, and the details that follow, like phonetic spelling, make it seem silly. Gurov thinks she is "unintelligent, narrow, inelegant" and he is "afraid of her." The list shows his dislike, but being afraid shows he is not as strong as he pretends. This helps explain why he looks for other women, and it makes the reader understand him a bit.

He first calls the gossip about Yalta untrue and says people who spread it "would themselves have been glad to sin," but then he remembers the same tales and the thought of an affair "suddenly took possession of him." The thought is the grammatical subject, acting on him, which makes it seem like he has no control. The ending, where he shakes his finger at the growling Pomeranian twice, is a small version of the whole thing, since he does it again even after the dog growls.

Overall, Chekhov uses irony, repetition, and the narrator's tone to show that Gurov's experience and scorn are not as strong as he thinks, and that his desire wins over what he knows.
- Row A: "shows Gurov as a man who believes he is experienced and above women, but whose behavior proves the opposite" - Defensible thesis that addresses the gap between Gurov's self-image and his actions, as the task requires. It is fairly general and does not yet state a distinctive claim about the narrator's attitude, but it earns the point.
- Row B: "The phrase "It seemed to him" shows that this is only Gurov's opinion of himself" - Good specific evidence with commentary on narrative voice and how it exposes his self-deception. This is one of the stronger moves in the essay.
- Row B: "The word "yet" turns the sentence around" - Identifies the key reversal and explains how it undercuts his scorn, linking a small technical choice to the argument. The explanation stays fairly brief.
- Row B: "The contrast between "light and charming" and "extreme intricacy" shows how much trouble he knows is coming." - Uses the contrast of diction accurately, but the commentary is thin and mostly restates the contrast rather than exploring its effect.
- Row C: "The structure of the passage acts this out, because the lesson is stated and then forgotten right away" - Notices that structure mirrors the cycle, which is a promising insight toward sophistication. It is a single observation and is not developed or sustained through the essay.
- Row B: "The list shows his dislike, but being afraid shows he is not as strong as he pretends." - Commentary on the wife passage is present but general. It does not fully explain the irony of 'intellectual' or tie the wife to the larger pattern beyond a short remark.
- Row C: "is a small version of the whole thing, since he does it again even after the dog growls" - Reads the dog scene as a model of his behavior, a good idea, but the commentary is brief and ends the essay without developing the reading. The conclusion mostly repeats the thesis, so it does not reach sustained sophistication.

lit_frq.title: Prose Fiction Analysis: The Lady with the Dog

prompt.lead: The following passage is from "The Lady with the Dog," a short story by Anton Chekhov (1899 in the original; English translation by Constance Garnett, 1917). In this passage, the narrator introduces Dmitri Dmitritch Gurov, a married man on holiday at Yalta, as he notices a young woman walking alone with a small white dog and begins to imagine an affair with her.
prompt.task: Read the passage closely. Then write an essay in which you analyze how Anton Chekhov uses literary elements and techniques to portray Gurov as a man whose claimed worldly experience and scorn for women are undercut by his dependence on them and his readiness to forget what experience has taught him.
requirements: Respond to the prompt with a thesis that offers a defensible interpretation of the passage.
Use specific evidence from the passage, and explain how that evidence supports your line of reasoning.
Explain how multiple literary elements and techniques contribute to the meaning you describe.
Write clearly, with appropriate grammar and punctuation.

passage.title: The Lady with the Dog
passage.attribution: by Anton Chekhov, translated by Constance Garnett
passage.headnote: The following passage from a short story is by Anton Chekhov, translated by Constance Garnett (1917). This is an excerpt.
stanzas: IT was said that a new person had appeared on the
sea-front: a lady with a little dog. Dmitri Dmitritch
Gurov, who had by then been a fortnight at Yalta, and so
was fairly at home there, had begun to take an interest
in new arrivals. Sitting in Verney's pavilion, he saw,
walking on the sea-front, a fair-haired young lady of
medium height, wearing a béret; a white Pomeranian dog
was running behind her.
And afterwards he met her in the public gardens and
in the square several times a day. She was walking
alone, always wearing the same béret, and always with
the same white dog; no one knew who she was, and every
one called her simply "the lady with the dog."
"If she is here alone without a husband or friends,
it wouldn't be amiss to make her acquaintance," Gurov
reflected.
He was under forty, but he had a daughter already
twelve years old, and two sons at school. He had been
married young, when he was a student in his second year,
and by now his wife seemed half as old again as he. She
was a tall, erect woman with dark eyebrows, staid and
dignified, and, as she said of herself, intellectual.
She read a great deal, used phonetic spelling, called
her husband, not Dmitri, but Dimitri, and he secretly
considered her unintelligent, narrow, inelegant, was
afraid of her, and did not like to be at home. He had
begun being unfaithful to her long ago--had been
unfaithful to her often, and, probably on that account,
almost always spoke ill of women, and when they were
talked about in his presence, used to call them "the
lower race."
It seemed to him that he had been so schooled by
bitter experience that he might call them what he liked,
and yet he could not get on for two days together
without "the lower race." In the society of men he was
bored and not himself, with them he was cold and
uncommunicative; but when he was in the company of women
he felt free, and knew what to say to them and how to
behave; and he was at ease with them even when he was
silent. In his appearance, in his character, in his
whole nature, there was something attractive and elusive
which allured women and disposed them in his favour; he
knew that, and some force seemed to draw him, too, to
them.
Experience often repeated, truly bitter experience,
had taught him long ago that with decent people,
especially Moscow people--always slow to move and
irresolute--every intimacy, which at first so agreeably
diversifies life and appears a light and charming
adventure, inevitably grows into a regular problem of
extreme intricacy, and in the long run the situation
becomes unbearable. But at every fresh meeting with an
interesting woman this experience seemed to slip out of
his memory, and he was eager for life, and everything
seemed simple and amusing.
One evening he was dining in the gardens, and the
lady in the béret came up slowly to take the next table.
Her expression, her gait, her dress, and the way she did
her hair told him that she was a lady, that she was
married, that she was in Yalta for the first time and
alone, and that she was dull there.... The stories told
of the immorality in such places as Yalta are to a great
extent untrue; he despised them, and knew that such
stories were for the most part made up by persons who
would themselves have been glad to sin if they had been
able; but when the lady sat down at the next table three
paces from him, he remembered these tales of easy
conquests, of trips to the mountains, and the tempting
thought of a swift, fleeting love affair, a romance with
an unknown woman, whose name he did not know, suddenly
took possession of him.
He beckoned coaxingly to the Pomeranian, and when
the dog came up to him he shook his finger at it. The
Pomeranian growled: Gurov shook his finger at it again.

rows.name: Thesis

descriptors.0: No defensible thesis: the response only restates the prompt, summarizes or describes the text, makes a comment that does not answer the prompt, or never states an interpretation that needs to be defended.
descriptors.1: The response states a defensible interpretation that answers the prompt (it may take more than one sentence and may appear anywhere in the essay).

rows.task_specific: A defensible thesis must make an interpretive claim about how the passage presents Gurov, and it must deal with the tension between what he says or believes (his contempt for women, his bitter experience, his scorn of Yalta gossip) and what he feels or does (needing women, forgetting his lessons, being carried away by the thought of an affair). Acceptable theses might say the narrator ironically exposes Gurov's contempt as a defense that hides his dependence, or that the passage shows a man trapped in a repeating cycle of disillusionment and renewed appetite, or that Chekhov's mix of detachment and sympathy makes Gurov both ridiculous and human. A thesis that only restates the prompt, only lists devices, only summarizes (for example, 'Gurov sees a lady and wants to meet her'), or only judges Gurov morally ('Gurov is a bad husband') without a claim about how he is portrayed does not earn the point.

rows.name: Evidence and commentary

descriptors.0: Restates the thesis or the prompt, repeats given information, or offers irrelevant material; no usable evidence or commentary.
descriptors.1: Evidence is mostly general; the response summarizes or paraphrases and does not explain how the evidence supports an argument.
descriptors.2: Some specific, relevant evidence, mixed with generalities. Explains how some evidence relates to the argument, but no line of reasoning is established or it is faulty.
descriptors.3: Specific evidence for the claims in a line of reasoning, and explains how some of that evidence supports the line of reasoning, including how at least one literary element or technique contributes to meaning.
descriptors.4: Specific evidence supports every claim in a line of reasoning, the commentary consistently explains how the evidence supports it, and it explains how multiple literary elements or techniques contribute to meaning. Errors that interfere with communication prevent this level.

rows.task_specific: Strong responses build a line of reasoning from specific textual details. Key evidence includes the reversal in 'he might call them what he liked, and yet he could not get on for two days together without "the lower race"'; the repeated 'Experience often repeated, truly bitter experience' set against 'this experience seemed to slip out of his memory'; the movement from 'a light and charming adventure' to 'a regular problem of extreme intricacy'; the ironic 'as she said of herself, intellectual' and the list of 'unintelligent, narrow, inelegant, was afraid of her'; his scorn for gossips 'who would themselves have been glad to sin' just before the same tales tempt him; the involuntary phrasing 'some force seemed to draw him' and 'suddenly took possession of him'; and the closing moment with the growling Pomeranian. Commentary has to explain how these choices show the gap between Gurov's self-image and his behavior, for example how the narrator's close, half-ironic voice ('It seemed to him') lets readers see past his own rationalizations. A score of 4 needs consistent, specific commentary that ties evidence to the thesis across the passage. A score of 3 explains several pieces of evidence well but unevenly. A score of 2 relies on summary, or names devices with little explanation. A score of 1 or 0 is mostly paraphrase or uses evidence that has nothing to do with the claim.

rows.name: Sophistication

descriptors.0: Does not meet the criteria for the point: contextualizing is limited to sweeping generalities, other readings are only hinted at, complexity is oversimplified, or elaborate language does not advance the argument.
descriptors.1: Shows sophistication of thought or develops a complex literary argument, sustained through the essay (not a phrase): explores tensions or complexities in the text, situates the interpretation in a broader context, accounts for alternative interpretations, or uses a consistently vivid and persuasive style.

rows.task_specific: Sophistication can be earned by tracing the complexity in how the narrator treats Gurov, who is mocked and also understood: the irony exposes his hypocrisy while the attention to his boredom with men and his marriage makes his longing believable. It can also be earned by showing how the passage's own structure acts out the cycle it describes, with a lesson stated and then immediately forgotten. Other routes are reading the final gesture with the dog as a small comic model of his whole approach to women (coaxing, then scolding, then repeating), or noting how the lady is reduced to a label and a set of readable signs ('the lady with the dog', 'whose name he did not know') in a way that shows how Gurov sees women. The point goes to responses that develop one of these readings throughout the essay. Passing mentions or sweeping claims about Chekhov or human nature do not earn it.

scoring_notes: Do not require or reward knowledge of later events in the story; responses must be grounded in this passage.
Moral condemnation of Gurov is acceptable only when it is tied to analysis of how the text presents him; disapproval alone is not analysis.
Do not credit readings that assume the narrator agrees with calling women 'the lower race' unless the response deals with the irony around that phrase.
Device identification without explanation of effect should not move a response above 2 in Row B.
Accept a range of interpretations of the dog ending (comic, symbolic, foreshadowing a pattern) as long as they are supported.

defensible_positions: The narrator's irony exposes Gurov's contempt for women as hypocritical and self-protective: he calls them 'the lower race' yet cannot do without them and feels like himself only in their company.
The passage presents Gurov as caught in a repeating cycle in which hard-won experience is forgotten at every new encounter, so his worldliness looks less like wisdom and more like self-deception.
Gurov is shown as oddly passive in his own desires, drawn by 'some force' and taken over by a 'tempting thought', which makes him both less responsible and less in control than he thinks.

Chekhov balances judgment with sympathy: the unhappy marriage, the fear of his wife, and his boredom with men make Gurov's restlessness understandable even while the narrator mocks his rationalizations.

Gurov's habit of reading women as types (decoding the lady's dress and gait, choosing her because she is nameless and unknown) shows how he turns women into objects of his own story, a habit the growling dog comically pushes back against.

devices.quote: he might call them what he liked, and yet he could not get on for two days together without "the lower race."
devices.effect: The turn on 'and yet' undercuts his contempt right away and shows that his scorn hides his dependence on women.

devices.quote: Experience often repeated, truly bitter experience
devices.effect: Repeating 'experience' stresses how heavily Gurov relies on his supposed wisdom, which makes its quick disappearance a few lines later more pointed.

devices.quote: this experience seemed to slip out of his memory, and he was eager for life, and everything seemed simple and amusing.
devices.effect: Putting his firm lesson next to its immediate forgetting shows the cycle of disillusionment and renewed appetite that rules him.

devices.quote: a light and charming adventure, inevitably grows into a regular problem of extreme intricacy
devices.effect: The shift from airy, pleasant words to heavy, bureaucratic ones traces how each affair goes sour, in Gurov's own weary terms.

devices.quote: as she said of herself, intellectual
devices.effect: Using the wife's own label lets the narrator mock her pretensions while also hinting at how one-sided Gurov's view of her is.

devices.quote: secretly considered her unintelligent, narrow, inelegant, was afraid of her, and did not like to be at home
devices.effect: The list of private insults ends in fear and avoidance, showing the weakness behind his contempt.

devices.quote: persons who would themselves have been glad to sin if they had been able
devices.effect: Gurov looks down on the gossips as hypocrites just before the same gossip tempts him, so the judgment turns back on him.

devices.quote: suddenly took possession of him
devices.effect: Treating the thought as something that takes hold of him presents Gurov as passive before his desires and avoiding responsibility.

devices.quote: Her expression, her gait, her dress, and the way she did her hair told him
devices.effect: The cataloguing sentence shows Gurov reading a woman as a set of signs, which reveals his practiced, objectifying eye.

devices.quote: always wearing the same béret, and always with the same white dog
devices.effect: Repeated 'always' and 'same' turn the lady into a fixed, anonymous figure, which fits the label 'the lady with the dog' and her appeal to him as an unknown.

devices.quote: The Pomeranian growled: Gurov shook his finger at it again.
devices.effect: The coax, scold, and repeat pattern with the dog is a small comic model of his approach to women, and the dog's resistance punctures his confidence.

devices.quote: It seemed to him that he had been so schooled by bitter experience
devices.effect: Staying close to Gurov's view while marking it with 'It seemed to him' lets the narrator present his self-justification and quietly put it in doubt.

common_pitfalls: Summarizing Gurov's background and his first sight of the lady without analyzing how the narration shapes our view of him.
Treating the 'lower race' remark as the narrator's view instead of recognizing the irony around it.
Moralizing about adultery instead of analyzing how the text presents Gurov's contradictions.
Bringing in events from later in the story that the passage does not support.
Ignoring the dog ending or treating it only as a cute detail.
Listing devices such as repetition or diction without explaining how they show the gap between Gurov's beliefs and his behavior.

samples.essay:
Gurov thinks of himself as a man who has seen through women, but Chekhov's narrator stays just close enough to his thoughts to show that the contempt is a cover. Using a close, half-ironic narrative voice, sentences that turn on "and yet" and "but," and a final comic moment with a dog, Chekhov presents Gurov's "bitter experience" as a lesson he keeps repeating and keeps forgetting. Still, the narrator never simply sneers at him. By paying attention to his loveless marriage and his loneliness among men, Chekhov makes Gurov ridiculous and believable at once.

The irony starts with how Gurov's opinions are framed. The narrator tells us he called women "the lower race," but the explanation comes from the narrator: he was unfaithful often, and "probably on that account" spoke ill of women. That small phrase flips the cause and effect Gurov would claim. He doesn't scorn women because experience taught him to. He scorns them because he has wronged them and needs a reason. The next paragraph opens with "It seemed to him," which marks his sense of being "schooled" as his own belief, not a fact the narrator confirms. Then the sentence pivots: he could call them what he liked, "and yet he could not get on for two days together" without them. The grammar acts out the contradiction, with the boast in the first half and the dependence in the second.

Chekhov does not let the irony go cold, though. The description of Gurov's wife cuts both ways. She is "intellectual" only "as she said of herself," which mocks her pretensions, and Gurov privately judges her "unintelligent, narrow, inelegant." But the list ends with "was afraid of her, and did not like to be at home." The last item gives him away, because a man who fears his wife is not the master of women he imagines. The same goes for the line that among men he is "bored and not himself," while with women "he felt free." These details make his chasing less like conquest and more like a hunt for the only place he can be himself, so the reader pities him even while seeing through him.

The paragraph about experience repeats its lesson in the way it is built. "Experience often repeated, truly bitter experience" is insistent, almost exhausted, as if Gurov is trying to drill the lesson into himself. The long sentence that follows moves from "a light and charming adventure" to "a regular problem of extreme intricacy," and its piled-up clauses feel as tangled as the affairs it describes. Then one short "But" wipes the lesson away: the experience "seemed to slip out of his memory." Here the experience is the grammatical subject and Gurov only undergoes the forgetting: he does not choose to forget, it just happens to him, the same way "some force seemed to draw him" and the thought of an affair "suddenly took possession of him." Chekhov lets Gurov feel like the victim of his own desire, but the repeated "seemed" keeps that excuse at a distance. The Yalta gossip works the same way. Gurov despises the storytellers as people "who would themselves have been glad to sin," which describes him exactly, and a sentence later "he remembered these tales." His scorn and his temptation sit inside one sentence.

The ending shrinks this whole pattern down to a gesture. The woman has no name. She is "the lady with the dog," and Gurov reads her gait and dress as signs that she is married, alone and "dull," confident in his worldly expertise. What attracts him is a woman "whose name he did not know," in other words someone he can't really know. Then he beckons "coaxingly" to the Pomeranian, shakes his finger at it, and when "The Pomeranian growled," he does it again. Coaxing, scolding and trying again regardless is exactly how he treats women, and the growl is a warning he ignores just as he ignores his experience. It is funny, but it also suggests that Gurov, for all his claims, has learned nothing at all.

samples.essay:
In this passage from "The Lady with the Dog," Chekhov shows Gurov as a man who believes he is experienced and above women, but whose behavior proves the opposite. Through irony and a narrator who stays close to Gurov's thoughts while still pointing out his contradictions, Chekhov makes Gurov both a little ridiculous and believable, a man who says one thing and does another.

The clearest contradiction is in how Gurov talks about women. The narrator says he "almost always spoke ill of women" and called them "the lower race." This sounds like contempt, but the next paragraph undercuts it. It says "It seemed to him that he had been so schooled by bitter experience that he might call them what he liked." The phrase "It seemed to him" shows that this is only Gurov's opinion of himself, and the narrator does not agree with it. Then comes the reversal, "yet he could not get on for two days together" without them. The word "yet" turns the sentence around, so the reader sees that the name-calling is not real superiority. He actually needs women, since with men he is "bored and not himself" but with women he feels "free." So his scorn seems more like a cover for dependence.

Chekhov also uses repetition to show how Gurov forgets what he has learned. The narrator writes "Experience often repeated, truly bitter experience," which makes the lesson sound heavy and serious. The lesson is that affairs start as "a light and charming adventure" and end as "a regular problem of extreme intricacy." The contrast between "light and charming" and "extreme intricacy" shows how much trouble he knows is coming. But then "this experience seemed to slip out of his memory," and "everything seemed simple and amusing." The structure of the passage acts this out, because the lesson is stated and then forgotten right away, just as Gurov forgets it with every new woman.

The description of his wife adds to this. She is described as "as she said of herself, intellectual," which is ironic because it is her own claim, and the details that follow, like phonetic spelling, make it seem silly. Gurov thinks she is "unintelligent, narrow, inelegant" and he is "afraid of her." The list shows his dislike, but being afraid shows he is not as strong as he pretends. This helps explain why he looks for other women, and it makes the reader understand him a bit.

Finally, the passage ends with Gurov teasing the dog. He first calls the gossip about Yalta untrue and says people who spread it "would themselves have been glad to sin," but then he remembers the same tales and the thought of an affair "suddenly took possession of him." The thought is the grammatical subject, acting on him, which makes it seem like he has no control. The ending, where he shakes his finger at the growling Pomeranian twice, is a small version of the whole thing, since he does it again even after the dog growls.

Overall, Chekhov uses irony, repetition, and the narrator's tone to show that Gurov's experience and scorn are not as strong as he thinks, and that his desire wins over what he knows.

First, Chekhov tells us about Gurov's family. He has a daughter who is twelve and two sons at school. He married young and his wife seems older than him. She is described as "staid and dignified" and she says she is intellectual. Gurov does not like her and he does not like to be at home. This is why he has been unfaithful to her many times. The narrator also says he calls women "the lower race" which is a bad thing to say about women.

Next, the passage says that Gurov has had "bitter experience" with women. He thinks that affairs always become a problem in the end. But when he meets a new woman he forgets all of this and thinks everything is simple and amusing. So he does not really learn from what happened before. The narrator says it "seemed to slip out of his memory" which shows that he forgets.

Then the lady comes to sit at the next table at dinner. Gurov thinks about the stories of Yalta and gets tempted. At the end he calls the dog over and shakes his finger at it and the dog growls. This is a small moment but it shows he is trying to get close to the lady.

In conclusion, Chekhov uses details about Gurov's marriage and his thoughts to show that he says one thing about women but does another. He is a man who is unfaithful and forgets his lessons, which makes him seem like a bad person.

annotations.quote: Chekhov shows Gurov as a man who has a lot of experience with women and who is also married.
annotations.comment: The thesis only restates the situation and the prompt's wording. It makes no claim about how Gurov is portrayed or about the tension between what he says and what he does, so it earns no thesis credit.

annotations.quote: This shows that Gurov is not a very good husband and that he does not respect women.
annotations.comment: This is a moral judgment of Gurov, not an interpretive claim about technique or about the gap between his self-image and his behavior. The task-specific guidance says this does not meet the thesis standard.

annotations.quote: She is described as "staid and dignified" and she says she is intellectual.
annotations.comment: The detail is specific and relevant, but the essay never notices the irony in 'as she said of herself'. It also skips Gurov's list of insults against her. The material is paraphrased and the paragraph ends without a point about Gurov.

annotations.quote: The narrator says it "seemed to slip out of his memory" which shows that he forgets.
annotations.comment: This is the best moment, because it quotes the key phrase and ties it to forgetting. The comment only repeats the quotation. It does not explain the repeated 'bitter experience' set against the forgetting, or how the narrator's voice exposes Gurov.

annotations.quote: This is a small moment but it shows he is trying to get close to the lady.
annotations.comment: The dog scene is summarized and its meaning is read too literally. The essay does not see the coaxing and scolding as a comic image of Gurov's whole approach to women. It also leaves out the earlier scorn for gossips, who are the very people he resembles when he is tempted.

annotations.quote: which makes him seem like a bad person.
annotations.comment: The conclusion ends on a flat moral verdict. It does not see that the narrator both mocks Gurov and understands him, through his boredom with men and his unhappy marriage. No complexity or alternative reading is developed, so no sophistication.

blueprint.central_idea: The opening of the story presents Gurov through a close, quietly ironic narration that sets his self-image as an experienced man who scorns women against his dependence on them, his fear of his wife, and his habit of forgetting every lesson when a new woman appears.
blueprint.complexity: The passage is neither a simple condemnation nor a simple endorsement. The narrator mocks Gurov's rationalizations and his hypocrisy toward the gossips, yet gives him an unhappy marriage, a believable loneliness, and a passivity before his desires that makes him human. The structure acts out the cycle it describes, and the comic gesture with the dog both sums up and deflates his practiced charm.

payload.title: The House That Holds

parts.label: A
parts.prompt:
In many works of literature, a home is more than a setting. It can be a farmhouse that keeps a family alive through a hard winter, a crowded apartment where a grandmother's rules decide who may marry whom, or a ship's cabin, a convent cell, or a borrowed room that a refugee is told to be grateful for. The same walls that keep out danger can also keep a person in, and the comfort of belonging can carry obligations, silences, and limits. Writers often use such places to test what characters owe the people and structures that shelter them, and what it costs either to stay or to leave.

Either from your own reading or from the list below, choose a work of fiction in which a home, or a place that functions as one, both protects a character and confines that character. Then, in a well-written essay, analyze how the home and its double nature contributes to an interpretation of the work as a whole. Do not merely summarize the plot.

Your essay should:
- State a defensible thesis about how the idea in the prompt contributes to an interpretation of the work as a whole.
- Support the argument with specific, accurate evidence from the work you chose, and explain how that evidence supports your line of reasoning.
- Do not merely summarize the plot.
- Write clearly, with appropriate grammar and punctuation.

parts.model_answer:
In Henrik Ibsen's A Doll's House, the Helmer apartment seems like the safest place a woman in nineteenth-century Norway could hope to live. It is warm and decorated for Christmas, and Torvald's new job at the bank will pay for it. Ibsen builds the play so that every comfort the house gives Nora is also a rule she has to follow, though. The home protects her only while she agrees to be the person it was designed for, and the play suggests that a shelter built on one person's performance is really a stage. That is why Nora's exit at the end is both freedom and a real loss: the walls that kept her in were also the only self she had ever been allowed to have.

The first scene sets up this double meaning with small objects. Nora comes in with packages and a Christmas tree that she tells the maid to hide until it is decorated, and she secretly eats macaroons that Torvald has forbidden. The tree is a lot like Nora. It is something beautiful that gets arranged for display, and Torvald treats her the same way when he calls her by pet names for little birds and squirrels and hands her money as if it were an allowance. Even the macaroons matter. In this house even a cookie has to be hidden, so Nora has to lie to enjoy a harmless pleasure. Still, Ibsen does not pretend the protection is fake. When Mrs. Linde arrives, widowed, worn out, and desperate for work, she shows the audience what waits outside a husband's house for a woman with no money. Next to her, Nora's cage looks like luck, and I think that is the point. The comfort is real, which is exactly what makes it hard to leave.

The secret loan turns the house's logic upside down. Years earlier Nora borrowed money from Krogstad to pay for the trip to Italy that saved Torvald's life, so it turns out the home was being protected by her, not by him. But since a wife could not legally borrow without a man's consent, she forged her father's signature. The same social structure that is supposed to shelter women makes their own acts of protection criminal. Ibsen shows this through the locked letterbox. Krogstad drops his letter exposing the forgery into it, and only Torvald has the key, so a piece of the home meant for privacy becomes the trap closing on Nora. Her wild tarantella, danced to keep Torvald away from the mail, shows how little power she has. Performing is the one tool the house ever taught her to use.

The ending is where the two sides of the home separate. Torvald explodes at Nora, and then, once Krogstad sends back the bond, he forgives her and promises to shelter her like something he has rescued. His forgiveness is what shows Nora she has been a doll first in her father's house and then in her husband's, which makes the title refer to the whole institution rather than one marriage. Ibsen does not make her leaving easy, though. She walks out at night and leaves her children behind, and the nurse, Anne-Marie, who had to give away her own child to survive, reminds us that women in this world pay for every choice. Early audiences thought this was so shocking that Ibsen was pushed into writing a different ending for a German production in which Nora stays for the children. That reaction actually backs up the play's argument, because it shows how strongly people believed a home's protection should outweigh a woman's selfhood. The door slamming at the end is so powerful because it sounds like escape and like loss at once. Nora is free, but she has no shelter yet, and Ibsen leaves us unsure whether the world outside will be any kinder than the dollhouse.

rubric_rows.criterion: A defensible thesis names a work and makes a claim about how the home's double nature, both protective and confining, contributes to a meaning of the whole work, for example that the work shows belonging cannot be separated from constraint. Summarizing that a character lives in a house, or just saying the home is both safe and limiting with no interpretation of the work, does not count. A thesis that deals with only one side of the home can earn the point only if it is still defensible and connected to meaning. The thesis may appear anywhere in the response.

Strong responses pick specific moments that show both the sheltering and the restricting functions of the home, such as a scene of rescue or comfort set against a scene of refusal, rule, or failed escape. Commentary must explain how these moments, and choices like setting details, symbols, characterization, or structure, build the interpretation, not just retell events. A score of 4 calls for consistent explanation of how the evidence supports a line of reasoning about the double nature. A score of 2 fits responses that are mostly summary with general claims. A score of 1 fits responses that have little relevant evidence or only repeat the plot.

Sophistication may come from exploring tensions, for example that the protective and confining sides are the same feature seen differently, or that leaving is both freedom and loss. It may also come from placing the work in a wider context, such as gender roles, migration, or class, or from a consistently vivid and persuasive style. A passing mention of complexity or of other works does not earn the point. The sophistication has to run through the argument as a whole.

- Row A: "The home protects her only while she agrees to be the person it was designed for, and the play suggests that a shelter built on one person's performance is really a stage." - This is a defensible thesis that covers both sides of the home and makes an interpretive claim about the whole play. It is more than just saying the house is safe and limiting.
- Row A: "the walls that kept her in were also the only self she had ever been allowed to have" - This adds a cost to the thesis. Leaving means both freedom and loss, and that sets up the essay's line of reasoning.
- Row B: "The tree is a lot like Nora." - This is specific, accurate evidence (the tree, the pet names, the allowance) with commentary that reads a symbol and a characterization choice as signs of confinement.
- Row B: "Next to her, Nora's cage looks like luck" - Using Mrs. Linde as a foil gives evidence for the protective side, so the argument shows both functions of the home. Writing about character contrast is one more literary element.
- Row B: "a piece of the home meant for privacy becomes the trap closing on Nora" - The essay reads the letterbox as a setting detail and a symbol and explains how it supports the claim. Commentary like this runs through every body paragraph, which fits a score of 4.
- Row B: "which makes the title refer to the whole institution rather than one marriage" - This links structure and the title to the whole-work interpretation. The essay draws on several techniques (symbol, foil, setting, the final staging), not just one.
- Row C: "The same social structure that is supposed to shelter women makes their own acts of protection criminal." - This puts the argument in the context of nineteenth-century gender law and treats protection and confinement as the same structure seen from two sides.
- Row C: "That reaction actually backs up the play's argument" - The essay brings in another way of seeing the ending, through the audience reaction and the alternate German ending, and folds it into the argument. Along with the Anne-Marie point and the escape/loss tension, the complexity is carried through the essay rather than stated once.

Sample essay (mid; scored 4/6: thesis 1, evidence 3, sophistication 0)
In Henrik Ibsen's A Doll's House, the Helmer home is a place that looks like safety but works like a cage. Ibsen uses the house to show that the comfort Nora gets from her marriage is bought with her freedom, so that the protection she receives is really a form of control. By the end, her leaving shows that a home built on someone's dependence cannot actually belong to her.

At the start of the play the home seems warm and protective. It is Christmas, Nora comes in with packages, and Torvald talks to her from his study like a pleased parent. He calls her pet names such as "little lark" and "squirrel," and these seem affectionate. The household has money coming in because Torvald is about to become a bank manager, so it appears to shelter Nora from the worries of the outside world. However, the nicknames also treat her like an animal or a child and not like an equal. The comfort of the home depends on Nora staying small and sweet, and this is the first sign that protection and confinement are the same thing. The stage setting of one living room, where almost the whole play takes place, also makes the home feel closed in.

The confinement becomes clearer once Nora's secret is brought in. Years before, she borrowed money by forging her father's signature to save Torvald's life, and she has hidden it in order to keep the peace of the house. She has to sneak macaroons and hide things from him, which shows that the home has rules she cannot openly break. The tarantella scene is another good example. Torvald makes her practice the dance and controls how she performs it, so even her body is directed by him. The house is a stage where Nora performs the role of the happy wife, and the title's image of a doll fits because a doll is kept safe only as long as it does what its owner wants.

The turning point is when Torvald reads Krogstad's letter and reacts by caring only about his reputation, not about what Nora did for him. He calls her names and says she is not fit to raise the children, but when the danger passes he wants to go back to normal. This shows that the protection he offered was always conditional. When Nora decides to leave, the slamming door at the end ends the play and is a symbol for her choice. Her departure is not simply freedom, because she leaves her children and the only security she has known, so it costs her a great deal.

Overall, Ibsen suggests that a home which protects only by keeping someone dependent is not really a home. Nora has to give up shelter to become a person, and the play asks the audience to consider what the comfort of belonging is worth.
- Row A: "the Helmer home is a place that looks like safety but works like a cage" - Defensible claim naming the work and the double nature of the home, and it moves toward an interpretation (protection as control). It is somewhat general, and the idea that the home is not truly hers is only loosely developed, but it earns the thesis point.
- Row B: "He calls her pet names such as "little lark" and "squirrel," and these seem affectionate." - Specific, accurate detail that shows the sheltering tone and the diminishing effect at once. The commentary explains how the nicknames connect to the argument, which is a strength, though the analysis of language stays brief.
- Row B: "The stage setting of one living room, where almost the whole play takes place, also makes the home feel closed in." - Mentions setting as a technique, but the point is stated rather than explored. It gets some credit for a literary element, though thinly handled.
- Row B: "The house is a stage where Nora performs the role of the happy wife" - Uses the tarantella and the doll image to explain confinement. Commentary is present but repetitive of the earlier point about control, and the evidence of the sheltering side is not revisited in this section.
- Row B: "This shows that the protection he offered was always conditional." - Good move connecting the letter scene to the claim that protection was conditional. The evidence is accurate but compressed, and the reasoning is stated more than demonstrated.
- Row C: "Her departure is not simply freedom, because she leaves her children and the only security she has known, so it costs her a great deal." - Acknowledges that leaving is both freedom and loss, which hints at complexity. It is a single sentence and not sustained across the essay, so it does not earn the sophistication point.
- Row C: "Nora has to give up shelter to become a person, and the play asks the audience to consider what the comfort of belonging is worth." - The conclusion gestures at a broader meaning but stays general. There is no wider context (such as marriage laws or gender roles of the period) to push this into sustained sophistication.

Sample essay (low; scored 3/6: thesis 1, evidence 2, sophistication 0)
In A Doll's House by Henrik Ibsen the home is a place that is both safe and limiting for Nora. The Helmer house protects her but it also traps her, and this shows the double nature of home in the play.

At the start of the play Nora is happy and she is shopping for Christmas. Her husband Torvald calls her pet names like little squirrel and lark. The house is warm and comfortable and she has everything she needs, so it protects her from the outside world. She has a nursery and children and a maid. Torvald has a good job at the bank now so they dont have to worry about money.

But the house also confines her. Torvald tells her what to do and he doesnt let her eat macaroons. Nora has to hide things from him. She also has a secret that she borrowed money from Krogstad by forging a signature to save Torvalds life. She has to keep this secret inside the house which makes it feel like a cage. Then she dances the tarantella and Torvald is controlling her again.

In the end Torvald finds out about the loan and he gets very angry and calls her names. He only cares about his reputation. Nora realizes that she has been treated like a doll first by her father and then by her husband. She decides to leave and she slams the door. This shows that the home was never really protecting her it was confining her the whole time.

In conclusion the home in A Doll's House is both protective and confining. Ibsen uses the house to show that Nora had to leave to find herself, and the ending is important because of that.
- Row A: "The Helmer house protects her but it also traps her, and this shows the double nature of home in the play." - The introduction mostly restates the prompt's protect/confine idea. The thesis point is earned only because the essay does state a defensible interpretation later (the home confined Nora the whole time, and Ibsen shows she had to leave to find herself); the rubric allows the thesis anywhere in the essay. It stays a basic claim.
- Row B: "The house is warm and comfortable and she has everything she needs, so it protects her from the outside world." - This is a general statement about comfort. It names no specific scene or setting detail and does not explain how the details build an interpretation, so it earns little evidence credit.
- Row B: "Torvald tells her what to do and he doesnt let her eat macaroons." - The macaroon detail is accurate and relevant, but it is only mentioned. The essay never explains what it shows about control or how Ibsen uses it, so this is summary rather than commentary.
- Row B: "Then she dances the tarantella and Torvald is controlling her again." - The tarantella is a real and useful moment, but the claim is vague and unexplained. The essay does not say how the scene shows confinement or tie it to a line of reasoning.
- Row C: "This shows that the home was never really protecting her it was confining her the whole time." - This is the closest the essay comes to an interpretation. It oversimplifies by dropping the protective side it set up earlier, and it does not explore the tension between the two. No sophistication is shown.
- Row C: "Ibsen uses the house to show that Nora had to leave to find herself, and the ending is important because of that." - The conclusion repeats earlier points and makes a generic claim. It names no technique and offers no wider context such as gender roles or marriage in the period, so it does not reach sophistication.

rows.name: Thesis

descriptors.0: No defensible thesis: the response only restates the prompt, summarizes or describes the text, makes a comment that does not answer the prompt, or never states an interpretation that needs to be defended.
descriptors.1: The response states a defensible interpretation that answers the prompt (it may take more than one sentence and may appear anywhere in the essay).

rows.task_specific: A defensible thesis names a work and makes a claim about how the home's double nature, both protective and confining, contributes to a meaning of the whole work, for example that the work shows belonging cannot be separated from constraint. rows.name: Evidence and commentary

descriptors.0: Restates the thesis or the prompt, repeats given information, or offers irrelevant material; no usable evidence or commentary.
descriptors.1: Evidence is mostly general; the response summarizes or paraphrases and does not explain how the evidence supports an argument.
descriptors.2: Some specific, relevant evidence, mixed with generalities. Explains how some evidence relates to the argument, but no line of reasoning is established or it is faulty.
descriptors.3: Specific evidence for the claims in a line of reasoning, and explains how some of that evidence supports the line of reasoning, including how at least one literary element or technique contributes to meaning.
descriptors.4: Specific evidence supports every claim in a line of reasoning, the commentary consistently explains how the evidence supports it, and it explains how multiple literary elements or techniques contribute to meaning. Errors that interfere with communication prevent this level.

descriptors.0: Does not meet the criteria for the point: contextualizing is limited to sweeping generalities, other readings are only hinted at, complexity is oversimplified, or elaborate language does not advance the argument.
descriptors.1: Shows sophistication of thought or develops a complex literary argument, sustained through the essay (not a phrase): explores tensions or complexities in the text, situates the interpretation in a broader context, accounts for alternative interpretations, or uses a consistently vivid and persuasive style.
